If that [being] were different from that [state], then one must say that the denizen of hell (nāraka) is severed and is reborn separately in the human realm; therefore, your statement is unreasonable.
If you do not say that one who has been severed from the *naraka* hell is reborn separately in the human realm, then you should not say that he is different from them;
to say that he is different from them is unreasonable.
If one were to say:
"It cannot be said that it is either that or different," one should ask them:
"Do you accept this?
That one who has passed away from the hells is born in the human realm—this statement cannot be said to be either 'that very person' or 'someone else.
He replied:"
It is not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If it cannot be said whether that [being] is "that" or "other," then one should likewise say that there is someone who, having passed away from hell, is born in the human realm; yet such a statement also cannot be said to be "that" or "other. Therefore, your assertion is unreasonable.

If you do not assert that there are those who pass away from hell and are reborn in the human realm, then such a statement as "it cannot be said whether they are those very persons or others" would be untenable; thus, one should not say that it cannot be said whether they are those very persons or others.
To say that it cannot be said whether they are those very persons or others is illogical.
Just as there are those who pass away from the hells and are reborn in the human realm, so it is for those who pass away from the hells and are reborn in the heavenly realms.
As it is with the hell realm, so it is with the animal, hungry ghost, human, and celestial realms.

Regarding the distinction here: one should not say that there is capacity within the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts; rather, one should say that there is capacity within the realms of gods and humans.

One should not say that there is an incapacity [to attain liberation] among those in the realms of gods and humans; rather, one should say that there is an incapacity among those in the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Proponents of the *pudgala* (person) speak thus:
"In the sense of truth and in the ultimate sense, the *pudgala* is obtainable, realizable, presently existing, and equally existent; therefore, the *pudgala* definitely exists."
The proponents of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnyatāvādin) raise this question: Do you accept this?

That in the sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, elegant phrasing, and excellent exposition, has definitively established these eight types of persons (*pudgala*) without confusion—namely, those who are candidates for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka*) and those who have realized the fruit of stream-entry, up to those who are candidates for the realization of the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala-pratipannaka*) and those who have realized the fruit of arhatship; that there definitely exists separately the candidate for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry and definitely exists separately the one who has realized the fruit of stream-entry, and so on, up to definitely existing separately the candidate for the realization of the fruit of arhatship and definitely existing separately the one who has realized the fruit of arhatship.
He replied, "Yes. He was asked again:
"Do you agree with this?
That a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry attains the fruit of stream-entry? He replied:
It is so. Listen, you are defeated.

If there were eight types of *pudgalas* established as distinct and without confusion—namely, those proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala-pratipannaka*) and the fruit of stream-entry itself, up to those proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala-pratipannaka*) and the fruit of arhatship itself—and if it were determined that there is a distinct individual proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of stream-entry and a distinct individual who has attained the fruit of stream-entry, and so on up to a distinct individual proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of arhatship and a distinct individual who has attained the fruit of arhatship, then one should not say that "a *pudgala* proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of stream-entry attains the fruit of stream-entry. Your statement is therefore unreasonable.

Now, if you say that a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry attains the fruit of stream-entry, then you should not say that these eight types of persons are definitively established as distinct and unmixed—namely, the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry and the one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry, up to the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship and the one who has attained the fruit of arhatship—and that there is definitely a distinct person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, and definitely a distinct person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry, up to definitely a distinct person practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship, and definitely a distinct person who has attained the fruit of arhatship.

To say that these eight types of persons (*pudgala*) are definitively established without confusion—that is, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka*) as distinct from the fruit of stream-entry itself, and so on up to the candidate for the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala-pratipannaka*) as distinct from the fruit of arhatship itself—and that there must definitively exist a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry separate from the fruit of stream-entry, and so on up to a definitive existence of a candidate for the fruit of arhatship separate from the fruit of arhatship—is not reasonable.
He says this: "A person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry will certainly attain the fruit of stream-entry.
One should ask him:
"Do you accept this? That is indeed that.
He replied:
Not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry necessarily attains the fruit of stream-entry, then one must say that he is that very same person; therefore, your statement is unreasonable.

If you do not assert that "that is indeed that," then one should not say that a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry will certainly attain the fruit of stream-entry;
to say that a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry will certainly attain the fruit of stream-entry is illogical.
If one says, "That is indeed that," one should ask that person:
"Do you accept this?
That which constitutes realization is itself abiding in the fruit.
He replied:
It is not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If that very person were identical to that [state], then you should say that the one who has realized and declared [the path] is identical to the one who abides in the fruit; yet, for you to speak thus is unreasonable.
If you do not state that the realization and the orientation toward it are themselves the abiding in the fruit, then you should not say that "that is itself that";
to say that "that is itself that" is illogical.
Furthermore, if someone were to say,
"That is indeed that," one should ask them:
Do you agree with this?
A person who is practicing toward the realization of the fruit of stream-entry does not possess that fruit; however, if they have realized the fruit of stream-entry, they do possess that fruit.
He replied, "Yes. He was asked again:
"Do you accept this?
That which is non-attainment is itself attainment.
He replied:
It is not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If the person who is practicing toward the realization of the fruit of stream-entry does not possess that fruit, yet that fruit of stream-entry is possessed by the fruit itself, then one must say that what is non-possession is itself possession; thus, your statement is unreasonable.
If you do not say that what is non-attainment is itself attainment, then you should not say that "that is itself that";
to say that "that is itself that" is not logical.
If one should say,
"That is different from that," one should ask that person:
"Do you agree with this?
That one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) produces a distinct arising of the fruit of stream-entry through the abandonment [of defilements]?
He replied:
Not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If that [candidate] were different from that [fruit], then one should say that the various fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) arise separately from the realization of the candidate for stream-entry; yet your statement to this effect is unreasonable.

If you do not say that the fruit of stream-entry arises as something distinct from the path of realization for the fruit of stream-entry—which is the abandonment [of defilements]—then you should not say that one is different from the other;
to say that one is different from the other is not logical.
If one were to say:
"It cannot be said whether it is that, or something else,
or different," one should ask him:
Do you agree with this?

That one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) and has attained the fruit of stream-entry—regarding such a person, it cannot be said that they are either "that" or "other."
He replied: "It is not so.
Listen, you have lost the debate."

If it cannot be said that it is either that, or something else, or different from that, then one must say that those who are practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry attain the fruit of stream-entry; yet such a statement as this also cannot be said to be either that, or something else, or different from that. Therefore, your assertion is not logical.

If you do not say that those who are practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry attain the fruit of stream-entry, and if such a statement cannot be described as being either "that" or "other," then you should not say that it is indescribable as being either "that" or "other"; thus, your assertion is unreasonable.

Just as one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry cannot be said to be either that [fruit] or something other than it, so too this statement cannot be said to be either that or other; thus, you should not say that it is "inexpressible" whether it is that or other, for such a claim is unreasonable.

Just as one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala-pratipannaka) is in relation to the fruit of stream-entry, so too is it for one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala-pratipannaka) in relation to the fruit of once-returning.

The distinction here is as follows: regarding those who are candidates for the realization of the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), one should not categorically state that they do not possess the fruit.
Proponents of the theory of the person (*pudgalavādin*) speak thus:
"In terms of the meaning of truth and the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the person is obtainable, realizable, presently existing, and equally existent; therefore, the person definitely exists."
The proponents of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnyatāvādin) raise this question: "Do you accept this?

That in the sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, eloquent phrasing, and skillful exposition, definitively established these eight types of persons (pudgala) as distinct and unmixed—namely, those proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) and those who have realized the fruit of stream-entry, up to those proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of arhatship and those who have realized the fruit of arhatship?"

There definitely exists a distinct candidate for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, and there definitely exists the fruit of stream-entry itself; likewise, up to and including, there definitely exists a distinct candidate for the realization of the fruit of arhatship, and there definitely exists the fruit of arhatship itself.
He replied, "Yes. He was asked again:
"Do you accept this?
That those who are practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) shall attain the fruit of non-returning? He replied:
Thus it is.
Listen, you are defeated.

If there were eight types of persons established as distinct and non-confounded—namely, those who are candidates for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka) and those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, up to those who are candidates for the realization of the fruit of arhatship and those who have attained the fruit of arhatship—and if it were determined that there is a distinct candidate for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry and a distinct one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry, up to a distinct candidate for the realization of the fruit of arhatship and a distinct one who has attained the fruit of arhatship, then you should not say that "one who is a candidate for the realization of the fruit of non-returning attains the fruit of non-returning. Your statement is unreasonable.

If you now claim that those who are "candidates for the realization of the fruit of non-returner" (anāgāmiphala-pratipannaka) are themselves already "non-returners," then you should not say that these eight types of persons are definitively established without confusion—namely, that there is a candidate for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala-pratipannaka) distinct from the fruit of stream-entry itself, and so on, up to a candidate for the realization of the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala-pratipannaka) distinct from the fruit of arhatship itself; [for in that case, each candidate would be identical to the fruit].

To say that there are eight types of persons established as distinct and non-overlapping—namely, those who are candidates for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka) and those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, up to those who are candidates for the fruit of arhatship (arhat-phala-pratipannaka) and those who have attained the fruit of arhatship—is not tenable; for it would mean that there must exist a distinct candidate for the fruit of stream-entry separate from the fruit of stream-entry itself, and so on, up to the existence of a distinct candidate for the fruit of arhatship separate from the fruit of arhatship itself. This is illogical.
He says this: "One who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returner will certainly attain the fruit of non-returner.
One should ask him:
"Do you accept this? That is indeed that.
He replied:
It is not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If one who is practicing toward the realization of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) is certain to attain that fruit, then it must be said that he is already that very fruit; therefore, your statement is unreasonable.

If you do not assert that "that is indeed that," then one should not say that those who are candidates for the realization of the fruit of non-return (anāgāmiphala-pratipannaka) will certainly attain the fruit of non-return;
to say that candidates for the realization of the fruit of non-return will certainly attain the fruit of non-return is illogical.
If one were to say,
"That is indeed that," one should ask them:
"Do you accept this?
That which constitutes realization and turning toward [the goal] is itself abiding in the fruit. He replied:
Not so. Listen, you are defeated.

If that very thing were itself that [result], then one should say that the candidate for realization (*sākṣātkriyābhimukha*) is itself abiding in the fruit (*phalastha*); thus, your statement is unreasonable.
If you do not state that the realization and the orientation toward it are themselves the abiding in the fruit, then you should not say that "it is that very thing";
to say that "it is that very thing" would be unreasonable.
Furthermore, if someone were to say,
"That is indeed that," one should ask them:
"Do you accept this?
One who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning possesses anger; that fruit of non-returning is free from anger. He replied:
"Is that so?
He then asked him again:
"Do you accept this?"
If he has ill will, he immediately abandons it. He replies: "No."
Listen, you are defeated.
If that were identical to that, then one would have to say that he who possesses anger is himself free from anger; thus, your statement is unreasonable.
If you do not say that one who possesses anger is the same as one who is free from anger, then it would not be right to say that "he is he";
to say that "he is he" is illogical.
If one were to say,
"That is different from that," one should ask that person:
"Do you accept this?
That those who are practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-return can, through the abandonment [of defilements], produce a distinct fruit of non-return?
He replied:
Not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If that [fruit] were different from that [path], then one would have to say that the various non-returners who are practicing for realization sever [the defilements] and subsequently give rise to a distinct non-returner fruit; yet your assertion is unreasonable.

If you do not say that the various candidates for realization of the fruit of non-return (anāgāmiphala-pratipannaka) produce a distinct fruit of non-return through abandonment, then you should not say that one is different from the other;
to say that one is different from the other would be unreasonable.
If one were to say:
"It cannot be said that it is either that, or something else," one should ask that person:
Do you agree with this?
That one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-return and attains the fruit of non-return—this cannot be said to be either that [person] or something else.
He replied: "It is not so.
Listen, you have lost the debate."

If it cannot be said that he is either that or different from that, then one must say that the one who has realized the fruit of non-returner and is proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of non-returner likewise cannot be said to be either that or different from that; therefore, your statement is unreasonable.

If you do not say that those who are practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) obtain the fruit of non-returning, and if such a statement cannot be said to be either "that" or "other," then one should not say that it is indescribable as being either "that" or "other";
to say it is indescribable as being either "that" or "other" is illogical.
The proponents of the *pudgala* speak thus:
"In truth, in the ultimate sense, the *pudgala* is obtainable, realizable, presently existent, and equally existent; therefore, the *pudgala* definitely exists."
The proponents of the theory of intrinsic emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) raise this question: "Do you accept this?

That in the sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, excellent phrasing, and skillful exposition, has definitively established these eight types of persons without confusion—namely, those who are candidates for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka*) and those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, up to those who are candidates for the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala-pratipannaka*) and those who have attained the fruit of arhatship—and that there definitely exists separately the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry, definitely exists separately the one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry, and so on, up to definitely existing separately the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and definitely existing separately the one who has attained the fruit of arhatship?"
He replied, "Yes. He was asked again:
"Do you accept this?
That one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship attains the fruit of arhatship. He replied:
It is so. Listen, you are defeated.

If there were eight distinct types of persons (*pudgala*) established without confusion—namely, those practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of stream-entry itself, and so on, up to those practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship, the fruit of arhatship itself—if it were the case that there were definitely distinct persons practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry and definitely distinct persons who have realized the fruit of stream-entry, and so on, up to definitely distinct persons practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship and definitely distinct persons who have realized the fruit of arhatship, then it would not be correct to say that one attains the fruit of arhatship by practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship; thus, your statement is unreasonable.

If you now claim that one who is "facing the realization" (pratipannaka) of the fruit of arhatship attains the fruit of arhatship, then you should not say that these eight types of persons are definitively established without confusion—namely, that there is a distinct person facing the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) who is the fruit of stream-entry itself, up to a distinct person facing the realization of the fruit of arhatship who is the fruit of arhatship itself; rather, there must be a distinct person facing the realization of the fruit of stream-entry who is distinct from the fruit of stream-entry itself, and so on, up to a distinct person facing the realization of the fruit of arhatship who is distinct from the fruit of arhatship itself.

To say that there are eight types of persons established as distinct and non-overlapping—namely, those who are candidates for the fruit of stream-entry or those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, up to those who are candidates for the fruit of arhatship or those who have attained the fruit of arhatship—is not tenable, because it would imply that there is a distinct candidate for the fruit of stream-entry separate from one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry, and so on, up to a distinct candidate for the fruit of arhatship being separate from one who has attained the fruit of arhatship. This is illogical.
He says this: "One who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship will certainly attain the fruit of arhatship.
One should ask him:
"Do you accept this? That is indeed that.
He replied:
It is not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If one who is practicing toward the realization of the fruit of arhatship will certainly attain the fruit of arhatship, then it must be said that the former is identical to the latter; yet your statement is unreasonable.

If you do not assert that "that is indeed that," then it would be improper to say that one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship will certainly attain the fruit of arhatship;
to say that one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship will certainly attain the fruit of arhatship would be illogical.
If one says, "That is indeed that," one should ask them:
"Do you accept this?
That which constitutes realization is itself abiding in the fruit.
He replied:
Not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.
If that very person were that [result], then one should say that the one who has realized the path toward it is identical to the one abiding in the fruit; thus, your statement is unreasonable.
If you do not state that the realization and the orientation toward it are themselves the abiding in the fruit, then you should not say that "it is that very same thing";
to say that "it is that very same thing" would be illogical.
Furthermore, if someone were to say,
"That is indeed that," one should ask them:
Do you agree with this?

Those who are practicing for the realization of the fruit of Arhatship have not yet completely abandoned greed, have not yet completely abandoned conceit, and have not yet completely abandoned ignorance; they are still learners with further tasks to perform.

The fruit of Arhatship is one who has completely abandoned craving, completely abandoned pride, and completely abandoned ignorance; such a person is one beyond training (aśaikṣa), having accomplished what was to be done.
He replied, "Yes. He was asked again:
"Do you agree with this?
That one who has something to do has already accomplished what was to be done.
He replied:
It is not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.
If that were identical to that, then it should be said that he who has something to do has already accomplished what was to be done; thus, your statement is unreasonable.
If you do not say that for him there is something to be done—that is, that what was to be done has already been accomplished—then you should not say that he is that very person;
to say that he is that very person would be unreasonable.
If one should say:
"That is different from that," one should ask him:
"Do you agree with this?
That one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship can, through the severance of distinct [defilements], produce the fruit of arhatship?
He replied:
It is not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If that [fruit] were different from that [path], then one would have to say that the various fruits of arhatship arise separately from the realization of the path leading toward their abandonment; yet your assertion is unreasonable.

If you do not say that those who are practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship produce a distinct fruit of arhatship through abandonment, then it would not be right to say that one is different from the other;
to say that one is different from the other would be illogical.
If one were to say:
"It cannot be said whether it is that, or something else,
or different," one should ask that person:
Do you agree with this?
That one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship attains the fruit of arhatship—this statement cannot be said to be either that [the same] or different.
He replied: "It is not so.
Listen, you have lost the debate."

If it cannot be said that he is either that or different from it, then one must say that the various fruits of arhatship are what are realized, and that the attainment of the fruit of arhatship is directed toward them; likewise, such a statement as this also cannot be said to be either that or different. Therefore, your assertion is unreasonable.

If you do not say that those who are practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship attain the fruit of arhatship, then this statement—that it cannot be said whether they are that or different—would be untenable;
one should not say that it cannot be said whether they are that or different, for such a claim is illogical.
The proponents of the *pudgala* speak as follows:
"In truth, in the ultimate sense, the *pudgala* is obtainable, realizable, presently existing, and equally existent; therefore, the *pudgala* definitely exists."
The proponents of the doctrine of intrinsic emptiness (śūnyatāvādin) raise this question: "Do you accept this?

That in the sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words and excellent phrasing, has well explained that these three groups are definitively established without confusion—namely, the group of the indeterminate, the group fixed in the wrong nature, and the group fixed in the right nature—and that there definitely exists a distinct group of the indeterminate, a definitely distinct group fixed in the wrong nature, and a definitely distinct group fixed in the right nature?"
He replied, "Yes. He was asked again:
"Do you accept this?
That there are those who enter the fixed category of wrong nature from the indeterminate category? He replied:
It is so. Listen, you are defeated.

If there were three groups established as definitively distinct and without confusion—namely, the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*), the group fixed in wrongness (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), and the group fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*)—and if there were a definitively distinct indeterminate group, a definitively distinct group fixed in wrongness, and a definitively distinct group fixed in rightness, then one should not say that there is an entry from the indeterminate group into the group fixed in wrongness; thus, what you have said is unreasonable.

If you now claim that there is one who enters the group of those fixed in wrongness from the group of the undetermined, then you should not say that these three groups—namely, the group of the undetermined, the group fixed in wrongness, and the group fixed in rightness—are established as definitively distinct and without confusion;

for it would be unreasonable to say that there are three groups established as definitively distinct and without confusion—namely, the group of the undetermined, the group fixed in wrongness, and the group fixed in rightness—and yet maintain that there is a definitively distinct group of the undetermined, a definitively distinct group fixed in wrongness, and a definitively distinct group fixed in rightness.
He says: "There certainly are those who enter the group of the definitely wrong-natured from the group of the indeterminate.
One should ask him:
"Do you agree with this?
That is precisely that.
He replied:
It is not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If it were certain that one enters the group of those fixed in wrongness from the group of the undetermined, then one should say that the former is identical to the latter; thus, your statement is illogical.

If you do not say that "that" is identical to "that," then one should not say that there is definitely a transition from the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) into the group fixed in wrongness (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi);
to say that there is definitely such a transition from the indeterminate group into the group fixed in wrongness is illogical.
If one were to say,
"That is indeed that," one should ask that person:
"Do you accept this?
That those who abide in the indeterminate group are themselves abiding in the group fixed in wrong nature?
He replied:
Not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If that were identical to that, then one must say that those abiding in the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) are themselves abiding in the group fixed in wrongness (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*); thus, your statement is unreasonable.
If you do not say that those who abide in the indeterminate group are themselves those who abide in the group fixed in wrongness, then it should not be said that "they are themselves they";
to say that "they are themselves they" is not logical.
Furthermore, if someone says, "That is indeed that," you should ask them:
Do you agree with this?

Those abiding in the group of the indeterminate have the capacity to give rise to the untainted faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, whereas those abiding in the group of the fixed in error lack such capacity.
He replied, "Yes. He was asked again:
"Do you accept this?
That which possesses capability is itself without capability.
He replied:
Not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.
If that very thing were identical to itself, then one would have to say that it both possesses capability and lacks capability; thus, your statement is unreasonable.
If you do not say that what is capable is itself incapable, then it should not be said that "it is that very thing";
to say that "it is that very thing" is not logical.
If one says, "That is different from that," one should ask that person:

"Do you accept this? That those abiding in the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) who have severed [the roots of goodness] will arise separately and abide in the group fixed in wrongness (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi)?
He replied:
It is not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If that [state] were different from this, then one would have to say that those abiding in the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi), having abandoned it, are born separately and abide in the fixed group of wrongness (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi); yet your assertion is unreasonable.

If you do not say that those abiding in the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) abandon it and are born separately into the group fixed in wrongness (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi), then you should not say that the one is different from the other;
to say that the one is different from the other is not logical.
If one says: "It cannot be said whether it is that, or something else,
or different," one should ask them:
"Do you accept this?
Regarding those who enter the group of fixed wrongness from the group of the undetermined, it cannot be said that they are either 'that' or 'other'.
He replied:
Not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If it cannot be said that they are either "that" or "other," then one must likewise say that the statement regarding those who enter the fixed group of the wrong nature from the indeterminate group cannot be said to be either "that" or "other"; thus, your assertion is unreasonable.

If you do not say that those who enter the group of the fixed in wrongness from the group of the undetermined are such that this statement cannot be said to be either "that" or "other," then you should not say that it cannot be said to be either "that" or "other";
to say that it cannot be said to be either "that" or "other" is illogical.
The proponents of the *pudgala* speak thus:
"In truth, in the ultimate sense, the *pudgala* is obtainable, realizable, presently existing, and equally existent; therefore, the *pudgala* definitely exists."
The proponents of the doctrine of intrinsic emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) raise this question: "Do you accept this?

That in the sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, eloquent phrasing, and excellent exposition, definitively established these three groups as being unmixed: namely, the group of the indeterminate (*aniyata-rāśi*), the group fixed in the wrong nature (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), and the group fixed in the right nature (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*); that there definitely exists a distinct group of the indeterminate, definitely exists a distinct group fixed in the wrong nature, and definitely exists a distinct group fixed in the right nature?"
He replied, "Yes. He was asked again:
"Do you agree with this?
That there is one who enters the fixed nature of rightness from the indeterminate group? He replied:
It is so. Listen, you are defeated.

If there were three groups established as distinct and non-confused—namely, the indeterminate group, the group fixed in wrongness, and the group fixed in rightness—and if there were a definitely separate indeterminate group, a definitely separate group fixed in wrongness, and a definitely separate group fixed in rightness, then one should not say that there is an entry from the indeterminate group into the group fixed in rightness; thus, your statement is unreasonable.

If you now claim that there is one who enters the fixed nature of rightness from the indeterminate group, then you should not say that these three groups—the indeterminate group, the fixed nature of wrongness, and the fixed nature of rightness—are established as definitively distinct and without confusion; that is, that there is a definitively separate indeterminate group, a definitively separate fixed nature of wrongness, and a definitively separate fixed nature of rightness.

To say that there are three groups established as definitively distinct and without confusion—namely, the indeterminate group, the fixed nature of wrongness, and the fixed nature of rightness—and yet maintain that there is a definitively separate indeterminate group, a definitively separate fixed nature of wrongness, and a definitively separate fixed nature of rightness, is unreasonable.
He says this: "There certainly is an entry from the indeterminate group into the group of those fixed in the rightness of nature.
One should ask him:
"Do you accept this? That is indeed that.
He replied:
It is not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat.

If it were certain that there is a transition from the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) into the group of those fixed in the right nature (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi), then one should say that the former is itself the latter; therefore, your statement is unreasonable.

If you do not assert that "that is indeed that," then one should not say that there is definitely a transition from the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) into the group of those fixed in the rightness of nature (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi); to say that there is definitely such a transition is illogical.
If one were to say,
"That is indeed that," one should ask that person:
"Do you agree with this?
That those who abide in the indeterminate group are themselves abiding in the group of those fixed in the right nature?
He replied:
Not so. Listen, you are defeated.

If that were identical to that, then one must say that those who abide in the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) are themselves those who abide in the group of those fixed in the right nature (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi); thus, what you have said is unreasonable.
If you do not state that those abiding in the indeterminate group are themselves abiding in the group of those fixed in the right nature, then you should not say that "they are themselves that";
to say that "they are themselves that" is not logical.
Furthermore, if someone were to say,
"That is indeed that," one should ask them:
"Do you agree with this?
Those who abide in the indeterminate group are finite fields of merit; those who abide in the group of those fixed in the right nature are infinite fields of merit.
They replied:
"Is that so?
He then asked him again:
"Do you accept this?"
"All those who are finite fields of merit are, in fact, infinite fields of merit.
He replied: "Not so."
Listen, you are defeated.
If that were indeed that, then one should say that all finite fields of merit are themselves infinite fields of merit; thus, your statement is unreasonable.
If you do not state that those which are finite fields of merit are themselves infinite fields of merit, then you should not say that "that is itself that";
to say that "that is itself that" is illogical.
If one should say:
"That is different from that," one should ask that person:

"Do you accept this? That those abiding in the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) who have severed [the roots of goodness] will be born separately and abide in the group of those fixed in the right nature (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi)?
He replied:
Not so. Listen, for you have fallen into defeat:

if that [state] were different from this, then one would have to say that those abiding in the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi), having abandoned it, are born separately and abide in the group of those fixed in the right nature (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi). Your assertion is therefore unreasonable.

If you do not assert that those abiding in the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) abandon it and are born separately into the group of those fixed in the right nature (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi), then you should not say that one is different from the other;
to say that one is different from the other would be unreasonable.
If one were to say:
"It cannot be said that it is either that or different," one should ask that person:
Do you agree with this?
That there are those who enter the fixed nature of correctness from the indeterminate group—such a statement cannot be said to refer either to them or to others.
He replied: "It is not so.
Listen, you have lost the debate."

If it cannot be said that they are either those, or others, or different, then one must also say that when those in the indeterminate group enter the group of those fixed in the right nature, such a statement as "either those or different" likewise cannot be said; therefore, your assertion is unreasonable.

If you do not say that those in the various states of existence enter the fixed nature of rightness from the indeterminate group, then such a statement as "it cannot be said whether they are that or different" is also untenable; thus, one should not say that it cannot be said whether they are that or different.
To say that it cannot be said whether they are that or different is not logical.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Chapter Two: *Vijñānakāya-pāda*.
*Abhidharma-vijñānakāya-śāstra*, Chapter Three.
Composed by the Arhat Devaśarman.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Two of the Second Section on the *Pudgala-skandha*. First, the Verse Summary (*Uddāna*): The Proponents of the *Pudgala* (Pudgalavādins) state as follows:
"In truth, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the *pudgala* is obtainable, realizable, presently existing, and equally existent; therefore, the *pudgala* definitely exists."
The proponents of the theory of intrinsic emptiness (śūnyatāvādin) raise this question: Do you accept this?

That in the sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, excellent phrasing, and skillful exposition, has definitively established these three types of persons (*pudgala*) without confusion—namely, the person in training (*śaikṣa*), the person beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the person who is neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
He replied: "Yes.
Dharmas are also of three kinds: namely, dharmas of training (śaikṣa), dharmas beyond training (aśaikṣa), and dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa)."
He replied, "Yes. He was asked again:
Do you accept this?

That first there is a person who is neither a learner nor one beyond learning, who subsequently becomes a learner; having become a learner, he later becomes one beyond learning; and having become one beyond learning, he again becomes a person who is a learner.
He replied, "Yes. He was asked again:
Do you agree with this?

That first there are dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, which subsequently become learner-dharmas; having become learner-dharmas, they later become non-learner-dharmas; and having become non-learner-dharmas, they again become learner-dharmas?
He replied: "No.
Listen, you have lost the debate."

If a person (pudgala) who was previously neither a learner (śaikṣa) nor one beyond learning (aśaikṣa) subsequently becomes a learner, and having become a learner, later becomes one beyond learning, and having become one beyond learning, again becomes a learner—then it must be said that first there were dharmas that were neither learner nor beyond learning, which subsequently became learner-dharmas, and having become learner-dharmas, later became dharmas beyond learning, and having become dharmas beyond learning, again became learner-dharmas. Your statement is therefore unreasonable.

If you do not say that one who was previously neither a learner (*śaikṣa*) nor a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) subsequently becomes a learner, and having become a learner, subsequently becomes a non-learner, and having become a non-learner, subsequently becomes a learner again;

then it would be improper to say that a person (*pudgala*) who was previously neither a learner nor a non-learner subsequently becomes a learner, and having become a learner, subsequently becomes a non-learner, and having become a non-learner, subsequently becomes a learner again—to say that a person who was previously neither a learner nor a non-learner subsequently becomes a learner, and having become a learner, subsequently becomes a non-learner, and having become a non-learner, subsequently becomes a learner again, is illogical.
The proponents of the *pudgala* theory speak thus:

"There exists a self (*ātman*), a sentient being (*sattva*), a life-principle (*jīva*), a living being (*jantu*), a nourisher (*poṣa*), a person (*puruṣa*), and a *pudgala*. Because of the existence of this *pudgala*, one is able to perform various karmas—those conducive to pleasant feeling, those conducive to painful feeling, or those conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."

Having performed karma conducive to pleasant feeling, one experiences pleasant feeling; having performed karma conducive to painful feeling, one experiences painful feeling; and having performed karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The proponents of the theory of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnyatāvādin) pose this question: "Do you accept this?
That suffering and pleasure are self-created?"
He replied: "No.
Listen, you have lost the debate."

If there were a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a person, or a pudgala, then by virtue of the existence of a pudgala, one would be able to perform various karmas—whether conducive to pleasant feeling, conducive to painful feeling, or conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Having performed karma conducive to pleasant feeling, one experiences pleasant feeling; having performed karma conducive to painful feeling, one experiences painful feeling; and having performed karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Thus, it must be said that one creates one's own pleasure and pain; your statement is therefore unreasonable.

If you do not assert that pleasure and pain are self-made, then you should not assert the existence of a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a spirit, or a person (pudgala); for it is because of the existence of a person that one can perform various karmas—whether they conduce to pleasant feeling, painful feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Having performed karma conducive to pleasant feeling, one experiences pleasant feeling; having performed karma conducive to painful feeling, one experiences painful feeling; and having performed karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

It is said that there is a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a person, and a pudgala; and because of the existence of this pudgala, one is able to perform various karmas—whether conducive to pleasant feeling, conducive to painful feeling, or conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

It would not be logical for one who has performed karma conducive to pleasant feeling to experience only pleasant feeling, or karma conducive to painful feeling to experience only painful feeling, or karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling to experience only neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
If someone were to say, "One creates one's own suffering and pleasure," one should ask them:
Do you agree with this?

That in the sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, excellent phrasing, and skillful exposition, spoke to the renunciant outsider Ghaṭīkāra, saying: "Ghaṭīkāra, you have accepted and understood that those who wish to create their own pleasure and pain [do so]—this, Ghaṭīkāra!"
"I never say such a thing.
He replied, "Indeed, it is so."
Listen, you are defeated.

If one were to create one’s own suffering and pleasure, then it would not have been right for the Blessed One to speak well, phrase well, and explain well in the Sūtra, saying to the ascetic outsider Caṅkī: “Caṅkī, whatever states there may be that one wishes to create as one’s own suffering and pleasure, these, Caṅkī, [one should neither affirm nor deny]. [Rather, he would have said: “Caṅkī, you yourself accept and admit them. Thus, you are defeated.
I have never said that what you say is not reasonable.

If you now claim that in the sūtras the Blessed One spoke well, with elegant phrasing and excellent exposition, for the sake of the renunciant outsider Ghaṭīkāra, saying: "Ghaṭīkāra, one who accepts and acknowledges that all those who wish to create their own pleasure and pain—this, Ghaṭīkāra!"—then [you are mistaken].
I never say that [suffering and pleasure are self-created]; therefore, one should not say that suffering and pleasure are created by oneself.
To say that suffering and pleasure are created by oneself is unreasonable.
If one were to say this:
If it is held that pleasure and pain are created by another, one should ask him:
"Do you accept this?"

That is to say, in the Sūtra, the Blessed One—speaking with skillful speech, skillful terminology, and skillful exposition—addressed the renunciant outsider Ghaṭīkāra, saying: "Ghaṭīkāra, you perceive one thing and experience another; if you wish to cause others to undergo suffering or happiness, [you are mistaken], O Ghaṭīkāra!"
"I certainly do not say that. He replied, "Yes."
Listen, you are defeated.

If suffering and pleasure were created by another, then it would not be right to say that in the Sūtra the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, eloquent speech, and excellent teaching, said to the renunciant outsider Caṅkī: "Caṅkī, you experience one thing and perceive another; you desire that others create your suffering and pleasure. O Caṅkī!"
I certainly do not say that what you have said is unreasonable.

If you now claim that in the Sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words and excellent terminology, spoke thus for the sake of the renunciant outsider Ghaṭīkāra: "Ghaṭīkāra, there are those who experience pleasure and pain differently and desire to cause others to experience them differently"—then, Ghaṭīkāra! [This is not so.]
I never say that; therefore, one should not say that suffering and pleasure are created by another.
To say that suffering and pleasure are created by another is unreasonable.
Those who propound the existence of a *pudgala* speak as follows:

There is a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a person, and a pudgala; because of the existence of this pudgala, one is able to perform various karmas—whether conducive to pleasant feeling, conducive to painful feeling, or conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Having performed karma conducive to pleasant feeling, one experiences pleasant feeling; having performed karma conducive to painful feeling, one experiences painful feeling; and having performed karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The proponents of the theory of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnyatāvādin) pose this question: "Do you accept this?
That this is the agent and this is the recipient?"
He replied: "No.
Listen, you have lost the debate."

If there were a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a person, or a pudgala, then by virtue of the existence of a pudgala, one would be able to perform various karmas—whether conducive to pleasant feeling, conducive to painful feeling, or conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Having performed karma conducive to pleasant feeling, one experiences pleasant feeling; having performed karma conducive to painful feeling, one experiences painful feeling; and having performed karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Thus, it should be said that "this is done and this is experienced. Your statement is therefore unreasonable.

If you do not say that "this performs" and "this experiences," then one should not speak of a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a spirit, or a person; for it is because of the existence of a person that one can perform various karmas—whether conducive to pleasant feeling, conducive to painful feeling, or conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Having performed karma conducive to pleasant feeling, one experiences pleasant feeling; having performed karma conducive to painful feeling, one experiences painful feeling; and having performed karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

It is said that there is a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a spirit, and a person (*pudgala*). Because of the existence of this *pudgala*, one is able to perform various karmas—whether conducive to pleasant feeling, conducive to painful feeling, or conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

It would not be logical for one who has performed karma conducive to pleasant feeling to experience a pleasant feeling, or karma conducive to painful feeling to experience a painful feeling, or karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling to experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
If one were to say:
"This is the agent and this is the experiencer," one should ask that person:
Do you agree with this?
That is to say, in the sūtra, the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, excellent phrasing, and skillful exposition, said to a certain brahmin: "Brahmin!
To say 'this is the agent' and 'this is the experiencer' is to fall into the extreme of eternalism."
He replied: "Yes. Listen, you have been defeated.

If this were the agent and this were the experiencer, then it would not be as the Blessed One, with his well-spoken words, excellent phrasing, and skillful exposition, said in a sutra when addressing a certain brahmin: "Brahmin!"
To say that "this is the agent and this is the experiencer" is to fall into the extreme of eternalism; thus, what you have said is unreasonable.
Now, if you were to claim that in the sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, elegant phrasing, and excellent exposition, spoke to a certain brahmin, saying: "Brahmin!..."
To say that "this is the agent and this is the experiencer" is to fall into the extreme of eternalism; thus, one should not say "this is the agent and this is the experiencer.
To say "this is the agent and this is the experiencer" is not logical.
If one were to speak as follows:
If one who acts is different from the one who experiences [the result], you should ask that person: "Do you accept this?"
That is to say, in the Sūtra, the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, eloquent phrasing, and excellent exposition, said to a certain brahmin: "Brahmin!
To hold that one acts and another experiences [the result] is to fall into the extreme of annihilationism."
He replied, "Yes.
Listen, you have been defeated.

If one were to perform an action and another were to experience its result, then it would not be right to say that, in the Sūtra, the Blessed One—using well-spoken words, eloquent phrasing, and excellent discourse—said this to a certain brahmin: "Brahmin!"
To hold that one performs an action and another experiences its result is to fall into the extreme of nihilism; therefore, what you have said is unreasonable.
If you now claim that in the Sūtra the Blessed One, with skillful speech, skillful terminology, and skillful exposition, spoke thus to a certain brahmin: "O brahmin!"... [then this is not so].

To claim that one person performs an action and another experiences its result is to fall into the extreme of nihilism; therefore, one should not say that one performs an action and another experiences its result.
To say that one performs an action and another experiences its result is unreasonable.
Proponents of the theory of the *pudgala* (person) speak as follows:

There is a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a person, and a pudgala; because of the existence of this pudgala, regarding those phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, and known, one has already attained or sought them, and the mind follows after discursive investigation and analysis.
The proponents of the theory of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnyatāvādin) pose this question: "Do you accept this?
That in the sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, eloquent phrasing, and excellent exposition, spoke to the bhikṣu Aṭṭhaka, the son of a donkey-breeder, saying: 'Bhikṣu!'"
Regarding all phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, and known—those already attained and those already sought—the mind follows after discursive investigation and analysis.
All such things are neither self nor belonging to a self, nor are they the self or the mine; one observes and sees them thus with right wisdom as they truly are.
He replied: "Yes. Listen now to your defeat.

If there were a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living soul, a nourisher, a spirit, or a person—and because of the existence of such a person—one were to engage in mental searching and investigation regarding those phenomena seen, heard, sensed, and known, having already attained or sought them, then one should not say that in the Sūtra the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, well-phrased expressions, and well-delivered teachings, spoke to the monk Aṭṭhaka, the son of a donkey-breeder, saying: "Monk!"
Regarding all phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, or cognized—those already attained and those sought after—the mind follows them through vitarka and vicāra.
To say that all such things are not "I" or "mine," nor "my self" or "belonging to my self," and to perceive this with right wisdom as it truly is, contradicts your statement; it is not reasonable.

If you now say that in the Sūtra the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, eloquent phrasing, and skillful exposition, spoke for the sake of the monk Aṭṭhaka, who was formerly a donkey herder, saying: "O monk!..."
Regarding all phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, and known—those already attained and those still sought—the mind follows after discursive thought and investigation.

All such things are neither "I" nor "mine," nor do they belong to a self; one should view them thus with right wisdom as they truly are. Therefore, one should not speak of a "self," a "sentient being," a "life-principle," a "creature," a "nourisher," a "person," or a "pudgala. Because of the existence of a pudgala, the mind would follow after discursive thought and investigation regarding phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, and known, whether already attained or still sought.

To say that there is a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a person, or a pudgala—and because of the existence of such a pudgala, for one to engage in mental seeking and investigation regarding phenomena seen, heard, sensed, and known, having already attained them or already sought them—is not reasonable.
Regarding what is said about the object of focus for loving-kindness (*maitrī*),

the proponents of the doctrine of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) state as follows: "The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-kāya*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*), the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are all obtainable [as objects]."
In the sense of ultimate truth and the highest meaning, a person (pudgala) is not obtainable, not realizable, not presently existent, and not substantially existent; therefore, no person exists.
The proponent of the theory of the person (pudgalavādin) asks:
"Venerable sir,
what is the object of focus (ālambana) of loving-kindness?"
He replied:

"The nature of all phenomena exists as it is; by means of conceptualization and re-conceptualization, one conventionally designates a 'sentient being. Within this context, loving-kindness takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates."
He asked: "Do you say that loving-kindness takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates? He replied:
"Yes. He asked again: "Do you accept this?"

This refers to what the Blessed One, with excellent speech, excellent phrasing, and excellent exposition, has taught in the sūtras: "One should cause sentient beings to possess all forms of happiness"; reflecting in this way, one enters the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
He replied: "Yes. He then said this:
Listen, you are defeated.

If loving-kindness (*maitrī*) takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates (*upāttaskandha-santati*), then it would be improper to say—as the Blessed One has well-spoken, well-phrased, and well-expounded in the sūtras—that one enters the meditative attainment of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*) with the thought, "May sentient beings possess all happiness. Your statement is therefore unreasonable.

If you now say that in the sūtras the Blessed One spoke well, with elegant phrasing and eloquent discourse, intending for sentient beings to be endowed with all happiness, and thus enters the meditative attainment of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*) through such reflection, then you should not say that loving-kindness takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates (*upātta-skandha-saṃtati*);
to say that loving-kindness takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates is illogical.
One should ask him: "Do you accept this?

That in the sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, eloquent phrasing, and skillful exposition, has declared that there are six groups of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness?"
He replied, “Yes. He was asked:
"Venerable one!
With which group of consciousnesses is loving-kindness associated?
Is it with eye-consciousness, or with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness?"
If one says it is associated with visual consciousness, then it does not take sentient beings as its object, because all visual consciousnesses take only visible form as their object.
If one says it is associated with auditory consciousness, then it does not take sentient beings as its object, because all auditory consciousnesses take only sound as their object.

If it is said that [this consciousness] is associated with olfactory consciousness, then it does not take sentient beings as its object, because all olfactory consciousnesses take only odors as their objects.
If it is said that it is associated with gustatory consciousness, then it does not take sentient beings as its object, because all gustatory consciousnesses take only tastes as their objects.

If one says it is associated with body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), then it does not take sentient beings as its object, because all body-consciousnesses take only tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*) as their objects.

If one says it is associated with mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), then it does not take sentient beings as its object, because all mental consciousnesses take only mental phenomena (*dharma*) as their objects.

If it is said that [the mind] is not associated with eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mental-consciousness, then there must be a separate seventh consciousness of sentient beings with which compassion is associated; yet the Blessed One did not fully awaken to this consciousness.
"Venerable ones!

In fearlessness, the Blessed One has declared: 'I have attained manifest, perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena; were there any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else who could rightfully challenge or remind me that I had not attained manifest, perfect enlightenment regarding these phenomena, [I would acknowledge it]. "

Regarding such right view, I have no self as an object for that right view; because there is no such object, I dwell in peace, free from fear and dread, proclaiming myself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage, turning the Great Brahma-wheel and roaring the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.
"Venerable sir!
If that were so, would it not be difficult to avoid charging the Buddha with being ignorant? He replied:
"Venerable friend!
I do not find fault with the Buddha for being ignorant; rather, although the Blessed One has fully awakened to this, he has not proclaimed it.
Venerable friend!"
The Blessed One once said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, I have proclaimed the teachings without interruption;

that is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path."
"Ānanda, for the Tathāgata there is no 'teacher's fist' regarding the Dharma—that is, he does not conceal anything out of fear that others might discover his lack of understanding.
Venerable One!"
If that is so, does this not challenge the Buddha by implying he has a "teacher's fist"?
He replied: "Venerable sir!"

I do not find fault with the Buddha for being ignorant, nor do I find fault with him for having a teacher’s fist; it is simply that although the World-Honored One has attained perfect enlightenment regarding those matters, he does not proclaim them.
"Venerable ones!

In the *Śāṇa-vana-sūtra*, the Blessed One said: 'O bhikṣus, even if the great earth were as high as the leaves of the Śāṇa forest, regarding those dharmas, I would spontaneously realize them; yet, though having attained perfect awakening, I would not teach them to others.'"
Therefore, although the Blessed One has attained perfect awakening regarding such consciousness, he did not proclaim it.
One should ask him:
"Venerable sir!"
Does that very sutra not contain further extensive passages?
That is to say, the Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus!

Those dharmas are unable to lead to the meaningful, unable to lead to the wholesome, unable to lead to the Dharma, do not lead to the holy life, do not result in the realization of supernormal powers, do not result in the realization of equal enlightenment, and do not result in the realization of nirvāṇa."

If there were such a person (pudgala) who could not lead to what is meaningful, could not lead to what is wholesome, could not lead to the Dharma, could not lead to the holy life (brahmacarya), could not realize supernormal powers (abhijñā), could not realize equal enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), and could not realize nirvāṇa, then they would be of no use; therefore, no such person exists.
The proponents of the theory of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnyatāvādin) state as follows:

"In terms of ultimate reality and the highest truth (*paramārtha*), the person (*pudgala*) is not obtainable, not realizable, not presently existent, and not substantially existent; therefore, the person does not exist."
The proponent of the theory of the person (pudgalavādin) asks:
"Venerable sir,
what is the object of focus for loving-kindness?"
He replied:

"The nature of all phenomena exists as it is; by means of conceptualization and re-conceptualization, one conventionally designates 'sentient beings. Within this context, loving-kindness takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates."
He asked: "Do you say that loving-kindness takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates?
He replied: "Yes."
"Yes. He asked again: "Do you accept this?"

This refers to what the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, excellent phrasing, and eloquent exposition, taught in the sūtras: "One should cause sentient beings to possess all forms of happiness"—reflecting in this way, one enters the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
He replied: "Yes. He then spoke as follows:
Listen, you are defeated.

If loving-kindness (*maitrī*) takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates (*upātta-skandha-saṃtati*), then it would be improper to say—as the Blessed One has well spoken, well phrased, and well taught in the sūtras—that one enters the meditative attainment of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*) with the thought, "May all sentient beings possess happiness. Your statement is therefore unreasonable.

If you now say that in the sūtras the Blessed One spoke well, with elegant phrasing and excellent exposition, intending for sentient beings to be endowed with all happiness, and thus entered the meditative attainment of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*) with such a thought, then you should not say that loving-kindness takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates (*upātta-skandha-saṃtati*);
to say that loving-kindness takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates is unreasonable.
One should ask him: "Do you accept this?

That in the sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, eloquent phrasing, and excellent exposition, taught the four foundations of mindfulness: the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena?"
He replied, "Yes. He asked:
"Venerable sir!
With which application of mindfulness is loving-kindness associated?
Is it with the application of mindfulness to the body, or with the applications of mindfulness to feelings, mind, or phenomena?"

If one says it is associated with the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), then it does not take sentient beings as its object, because the application of mindfulness to the body takes only the body as its object.

If one says it is associated with the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*), then it does not take sentient beings as its object, because the application of mindfulness to feelings takes only feelings as its object.
If one says it is associated with the mindfulness of mind, then it does not take sentient beings as its object, because the mindfulness of mind takes only the mind as its object.
If one says it is associated with the mindfulness of phenomena, then it does not take sentient beings as its object, because the mindfulness of phenomena takes only phenomena as its object.

If it were said that [loving-kindness] is not associated with the applications of mindfulness of body, feeling, mind, or phenomena, then there would have to be a separate fifth application of mindfulness, namely "sentient-being mindfulness," with which loving-kindness would be associated; yet the Blessed One did not fully awaken to such an application of mindfulness.
"Venerable ones!

In the state of fearlessness, the Blessed One has declared: 'I have attained manifest and perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena. Should any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else challenge me with a legitimate objection or cause me to reflect upon these phenomena, there is nothing therein that I have not realized through manifest and perfect enlightenment.'"

Regarding such right view, I have no self as an object for that right view; because there is no such object, I dwell in peace, free from fear and dread, proclaiming myself to be established in the position of a Great Sage, turning the Great Brahma-wheel, and roaring the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.
"Venerable sir!
If that were so, would it not be difficult to avoid charging the Buddha with being ignorant? He replied:
"Venerable friend!
It is not that I consider the Buddha to be lacking in wisdom; rather, although the Blessed One has attained perfect awakening regarding this matter, he has not proclaimed it.
Venerable friend!"
The Blessed One once said to the Venerable Ānanda:

"Ānanda, I have proclaimed the Dharma to you without interruption—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path."
"Ānanda! The Tathāgata has no 'teacher’s fist' regarding the Dharma—that is, he does not conceal it out of fear that others might discover his own lack of understanding.
Venerable one!"
If that is so, does this not challenge the Buddha by implying he has a "teacher's fist"?
He replied: "Venerable sir!"

I do not find fault with the Buddha for being ignorant, nor do I find fault with him for having a teacher’s fist; it is simply that although the World-Honored One has attained perfect enlightenment regarding those matters, he does not proclaim them.
"Venerable ones!
In the *Śāṇa-vana-sūtra*, the Blessed One said: 'O bhikṣus!

Even if the great earth were as high as the height of the leaves of a Śāṇa forest, regarding those dharmas, I have personally realized them through my own knowledge; yet, although I have attained perfect awakening, I did not teach them to others.'"
Therefore, although the Blessed One has attained perfect awakening regarding those foundations of mindfulness, he did not proclaim them.
One should ask him: "Venerable sir," [why is this so?]
Regarding that very sutra:
Are there not further extensive passages?
Namely, the Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus!"

However, those phenomena cannot lead to the meaningful, cannot lead to the wholesome, cannot lead to the Dharma, do not lead to the holy life, do not result in the realization of supernormal powers, do not result in the realization of equal enlightenment, and do not result in the realization of nirvana.

If there were such a person (pudgala) who could not lead to what is meaningful, could not lead to what is wholesome, could not lead to the Dharma, could not lead to the holy life (brahmacarya), and could not realize supernormal powers, perfect enlightenment, or nirvana, then they would be of no use; therefore, no such person exists.
The proponents of the theory of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnyatāvādin) speak thus:

"In the sense of ultimate truth and the highest meaning, the person (pudgala) is not obtainable, not realizable, not presently existing, and not substantially existent; therefore, the person does not exist."
The proponent of the theory of the person (pudgalavādin) asked:
"Venerable sir,
what is the object of focus (ālambana) of loving-kindness?"
He replied:

"The nature of all phenomena exists as it is; by means of conceptualization and re-conceptualization, one conventionally designates 'sentient beings. Within this context, loving-kindness takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates."
He asked: "Do you say that loving-kindness takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates? He replied:
"So it is. He then asked again:
"Do you accept this?"

That is to say, in the sūtras, the Blessed One, with skillful speech, skillful terminology, and skillful exposition, has taught that one should enter the meditative attainment of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*) with the following reflection: "I shall cause all sentient beings to be endowed with every form of happiness."
He replied: "Yes. The other said this:
Listen, you are defeated.

If loving-kindness (*maitrī*) takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates (*upādatta-skandha-saṃtati*), then it would be incorrect to say that in the Sūtra the Blessed One, with well-spoken words and excellent phrasing, said: "One should cause sentient beings to possess all happiness," and that one enters the meditative attainment of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*) by reflecting in this way; for your statement is unreasonable.

If you now say that in the sūtras the Blessed One spoke well, with elegant phrasing and excellent exposition, intending for sentient beings to be endowed with all happiness, and thus entered the meditative attainment of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*) through such reflection, then you should not say that loving-kindness takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates (*upātta-skandha-saṃtati*);
to say that loving-kindness takes as its object the continuity of the appropriated aggregates is unreasonable.
One should ask him: "Do you accept this?

That in the sūtras the Blessed One, with well-spoken words, excellent phrasing, and skillful exposition, has declared that there are seven factors of enlightenment: the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, and the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity?"
He replied: "Yes. He asked:
"Venerable sir!
With which factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) is loving-kindness associated?
Is it with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, or with the factors of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, or equanimity?"

If one says it is associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness, then it does not take sentient beings as its object, because the awakening factor of mindfulness takes only phenomena (*dharma*) as its object.

If one says it is associated with the awakening factors of discrimination of phenomena, diligence, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, then it does not take sentient beings as its object, because the awakening factor of equanimity takes only phenomena as its object.

If it is claimed that [loving-kindness] is not associated with the factors of enlightenment such as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, then there must exist a separate eighth factor of enlightenment for sentient beings—namely, loving-kindness—that is associated with them; yet the Blessed One did not fully awaken to this as a factor of enlightenment.
"Venerable ones!

In fearlessness, the Blessed One has declared: 'I have attained manifest, perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena. Should any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else challenge me according to the Dharma or cause me to reflect upon these phenomena, there is not a single phenomenon regarding which I have not attained manifest, perfect enlightenment.'"

Regarding such right view, I have no basis for a "right view of self. Because that [basis] does not exist, I dwell in security, free from fear and dread; I declare myself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage and turn the Great Brahma-wheel, uttering the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.
"Venerable sir!
If that were so, would it not be difficult to avoid charging the Buddha with being ignorant? He replied:
"Venerable friend!
I do not find fault with the Buddha for being ignorant; rather, although the Blessed One has fully awakened to this, he has not proclaimed it.
Venerable friend!"
The Blessed One once said to the Venerable Ānanda:

"Ānanda, I have proclaimed the Dharma to you without interruption—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path."
"Ānanda! The Tathāgata has no 'teacher's fist' regarding the Dharma—that is, he does not conceal it out of fear that others might discover his own lack of understanding.
Venerable One!"
If that is so, does this not challenge the Buddha by implying he has a "teacher’s fist"?
He replied: "Venerable sir!"

I do not find fault with the Buddha for being ignorant, nor do I find fault with him for having a teacher’s fist; it is simply that although the World-Honored One has attained perfect enlightenment regarding this matter, he does not proclaim it.
"Venerable ones!
In the *Śāṇa-parṇopama Sūtra*, the Blessed One said:
