Regarding "not increasing by way of being an object, yet not not being a cause": this refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that, acting as causes, can bring about the maturation (vipāka) of this mind; specifically, those very latent dispositions do not take this [mind] as their object, or if they did, they have already been abandoned.

Regarding those that cannot act as causes and do not increase [by way of association]: this refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) which do not act as causes for the production of the maturation (*vipāka*) of this mind; specifically, those latent dispositions which do not take this [mind] as their object, or which, though taking it as an object, have already been abandoned; or those which take other objects; or other latent dispositions; or universal latent dispositions belonging to a different realm (*dhātu*).

"Not being non-causes and not being non-increasing" means that the various underlying tendencies (anuśaya) act as causes capable of producing the maturation (vipāka) of this mind, and those very same underlying tendencies take this [mind] as their object and have not yet been abandoned.
Just as the past mind associated with the desire realm that is to be abandoned through cultivation and is non-defiled, so it is for the future and present [minds].
Just as it is for the mind associated with the desire realm, so it is for the minds associated with the form realm and the formless realm.

The distinction here is that one should not say that minds bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or minds bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) possess the maturation (*vipāka*) of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
There are six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*), namely: eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
These six groups of consciousness are either wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, or unobscured-neutral.

Regarding the fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and outbursts associated with a wholesome eye-consciousness: how many should be said to act as causes and as conditions; and how many should be said to act as conditions but not as causes?

Regarding unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified eye-consciousness, among all its fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), how many should be said to function as causes (*hetu*) and as conditions (*pratyaya*), and how many should be said to function as conditions but not as causes?
As it is with visual consciousness, so it is with auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness.

Regarding wholesome visual consciousness, all fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) should be said to act as conditions (*pratyaya*) but not as causes (*hetu*).

Regarding unwholesome eye-consciousness, there are seven fetters (*saṃyojana*), seven bonds (*bandhana*), fifteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and twenty secondary afflictions and envelopments (*upakleśa-paryavasthāna*); these should be said to act as both causes and conditions. All remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding obscured-unspecified eye-consciousness, there are six fetters, six bonds, fourteen proclivities, and sixteen secondary afflictions and envelopments; it should be said that these act as causes and as conditions, while all remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Within unobscured-neutral visual consciousness—excluding that which is associated with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) or is a result of maturation (*vipāka*)—with respect to all other unobscured-neutral visual consciousnesses, it should be said that all fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent dispositions, secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) act as conditions (*pratyaya*) but do not act as causes (*hetu*).

Regarding the eye-consciousness that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), there are seven fetters (*saṃyojana*), seven bonds (*bandhana*), thirty-four latent dispositions, and thirty-nine secondary afflictions and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*); these should be said to act as both causes and conditions. As for all the remaining factors, they should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.
"Is it one mind? He replied, "No."

Regarding the visual consciousness that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), there are two fetters (*saṃyojana*), two bonds (*bandhana*), two latent tendencies, and seven secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*); these should be said to act as causes (*hetu*) and as conditions (*pratyaya*). As for all the remaining factors, they should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Just as the eye-consciousness that is the maturation of the latent tendency of false view abandoned through the vision of suffering is so described, the same applies to the eye-consciousness that is the maturation of the latent tendencies of views about grasping at views, grasping at precepts and observances, doubt, greed, hatred, and pride.

Regarding the visual consciousness that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of non-common ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering: it should be said to have one fetter (*saṃyojana*), one bond (*bandhana*), one latent tendency, and six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) as its entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), acting as both cause (*hetu*) and condition (*pratyaya); all remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the visual consciousness that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of false view abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), it should be said that there are two fetters (*saṃyojana*), two bonds (*bandhana*), two latent tendencies, and seven secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) that act as causes and act as conditions; for all the remaining factors, it should be said that they act as conditions but do not act as causes.

Just as the eye-consciousness that is the maturation of the latent tendency of false view abandoned through the vision of the origin is thus, so too are the eye-consciousnesses that are the maturations of the latent tendencies of adherence to views, doubt, greed, hatred, and pride.

Regarding the visual consciousness that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the latent tendency of uncommon ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), there is one fetter (*saṃyojana*), one bond (*bandhana*), one latent tendency, and six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) as active entanglements (*paryavasthāna*); these should be said to function as both causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*pratyaya*). As for all the remaining factors, they should be said to function as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the visual consciousness that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), it should be said that there are two fetters (*saṃyojana*), two bonds (*bandhana*), two latent tendencies, and seven secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) which act as causes and act as conditions; for all remaining factors, it should be said that they act as conditions but do not act as causes.

Just as the eye-consciousness that is the maturation of the latent tendency of false view abandoned through the vision of cessation is so, the eye-consciousness that is the maturation of the latent tendencies of views about grasping, doubt, greed, hatred, and pride is likewise.

Regarding the visual consciousness that is the maturation of the latent tendency of uncommon ignorance to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, there is one fetter, one bond, one latent tendency, and six secondary afflictions and envelopments; these should be said to act as causes and as conditions. As for all the remaining factors, they should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the visual consciousness that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are two fetters (*saṃyojana*), two bonds (*bandhana*), two latent tendencies, and seven secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*); it should be said that these act as causes and as conditions, while all remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Just as the retribution of eye-consciousness resulting from the latent tendencies of false view abandoned through the path of seeing is such, so too are the retributions of eye-consciousness resulting from the latent tendencies of adherence to views, adherence to precepts and observances, doubt, greed, hatred, and pride.

Regarding the eye-consciousness that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of uncommon ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing: it should be said to have one fetter (*saṃyojana*), one bond (*bandhana*), one latent tendency, and six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) as its entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), acting as both cause (*hetu*) and condition (*pratyaya*); all other factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the resultant eye-consciousness of the latent tendency of attachment abandoned through cultivation, it should be said that there are two fetters, two bonds, two latent tendencies, and seven secondary afflictions and entanglements that act as causes and act as conditions; for all others, it should be said that they act as conditions but do not act as causes.

Just as the eye-consciousness that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of greed abandoned by cultivation is so, the same applies to the eye-consciousness that is the maturation of the latent tendencies of hatred and pride.

Regarding the eye-consciousness that is the maturation of the latent tendency of non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) abandoned by cultivation, it should be said that one fetter (*saṃyojana*), one bond (*bandhana*), one latent tendency, and six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) act as its cause and its condition; all remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.
As it is with visual consciousness, so it is with auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses.
The distinction here is that one should not say that olfactory and gustatory consciousness possess the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) state.
Regarding the wholesome mental consciousness, all fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and envelopments should be said to function as conditions, but not as causes.

Regarding unwholesome mental consciousness, there are seven fetters (*saṃyojana*), seven bonds (*bandhana*), thirty-six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and forty-one secondary afflictions and entanglements (*upakleśa-paryavasthāna*); these should be said to act as both causes and conditions. All remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.
"Is it a single mind? He replied: "No."

Regarding the unwholesome mental consciousness abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), there are seven fetters (*saṃyojana*), seven bonds (*bandhana*), fourteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and nineteen secondary afflictions and envelopments (*upakleśa-paryavasthāna*); it should be said that these act as causes and as conditions, while all remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the unwholesome mental consciousness abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering], there are seven fetters (*saṃyojana*), seven bonds (*bandhana*), fourteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and nineteen secondary afflictions and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*); these should be said to act as both cause and condition. As for all the remaining factors, they should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the unwholesome mental consciousness to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, there are seven fetters (*saṃyojana*), seven bonds (*bandhana*), eighteen latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and twenty-three secondary afflictions and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*); it should be said that these act as both causes and conditions, while all remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the unwholesome mental consciousness to be abandoned by the path of seeing, there are seven fetters (*saṃyojana*), seven bonds (*bandhana*), nineteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and twenty-four secondary afflictions and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*); these should be said to act as both causes and conditions. All remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the unwholesome mental consciousness to be abandoned through cultivation, there are seven fetters (*saṃyojana*), seven bonds (*bandhana*), fifteen latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and twenty secondary afflictions and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*); these should be said to act as both causes and conditions. All remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-manovijñāna*), there are seven fetters (*saṃyojana*), seven bonds (*bandhana*), seventy-six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and eighty-one secondary afflictions and entanglements (*upakleśa-paryavasthāna*); these should be said to act as both causes and conditions. All remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.
"Is it one mind? He replied: "No."

Regarding the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are seven fetters (*saṃyojana*), seven bonds (*bandhana*), fourteen proclivities (*anuśaya*), and nineteen secondary afflictions and outbursts (*upakleśa-paryavasthāna*); it should be said that these act as causes and act as conditions. As for all remaining factors, they should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the form realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, there are six fetters, six bonds, thirteen underlying tendencies, and fifteen secondary afflictions and entanglements; it should be said that these act as both causes and conditions, while all remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), there are six fetters (*saṃyojana*), six bonds (*bandhana*), thirteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and fifteen secondary afflictions and entanglements (*upakleśa-paryavasthāna*); it should be said that these act as both causes and conditions, while all remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the form realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, there are six fetters, six bonds, seventeen underlying tendencies, and nineteen secondary afflictions and outbursts; it should be said that these act as causes and act as conditions, while all remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that is to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are six fetters (*saṃyojana*), six bonds (*bandhana*), eighteen latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and twenty secondary afflictions and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*). It should be said that these act as causes and act as conditions; all remaining factors should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.

Regarding the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there are six fetters (*saṃyojana*), six bonds (*bandhana*), fourteen latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and sixteen secondary afflictions and entanglements (*upakleśa-paryavasthāna*); it should be said that these act as causes and act as conditions. As for all remaining factors, they should be said to act as conditions but not as causes.
Regarding the non-obscured neutral mental consciousness, it should be said that all fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and envelopments act as conditions but not as causes.
There are six groups of consciousness, namely: eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
These six groups of consciousness are either wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, or unobscured-neutral.

Regarding all fetters, bonds, latent dispositions, secondary afflictions, and envelopments associated with wholesome visual consciousness, how many should be said to be associated and how many to be dissociated?

Regarding the eye-consciousness that is unwholesome, obscured-unneutral, or unobscured-unneutral: with how many fetters (saṃyojana), bonds (bandhana), latent dispositions (anuśaya), secondary afflictions (upakleśa), and envelopments (paryavasthāna) should it be said to be associated, and with how many dissociated?
As it is with visual consciousness, so it is with auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness.

Regarding wholesome visual consciousness, one should say that all fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are entirely dissociated from it.

Regarding unwholesome eye-consciousness, it should be said that the three fetters (saṃyojana), the three bonds (bandhana), the three latent dispositions (anuśaya), and the seven secondary afflictions (upakleśa) and envelopments (paryavasthāna) are associated with it.
Is this within a single moment of mind?
He said: Not so.

In an unwholesome eye-consciousness associated with greed, there are two fetters, two bonds, two underlying tendencies, and six secondary afflictions and entanglements; it should be said that these are associated.
Just as with unwholesome eye-consciousness associated with greed, so it is with unwholesome eye-consciousness associated with hatred.
Regarding obscured-unspecified eye-consciousness, it should be said that it is associated with two fetters, two bonds, two underlying tendencies, and four secondary afflictions and outbursts.
Regarding the non-obscured, neutral visual consciousness, it should be said that all fetters, bonds, latent dispositions, secondary afflictions, and envelopments are entirely dissociated from it.
As it is with visual consciousness, so it is with auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses.
The distinction here is that olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses should not be said to possess obscured-neutral [states].

Regarding wholesome mental consciousness, it should be said that all fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are entirely dissociated from it.

Regarding unwholesome mental consciousness, there are seven fetters, seven bonds, thirty-four latent tendencies, and thirty-nine secondary afflictions and envelopments; it should be said that these are associated with it.
"Is it a single mind? He replied: "No."

In an unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), there are two fetters (*saṃyojana*), two bonds (*bandhana*), and two latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
If in a state of wakefulness, it should be said that it is associated with six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*);
if in a state of sleep, a seventh [entanglement] is added.

Just as it is with the unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of false view abandoned through the vision of suffering, so it is also with the unwholesome mental consciousnesses associated with the latent tendencies of views about grasping at extremes, adherence to rules and observances, doubt, greed, hatred, and pride.

In the case of an unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, there is one fetter (*saṃyojana*), one bond (*bandhana*), and one latent tendency;
if in a state of wakefulness, it should be said to be associated with five secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*);
if in a state of sleep, the sixth, torpor (*middha*), is added.

In the case of an unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), there are two fetters (*saṃyojana*), two bonds (*bandhana*), and two latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
If it is in a state of wakefulness, it should be said that it is associated with six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*);
if it is in a state of sleep, a seventh [secondary affliction] is added.

Just as it is with the unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of false view abandoned through the vision of origin, so too it is with the unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendencies of adherence to views, doubt, greed, hatred, and pride.

In the case of an unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of uncommon ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyānuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*), there is one fetter (*saṃyojana*), one bond (*bandhana*), and one latent tendency (*anuśaya*).
If it is in a state of wakefulness, it should be said to be associated with the five secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) as active entanglements (*paryavasthāna*);
if it is in a state of sleep, a sixth [factor], sleep (*middha*), is added.
In the unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of false view to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, there are two fetters, two bonds, and two latent tendencies;
if in the state of wakefulness, it should be said that it is associated with six secondary afflictions as active outbursts;
if in the state of sleep, the seventh [secondary affliction] increases.

Just as it is with the unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of false view abandoned through the vision of cessation, so it is also with the unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendencies of views-attachment, doubt, greed, hatred, and pride.

In relation to the unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of uncommon ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), there is one fetter (*saṃyojana*), one bond (*bandhana*), and one latent tendency (*anuśaya*).
If it is in a state of wakefulness, it should be said to be associated with the five secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) as active entanglements (*paryavasthāna*);
if it is in a state of sleep, the sixth, torpor (*middha*), is added.

In the unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are two fetters (*saṃyojana*), two bonds (*bandhana*), and two latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
If it is in a state of wakefulness, one should say that it is associated with six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) as active entanglements (*paryavasthāna*);
if it is in a state of sleep, a seventh [secondary affliction] is added.

Just as it is with the unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing, so it is also with the unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendencies of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), hatred (*pratigha*), and pride (*māna*).

In the case of unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of non-shared ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā-anuśaya*) which is to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*), there is one fetter (*saṃyojana*), one bond (*bandhana*), and one latent tendency (*anuśaya*).
If it is in a state of wakefulness, it should be said to be associated with the five secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) as active obsessions (*paryavasthāna*);
if it is in a state of sleep, the sixth, torpor (*middha*), is added.
In the case of unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of attachment to be abandoned through cultivation, there are two fetters, two bonds, and two latent tendencies;
if in a state of wakefulness, it should be said that it is associated with the six secondary afflictions as active entanglements;
if in a state of sleep, a seventh, namely torpor, is added.

Just as there is an unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of greed (*rāgānuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation, so it is for unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendencies of hostility (*pratigha*) and pride (*māna*).

Regarding the unwholesome mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of non-specific ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation, there is one fetter (*saṃyojana*), one bond (*bandhana*), and one latent tendency;
if in the state of awakening, it should be said that it is associated with the five secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).
If one is in the state of sleep, the sixth [type of] torpor (*middha*) increases.

Regarding the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mental consciousness, it should be said that six fetters (*saṃyojana*), six bonds (*bandhana*), sixty-five latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and sixty-eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are associated with it.
"Is it with a single mind? He replied: "No."

In the case of the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) bound to the desire realm, there are two fetters (saṃyojana), two bonds (bandhana), and two latent dispositions (anuśaya);
if in a state of wakefulness, it should be said that four secondary afflictions (upakleśa) and entanglements (paryavasthāna) are associated;
if in a state of sleep, a fifth, sleep (middha), is added.

Just as it is with the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) bound to the desire realm, so it is also with the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).

In the case of the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) bound to the realm of form, it should be said that it is associated with two fetters, two bonds, two latent tendencies, and four secondary afflictions and outbursts.

Just as the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) bound to the realm of form is so described, the same applies to the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendencies of the view of extremes, false views, grasping at views, grasping at precepts and observances, doubt, greed, and pride, which are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.

In the case of the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of uncommon ignorance abandoned through the vision of suffering within the realm of form, there is one fetter, one bond, one latent tendency, and three secondary afflictions and entanglements; it should be said that these are associated.

In the case of the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of false view abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) which is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), it should be said that there are two fetters (*saṃyojana*), two bonds (*bandhana*), two latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and four secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) that are associated with it.

Just as there is an obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of false view abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) which is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), so too it is for the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendencies of adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), and pride (*māna*).

In the case of the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of uncommon ignorance abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), there is one fetter (*saṃyojana*), one bond (*bandhana*), one latent tendency (*anuśaya*), and three secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*); it should be said that these are associated (*saṃprayukta*).

In the case of the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of false view to be abandoned by the vision of cessation within the realm of form, it should be said that there are two fetters, two bonds, two latent tendencies, and four secondary afflictions and envelopments that are associated with it.

Just as there is an obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of false view to be abandoned by the vision of cessation within the realm of form, so too is it for the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendencies of grasping at views, doubt, greed, and pride.

In relation to the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of uncommon ignorance—which is abandoned through the vision of cessation and bound to the form realm—one should say that there is one fetter, one bond, one latent tendency, and three secondary afflictions and envelopments in association.

In the case of the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of false view abandoned through the path of vision within the realm of form, it should be said that there are two fetters, two bonds, two latent tendencies, and four secondary afflictions and envelopments with which it is associated.

Just as there is a defiled-neutral mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of false view that is abandoned by the path of seeing and bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), so too is it for the defiled-neutral mental consciousness associated with the latent tendencies of adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), and pride (*māna*).

In the case of the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of uncommon ignorance abandoned by the path of seeing within the realm of form, there is one fetter, one bond, one latent tendency, and three secondary afflictions and envelopments; it should be said that these are associated.

In the case of the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of greed to be abandoned through cultivation within the realm of form, it should be said that it is associated with two fetters, two bonds, two latent tendencies, and four secondary afflictions and outbursts.

Just as there is a concealing-neutral mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of greed to be abandoned through cultivation that is tied to the realm of form, so too is there a concealing-neutral mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of pride.

In the case of the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) mental consciousness associated with the latent tendency of non-shared ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā-anuśaya), which is abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) and bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), there is one fetter (saṃyojana), one bond (bandhana), one latent tendency (anuśaya), and three secondary afflictions (upakleśa) and envelopments (paryavasthāna); it should be said that these are associated.

As it is with the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), so it is with the obscured-unspecified mental consciousness associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding the unobscured-unspecified mental consciousness, one should say that all fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are entirely dissociated from it.
The *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda School,
Volume Five. The *Abhidharma-vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra*,
composed by the Arhat Devaśarman, Volume Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree:
Questions concerning the past and so forth; questions concerning the wholesome and so forth; Questions concerning the two sets of four minds that have understood blue and so forth;
Questions concerning the twelve minds, which are of two kinds; Questions concerning the fifteen minds, which are of five kinds.
There are six groups of consciousness, namely: eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
These six groups of consciousness are either past, future, or present.
Regarding past eye-consciousness: is there that which has an object in the past but not in the future or the present?
Is there that which has an object in the future but not in the past or the present?
Is there that which has an object in the present but not in the past or the future?
Is there that which has an object in the past and the present, but not in the future?
Is there that which has an object in the future and the present, but not in the past?
Is there that which has an object in the past and the future, but not in the present?
Is there an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for the past, future, and present?
As it is with past eye-consciousness, so it is with future and present eye-consciousness.
As it is with eye-consciousness, so it is with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
All past visual consciousnesses take only the past as their object; other [temporal] categories are not obtainable.
Future visual consciousness may take the past as its object, or the future, or the present.
All present visual consciousnesses take only the present as their object; other categories are not applicable.
As it is with visual consciousness, so it is with auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses.
The mental consciousnesses of the past, future, and present should all be said to take all phenomena as their objects.
There are six groups of consciousness, namely: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mental consciousness.
Thus, these six groups of consciousness are either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Regarding wholesome visual consciousness: is there that which is associated with the wholesome, yet not unwholesome or indeterminate?
Are there objects of condition that are unwholesome but neither wholesome nor indeterminate?
Are there objects of condition that are indeterminate but neither wholesome nor unwholesome?
Are there objects of condition that are both wholesome and unwholesome but not indeterminate?
Are there conditioned phenomena that are wholesome or indeterminate, but not unwholesome?
Are there conditioned phenomena that are unwholesome or indeterminate, but not wholesome?
Are there conditioned phenomena that are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate?
As it is with wholesome eye-consciousness, so it is with unwholesome and indeterminate eye-consciousness.
As it is with eye-consciousness, so it is with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
Wholesome eye-consciousness may take a wholesome object, an unwholesome object, or an indeterminate object.
Unwholesome eye-consciousness takes as its object that which is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Indeterminate eye-consciousness takes as its object that which is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
As it is with visual consciousness, so it is with auditory and mental consciousness.
Regarding the remaining three groups of consciousness—whether they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—all should be said to take only the indeterminate as their object.
There are six groups of consciousness, namely: eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
Eye-consciousness can only discern blue color; it cannot discern that "this is blue."
The mental consciousness can also discern blue color; however, as long as it has not yet discerned its name, it cannot discern that "this is blue.
Once it can discern its name, at that time it can both discern the blue color and discern that "this is blue."
As it is with the color blue, so it is with yellow, red, white, and other colors.
Ear-consciousness can only discern sound; it cannot discern that "this is sound.
Mental consciousness also discerns sound, yet as long as it has not yet discerned its name, it cannot discern that "this is sound."
If one can discern its name, at that time one can also discern the sound and discern, "This is a sound.
Olfactory consciousness can only discern fragrance; it cannot discern, "This is fragrance."
The mental consciousness can also discern odors; however, as long as it has not yet discerned their names, it cannot discern that "this is an odor.
Once it can discern their names, at that time it can both discern the odor and discern that "this is an odor."
The gustatory consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*) can only discern taste; it cannot discern that "this is taste.
The mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) can also discern taste, yet as long as it has not yet discerned its name, it cannot discern that "this is taste";
once it can discern its name, at that time it can both discern the taste and discern that "this is taste."
The body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) can only discern touch; it cannot discern that "this is touch.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can also discern touch, yet as long as it has not yet discerned its name, it cannot discern that "this is touch";
once it can discern its name, at that time it can both discern touch and discern that "this is touch."

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is also able to discern all phenomena (*dharma*), namely: either grasping them as a self (*ātman*), or grasping them as belonging to a self (*ātmīya*); or grasping them as annihilated (*uccheda*), or grasping them as permanent (*śāśvata*); or denying causes (*ahetuka*), or denying actions (*akriyā*); or further deprecating [them]; or grasping them as venerable, or grasping them as superior, or grasping them as supreme, or grasping them as foremost; or grasping them as pure, or grasping them as liberation, or grasping them as transcendence; or being deluded, or doubting, or hesitating; or being attached, or resentful, or conceited, or ignorant; or regarding them as coarse, or suffering, or obstructive; or regarding them as calm, or sublime, or detached; or regarding them as like a disease, or like an abscess, or like an arrow, or like an affliction; or regarding them as impermanent, or suffering, or empty, or non-self.

If one regards the cause as the cause, as origination, as arising, and as condition; if one regards cessation as cessation, as tranquility, as excellence, and as liberation; and if one regards the path as the path, as suchness, as practice, and as departure.

Whether there is a cause, whether there is an origination, whether there is such a basis, or whether there is such a matter; whether it is a discernment induced by what is reasoned, or a discernment induced by what is unreasoned, or a discernment induced by what is neither reasoned nor unreasoned.

There are four kinds of mind: namely, mind bound to the desire realm, mind bound to the form realm, mind bound to the formless realm, and unbound mind.
Regarding those minds bound to the desire realm that can discern phenomena bound to the desire realm: how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in association with them?
Regarding those [minds] that can discern other phenomena: how many underlying tendencies increase in association with them?
Furthermore, regarding those unconditioned minds that can discern unconditioned phenomena, how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase therein?
And regarding those [minds] that can discern all other remaining phenomena, how many underlying tendencies increase therein?

When any mind bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-citta*) can discern phenomena bound to the desire realm, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with the entanglements of desire (*kāma-kaṣāya*) that take outflows as their object (*sāsrava-ālambana*) increase therein.

When any mind bound to the desire realm can discern phenomena bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*), the latent dispositions belonging to the three categories (*tri-koṭi-anuśaya*) associated with the entanglements of desire increase therein.

When any mind bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) discerns phenomena bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three categories of the desire-entanglements (*kāma-bandhana*) increase therein.

When any mind bound to the desire realm discerns unbound phenomena (*apratisaṃyukta*), the latent dispositions of the three categories of the desire-entanglements as well as the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) increase therein.

When any mind bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) can discern phenomena bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three categories of the desire-entanglements (*kāma-vyāpāda*) increase therein.

If one can discern other dharmas, then within this [state], the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) bound by desire and the latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation are those that increase as latencies.

If a mind bound to the realm of form can discern dharmas bound to the realm of form, then within this [state], the latent dispositions bound by form and having outflows as their object are those that increase as latencies.

When any mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) discerns phenomena bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three categories belonging to the form-realm fetters (*rūparāga-saṃyojana*) increase therein.

When any mind bound to the form realm discerns phenomena that are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*), the latent dispositions of the three categories belonging to the form-realm fetters as well as the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) increase therein.

When a mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) is able to discern phenomena bound to the form realm or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three categories belonging to the fetters of the form realm (*rūparāga-saṃyojana*) increase therein.

If one can discern other phenomena, among these, the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bound by the form realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation are those that increase as latencies.

Regarding all minds associated with the formless realm that can discern phenomena associated with the formless realm, the latent dispositions associated with the formless realm that take contaminated objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) are those that increase as latencies.

When any mind bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) can discern phenomena that are not so bound, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three categories of formless fetters (*ārūpyasaṃyojana*) and the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatragānuśaya*) increase in accordance with it.

If one can discern other dharmas, within these there are the omnipresent latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the formless realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation which increase as latent tendencies.
If the various unconditioned minds can discern unconditioned phenomena, there are no underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) therein that increase through association.
If they can discern other remaining phenomena, there likewise are no underlying tendencies therein that increase through association.

Is there one who can discern phenomena associated with the desire realm, phenomena associated with the form realm, phenomena associated with the formless realm, and phenomena that are unassociated?
As it is with a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, so it is even for a mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Can a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm discern phenomena bound to the desire realm?

It is said: one is able to discern. That is to say, whether it be coarse, or suffering, or an obstruction; or like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, or like an affliction; or impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; or regarding the cause as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; or that which has a cause, that which has an origination, that for which there is a possibility, or that for which there is a fact; or that which is discerned in accordance with reality. This is what is meant by discernment.
Is it possible to discern phenomena associated with the realm of form?
He replied:
"It is possible to discern them."

That is to say: [discerning] whether something is coarse, painful, or an obstacle; whether it is calm, sublime, or renounced; whether it is like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, or like an affliction; whether it is impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; or regarding causes as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; or that there is a cause, that there is an origination, that there is such a possibility, or that there is such a fact—discerning these in accordance with reality.
Is it possible to discern phenomena associated with the formless realm?
He replied:
It is possible to discern them.

That is to say: whether it be coarse, painful, or an obstacle; whether it be calm, sublime, or renounced; whether it be like a disease, like an ulcer, like an arrow, or like an affliction; whether it be impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; whether regarding causes as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; whether there is a cause, an origination, a possibility, or a factual occurrence; or whatever is discriminated in accordance with reality.
Is it possible to discern phenomena that are unconditioned?

It is possible to discern them.

That is to say: regarding cessation, one discerns it as cessation, as peace, as sublime, and as renunciation; regarding the path, one discerns it as the path, as suchness, as practice, and as deliverance; or [one discerns] impermanence, emptiness, or non-self; or that there is a cause, that there is an origination, that there is this possibility, or that there is this fact—discerning in accordance with what is drawn forth by correct reasoning.

Answer: It is possible to discern them.

Can unwholesome states of mind discern phenomena associated with the desire realm?
Answer: They can discern them.

That is to say: either denying the cause, or denying the action, or deprecating it; or clinging to it as venerable, or clinging to it as superior, or clinging to it as excellent, or clinging to it as foremost; or clinging to it as pure, or clinging to it as liberation, or clinging to it as deliverance; or being confused, doubtful, or hesitant; or being characterized by greed, hatred, pride, or delusion; or any discernment that is improperly induced.
Is it possible to discern phenomena associated with the realm of form?
He replied:
It is possible to discern them.

That is to say: either denying the cause, or denying the action, or deprecating it; or grasping at it as venerable, or grasping at it as superior, or grasping at it as excellent, or grasping at it as foremost; or grasping at it as pure, or grasping at it as liberation, or grasping at it as renunciation; or being confused, or doubtful, or hesitant; or lacking wisdom, or being in darkness, or being deluded; or any discernment that is not brought about by correct reasoning.
Is it possible to discern phenomena associated with the formless realm?
He replied:
"It is possible to discern them."

That is to say: either denying the cause, or denying the action, or deprecating it; or grasping it as venerable, or grasping it as superior, or grasping it as preeminent, or grasping it as foremost; or grasping it as pure, or grasping it as liberation, or grasping it as transcendence; or whatever confusion, doubt, or hesitation; or lack of knowledge, obscurity, or delusion; or any discernment induced by improper mental application.
Is there the ability to discern phenomena that are unconditioned? He replied: "There is."
That is to say: if there is the denial of cessation, or the denial of the path; if there is discernment accompanied by doubt, or discernment accompanied by delusion;
or if there is discernment induced by improper mental application—can such [discernment] discern phenomena associated with the form realm or the formless realm?
It is said: it is the act of discerning. That is to say:

either denying the cause, or denying the action, or further deprecating [it]; or grasping [it] as venerable, or grasping it as superior, or grasping it as supreme, or grasping it as foremost; or grasping it as pure, or grasping it as liberation, or grasping it as transcendence; or being deluded, or doubting, or hesitating; or lacking wisdom, or being in darkness, or being ignorant; or any discernment induced by what is not in accordance with reality.
Thus it is distinguished, while others are not so distinguished.
Can a mind that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and bound to the desire realm distinguish phenomena bound to the desire realm?
It is said:
It is the act of discerning;

that is to say, either apprehending it as a self, or apprehending it as belonging to a self, or apprehending it as annihilated, or apprehending it as eternal—such being a discernment induced by what is not in accordance with reality.
Thus it is discerned, while other things are not discerned.
Can those unobscured-neutral minds associated with the desire realm discern phenomena associated with the desire realm?
It is said: Yes.
It is capable of discerning;
that is to say, it discerns that which is neither induced by correct reasoning nor induced by incorrect reasoning.
It discerns in this manner, whereas others do not discern.

Uddāna Verse: The Second Part of the Fourth Aggregate on the Object-condition (ālambanapratyaya). Can a wholesome mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) discern phenomena bound to the form realm?
It is said: one is able to discern.

That is to say, whether it be coarse, suffering, or an obstruction; or calm, sublime, or renunciation; or like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, or like an affliction; or impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; or regarding causes as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; or that there is a cause, that there is an origination, that there is such a possibility, or that there is such a fact—one discerns these as they are led by correct reasoning.
"Is there the ability to discern phenomena associated with the desire realm?
He replied,
"There is the ability to discern them."

That is to say: whether it be coarse, or painful, or an obstruction; or like a disease, like an abscess, or like an arrow, or a source of affliction and harm; or impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; or regarding the cause as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; or that which has a cause, that which has an origination, that for which there is a possibility, or that for which there is a reality; or that which is discerned in accordance with reason.
Is it possible to discern phenomena associated with the formless realm? One says: it is possible to discern them. That is to say:

as coarse, as suffering, as an obstruction; or as calm, as sublime, as renunciation; or as like a disease, as like an ulcer, as like an arrow, as affliction; or as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, as non-self; or regarding the cause, as cause, as origin, as arising, as condition; or as having a cause, as having an origination, as there being such a possibility, as there being such a fact; or as discerned in accordance with reality.
Is it possible to discern phenomena that are unconditioned?
He replied:
It is possible to discern them.

That is to say: regarding cessation, one discerns it as cessation, as peace, as excellence, and as renunciation; regarding the path, one discerns it as the path, as suchness, as practice, and as emergence; or [discerns] impermanence, suffering, emptiness, or non-self; or that there is a cause, that there is an arising, that there is this possibility, or that there is this fact; or that which is discerned in accordance with reality.
Is it possible to discern phenomena associated with the desire realm and phenomena associated with the form realm?
Answer: It is possible to discern them.

Answer: It is possible to discern them.

Answer: It is possible to discern them.

That is to say: whether it be impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; whether there be a cause, an arising, a possibility, or a factual occurrence; or whatever is discerned as being drawn forth in accordance with reality.
Can a mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that is obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) discern phenomena associated with the form realm?

It is said: it can discern them. That is to say: either grasping [them] as a self, or grasping [them] as belonging to a self; or grasping [them] as annihilated, or grasping [them] as permanent; or denying causes, or denying actions; or further deprecating [them]; or grasping [them] as venerable, or grasping [them] as superior, or grasping [them] as supreme, or grasping [them] as foremost; or grasping [them] as pure, or grasping [them] as liberation, or grasping [them] as renunciation; whether through delusion, doubt, or hesitation; or through greed, pride, or ignorance; or discerning [them] as induced by improper mental application (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
Is it possible to discern phenomena associated with the formless realm?
He replied:
It is possible to discern them.

That is to say: either denying the cause, or denying the action, or deprecating it; or grasping at it as venerable, or grasping at it as superior, or grasping at it as excellent, or grasping at it as foremost; or grasping at it as pure, or grasping at it as liberation, or grasping at it as transcendence; or whatever confusion, doubt, or hesitation there may be; or lack of knowledge, darkness, or delusion; or any discernment that is not brought about by correct reasoning.
Is there that which can cognize phenomena not bound [to any realm]?
He replied:
"It can cognize them."

That is to say: if there is a denial of cessation, or a denial of the path; if there is discernment accompanied by doubt, or discernment accompanied by delusion; or if there is discernment induced by improper mental application.
Is it possible to discern phenomena pertaining to the form realm or the formless realm?

It is said: it is the discernment that is capable of such [erroneous] apprehension. That is to say: either denying the cause, or denying the action, or further deprecating [the truth], or grasping [it] as venerable, or grasping it as superior, or grasping it as supreme, or grasping it as foremost, or grasping it as pure, or grasping it as liberation, or grasping it as transcendence; or being deluded, or doubtful, or hesitant; or lacking wisdom, or being in darkness, or being ignorant; or any discernment induced by improper mental application.
Thus it is distinguished, while others are not so distinguished.
Can a mind that is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), unobscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), distinguish phenomena bound to the form realm?
It is said:
It is capable of discerning; that is to say, it is a discernment that is neither induced by correct reasoning nor induced by incorrect reasoning.
Is there anything capable of discerning phenomena associated with the desire realm?
He replied:
It is capable of discerning; that is to say, it discerns neither what is induced by correct reasoning nor what is induced by incorrect reasoning.
Such discernment is not shared by other [minds].
Can those wholesome minds associated with the formless realm discern phenomena associated with the formless realm?

It is said: It is capable of discerning. That is to say, it discerns whether something is coarse, suffering, or an obstacle; or whether it is calm, sublime, or renounced; or whether it is like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, or a source of affliction and harm; or whether it is impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; or regarding its cause, it discerns it as a cause, as an origin, as arising, or as a condition; or that there is a cause, there is an origination, there is such a possibility, or there is such a fact; or it discerns in accordance with what is drawn forth by correct reasoning.
Is it possible to discern phenomena associated with the realm of form?
He replied:
It is possible to discern them.
That is to say: whether it be coarse, or painful, or an obstruction, or that which is discerned in accordance with reason—can there be that which discerns phenomena not bound [to the realms]?
He replied:

It is the discernment that is capable of such recognition: namely, regarding cessation as cessation, as peace, as excellence, and as liberation; regarding the path as the path, as suchness, as practice, and as emergence; or regarding [phenomena] as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self; or as having a cause, as having an origin, as having a basis, and as having a factual occurrence; or as being discerned in accordance with reality.
Is it possible to discern phenomena associated with the formless realm as well as those that are unconditioned?
He replied:
It is possible to discern them.

That is to say: whether it be impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; whether there is a cause, an origination, a possibility, or a factual occurrence; or whatever is discerned as being led by correct reasoning.
Having distinguished it in this way, others do not distinguish it.
Can those minds associated with the formless realm that are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) distinguish phenomena associated with the formless realm?
It is said: it is that which is capable of discerning.

That is to say, it may be grasped as a self, or as belonging to a self, or as annihilated, or as eternal; or it may be the denial of cause, or the denial of action; or it may be a deprecation; or it may be grasped as venerable, or as superior, or as excellent, or as foremost; or it may be grasped as pure, or as liberation, or as transcendence; or it may be confusion, or doubt, or hesitation; or it may be greed, or pride, or delusion—namely, that discernment which is induced by what is not in accordance with reality.
Is there the ability to discern phenomena that are not bound?
He replied:
"There is the ability to discern them."

That is to say: if there is a denial of cessation, or a denial of the path, or discernment accompanied by doubt, or delusion, or discernment induced by improper reflection—such discernment is [discernment], while other forms of discernment are not.
Can the various unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm discern phenomena associated with the formless realm?
It is said that they can discern them; specifically, this refers to discerning [phenomena] that are neither induced by correct reasoning nor induced by incorrect reasoning.
Thus they are discerned, while others are not.
Can the minds of those in training discern phenomena that are unconditioned?
It is said: they can discern them.

That is to say: regarding cessation, one perceives it as cessation, as peace, as excellence, and as renunciation; regarding the path, one perceives it as the path, as suchness, as practice, and as emergence; and whether there is a cause, an origination, a possibility, or a factual occurrence, one discriminates in accordance with reality.
Is there the discernment of phenomena associated with the desire realm?

It is said: there is discernment. That is to say: as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, or as non-self; regarding the cause as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; as having a cause, as having an origination, as having this possibility, or as having this reality; and as discerned in accordance with reason.
Is it possible to discern phenomena associated with the realm of form?
He replied:
It is possible to discern them.

That is to say: whether it be impermanence, suffering, emptiness, or non-self; or regarding causes as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; or where there is a cause, where there is an origination, where there is such a possibility, or where there is such a fact; or whatever is discerned in accordance with reality.
Is it possible to discern phenomena associated with the formless realm?
He replied:
"It is possible to discern them."

That is to say: whether it be impermanence, suffering, emptiness, or non-self; or regarding causes as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; or where there is a cause, where there is an origination, where there is such a possibility, or where there is such a fact; or whatever is discerned in accordance with reality.
Is it possible to discern phenomena associated with the form realm and the formless realm?
He replied:
It is possible to discern them.

That is to say: whether it be impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; whether regarding causes as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; whether there is a cause, or an origination, or such a possibility, or such a fact; or whatever is discerned in accordance with reality.
Thus they are discerned, while others are not so discerned.
As it is with the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*), so it is with the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). There are twelve minds, namely:

the wholesome mind, the unwholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the desire realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the formless realm; and the mind of one in training and the mind of one beyond training.
Regarding wholesome minds bound to the desire realm that can discern phenomena bound to the desire realm: how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase therein?
Regarding those same minds that can discern other phenomena: how many underlying tendencies increase therein?

Furthermore, regarding the minds of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), if they can discern phenomena that are not bound (*apratisaṃyukta*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase therein?
And if they can discern all other remaining phenomena, how many underlying tendencies increase therein?

When any wholesome mind bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) discerns phenomena bound to the desire realm, the pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) associated with the entanglements of desire (*kāma-kaṣāya*) and the underlying tendencies to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are those that increase in accordance with it.

If one can discern other dharmas as well, within those too there are pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the desire realm and latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation which increase in accordance [with the object].

If any unwholesome mind is able to discern phenomena pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), then among these, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the entanglements of desire (*kāma-kaṣāya*) that have outflow as their object (*sāsrava-ālambana*) are those that increase in accordance with it.

If it is able to discern phenomena pertaining to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), then among these, the latent tendencies belonging to both categories associated with the entanglements of desire are those that increase in accordance with it.

If one can discern phenomena associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the two categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bound by desire (*kāmacaryā*) are those that increase therein.

If one can discern unconditioned phenomena (*apratisaṃyukta*), the two categories of latent dispositions bound by desire as well as the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) are those that increase therein.

If one can discern phenomena associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the two classes of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bound by desire (*kāmacaryā*) are those that increase therein.

Regarding all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the desire realm, they can only discern phenomena associated with the desire realm; herein, all latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) bound by desire, as well as the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), are those that increase therein.

The various unobscured-neutral minds bound to the desire realm can only discern phenomena bound to the desire realm; herein, the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the entanglements of desire and those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation are the factors that increase as concomitants.

When any wholesome mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) discerns phenomena bound to the form realm, the pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) associated with the fetters of the form realm (*rūparāga-bandhana*) and those latent dispositions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase therein through association.

If one can discern other dharmas, among them, the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) bound by the form realm and those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation are the ones that increase as underlying tendencies.

Regarding any obscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm that can discern dharmas bound to the form realm, among them, the latent dispositions with outflows directed toward objects are the ones that increase as underlying tendencies.

If one can discern phenomena associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), therein the two categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bound by the form-aggregate (*rūpa-gredha*) increase.

If one can discern unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*) phenomena, therein the two categories of latent dispositions bound by the form-aggregate as well as the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) increase.

If one can discern phenomena associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), among these there are the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two categories belonging to the fetters of the form realm that increase in accordance [with them].

Regarding all unobscured-neutral minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the form realm that can discern phenomena associated with the form realm, among these there are the pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) and the latent tendencies to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*) belonging to the fetters of the form realm that increase in accordance [with them].

If one can discern other phenomena, among them, the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bound to the form realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation are the latent dispositions that increase therein.

Regarding wholesome minds bound to the formless realm that can discern phenomena bound to the formless realm, among them, the pervasive latent dispositions bound to the formless realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation are the latent dispositions that increase therein.

If one is able to discern other dharmas, within these there are the omnipresent latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bound to the formless realm and those latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation which increase as accompanying tendencies.

Regarding those obscured-unspecified minds bound to the formless realm that can discern phenomena bound to the formless realm, within these, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the fetters of the formless realm that take outflows as their object increase in accordance [with the mind].

If one can discern dharmas that are not bound [to any realm], within this there are the two categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm’s fetters (*rūpāvacara-saṃyojana*) and the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) which increase through association.

Regarding all unobscured-neutral minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the formless realm, they can only discern dharmas bound to the formless realm; within these, there are the universal latent dispositions of the formless realm’s fetters and the latent dispositions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-anuśaya*) which increase through association.
If the various minds in training are able to discern phenomena that are not bound [to the realms], there are no underlying tendencies (anuśaya) therein that can increase through association.
If they are able to discern other remaining phenomena, there likewise are no underlying tendencies therein that can increase through association.
As it is with the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*), so it is with the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

There are ten types of minds: namely, the wholesome mind, unwholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and unobscured-neutral mind bound to the desire realm; the wholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and unobscured-neutral mind bound to the form realm; and the wholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and unobscured-neutral mind bound to the formless realm.

Regarding all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-citta*): if their substance (*svabhāva*) has not been abandoned, have their objects (*ālambana*) also not been abandoned?
Conversely, if their objects have not been abandoned, has their substance also not been abandoned?

This continues up to all non-obscured neutral minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): if their substance has not been abandoned, have their objects also not been abandoned?
If the object of focus (*ālambana*) has not been abandoned, has its substance (*svabhāva*) also not been abandoned?
Regarding all wholesome minds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), if their substance has not been abandoned, has their object also not been abandoned?

There are cases where both the substance and the object have not been abandoned; cases where the substance has not been abandoned but the object has already been abandoned; cases where the substance has not been abandoned and the object is both already abandoned and not yet abandoned; and cases where the substance has not been abandoned, yet it cannot be distinguished whether the object of this mind has been abandoned or not.

Regarding those whose substance is not yet severed and whose objects of perception are not yet severed: this refers to all *pudgalas* bound by all fetters, whose wholesome minds associated with the desire realm take as their objects those things bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm, those bound to the formless realm; those bound to both the desire and form realms; those bound to both the desire and formless realms; those bound to both the form and formless realms; and those bound to all three—the desire, form, and formless realms.

If one has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by seeing origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those things to be abandoned by seeing cessation, by seeing the path, and by cultivation.

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those things to be abandoned by seeing the path and by cultivation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, then those wholesome minds bound to the desire realm that take as their object what is to be abandoned by cultivation are said to have "the entity not yet abandoned and the object not yet abandoned."

Regarding those whose substance has not been severed but whose objects have already been severed: this refers to one who has not yet abandoned the craving of the desire realm, for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; their various wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origination.

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origination, and cessation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire, and his wholesome minds bound to the realm of desire take as their objects those things to be abandoned by insight—
this is called "the entity is not abandoned, but the object has been abandoned."

Regarding those whose substance has not been severed, while their objects have been severed or their objects have not yet been severed: this refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; their various wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as what is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds associated with the desire realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds associated with the desire realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

If one observes that a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision, but has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire, possesses wholesome minds bound to the realm of desire that take as their objects states to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation:
this is called "the entity is not yet abandoned while the object is already abandoned, and the object is also not yet abandoned."

Regarding the statement that "when its substance has not been severed, one cannot distinguish whether the object of this mind has been severed or not yet severed," this refers to the wholesome minds bound to the desire realm belonging to individuals who are still bound by all fetters; these take as their objects that which is not to be severed.

If one has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the realm of desire take as their object that which is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).

When the knowledge of origin has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the realm of desire take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.

When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.

Furthermore, for a disciple of the Blessed One who is perfected in vision but has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.
This is called "the substance not yet severed," such that one cannot distinguish whether the object of this mind has been severed or not.
Even if the object has not been severed, is its substance not yet severed?
