When the subsequent knowledge of origin (samudaya-anvaya-jñāna) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta) belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
The obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the path of seeing takes as its object that which is abandoned through the path of seeing;
the obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through cultivation takes as its object that which is abandoned through cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing take as their object those [defilements] to be abandoned by the path of seeing.
The obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) takes that which is to be abandoned by cultivation as its object.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision (*dṛṣṭi-sampanna*) has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), then all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation take that which is to be abandoned by cultivation as their object.
This is called "the entity is not yet abandoned and the object is not yet abandoned.

Regarding that which has an entity not yet abandoned but an object already abandoned: this refers to a mind that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), which takes as its object that which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*)—at a time when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.
This is called "the entity is not yet abandoned while the object has been abandoned.

Regarding that which is "the entity is not yet abandoned while the object has been abandoned" as well as "the object is not yet abandoned": it refers to those minds associated with the formless realm that are obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and to be abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), occurring when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, and which take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
This is called "the entity is not yet abandoned while the object is already abandoned, as well as the object is not yet abandoned.

Regarding that which has an entity not yet abandoned for which it is impossible to distinguish whether the mind’s object is already abandoned or not yet abandoned: this refers to the obscured-unspecified minds bound to the formless realm belonging to individuals who are fully fettered, which take as their objects that which is not to be abandoned.

For one who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, and for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta) associated with the formless realm take as their object that which is not to be abandoned (aprahātavya).

Having already abandoned craving for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), while the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the formless realm take as their object that which is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of suffering has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the formless realm take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path take as their object that which is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, those obscured-neutral minds of the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.
This is called "the substance not yet severed, such that it cannot be distinguished whether the object-condition of this mind has been severed or not.
Furthermore, if the object-condition has not been severed, is its substance also not yet severed?

Either the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is not abandoned while its substance (*svabhāva*) is not abandoned; or the object of cognition is not abandoned while its substance has already been abandoned; or both the object of cognition and the object of cognition that has been abandoned have their substance not yet abandoned; or both the object of cognition and the object of cognition that has been abandoned have their substance already abandoned.

Regarding those whose objects of perception have not been abandoned and whose essential nature has not been abandoned: this refers to the obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm belonging to individuals who are bound by all fetters, which take as their object that which is associated with the formless realm.

Having already abandoned craving for the desire realm but not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, and while the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (nivṛta-avyākṛta-citta) associated with the formless realm take that which is associated with the formless realm as their object.

Having already become detached from the craving of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), but before the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) take as their object those things associated with the formless realm.

Once the subsequent knowledge of suffering has arisen, but before the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of origin take as their object those things to be abandoned by the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of the origin conditions that which is abandoned through the vision of the origin;
the obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of cessation conditions that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation.
The obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the path of seeing takes as its object that which is abandoned through the path of seeing;
the obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through cultivation takes as its object that which is abandoned through cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (samudayānvaya-jñāna) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodhānvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta) associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
The obscured-unspecified mind abandoned by the path of seeing takes as its object that which is abandoned by the path of seeing;
the obscured-unspecified mind abandoned by the path of cultivation takes as its object that which is abandoned by the path of cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing take as their object those factors to be abandoned by the path of seeing.
The obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) takes that which is to be abandoned by cultivation as its object.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision (*dṛṣṭi-paripūrṇa*) has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), then all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation take that which is to be abandoned by cultivation as their object.
This is called "the object of cognition is not abandoned and its substance is not abandoned.

Regarding "the object of cognition is not abandoned but its substance is already abandoned": this refers to when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; at that time, all obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) minds associated with the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering take as their objects those states to be abandoned by the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin take as their objects those states to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all obscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of origination take as their objects both the path of vision and what is to be abandoned by cultivation.

If one sees that a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision, but has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, possesses obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by insight, which take as their object that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.
This is called "the object of cognition is not yet abandoned while its substance is already abandoned.

Regarding "the object of cognition is not yet abandoned and the object of cognition is already abandoned while its substance is not yet abandoned," this refers to the following: when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, the obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛta-avyākṛta-citta*) associated with the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of origin, which take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
This is called: "the object of cognition is not yet abandoned and its substance is not yet abandoned," and "the object of cognition is already abandoned and its substance is already abandoned.

Regarding the latter—where the object of cognition is already abandoned and its substance is already abandoned—it refers to the obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), at a time when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaye ’nvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; these minds take as their objects the truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (samudaya-anvaya-jñāna) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (nivṛta-avyākṛta-citta) belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛtacitta*) of the formless realm associated with the truths of suffering and origin—which abandon [afflictions] through seeing—and which take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation.

If one considers a perfected disciple of the Blessed One who has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, their obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by insight take as their objects those states to be abandoned by both insight and cultivation.
This is called "the object of focus is not yet abandoned and the entity itself is already abandoned.
Regarding those unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), if their entity is not yet abandoned, is their object of focus also not yet abandoned?

Either the entity is not yet abandoned while the object is not yet abandoned; or the entity is not yet abandoned while the object has already been abandoned; or the entity is not yet abandoned while both the object has already been abandoned and the object is not yet abandoned.

Regarding those whose essence is not severed and whose objects are not severed: this refers to the unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm belonging to individuals who are bound by all fetters, which take as their objects those things associated with the formless realm.

Having already abandoned craving for the desire realm but not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, and before the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm take that which is associated with the formless realm as their object.

For one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛtacitta*) bound to the formless realm take as their object that which is bound to the formless realm.

For one for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaye ’nvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds bound to the formless realm take as their object those things to be abandoned through seeing origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of origination has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds bound to the formless realm take as their objects those states to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all unobstructed-neutral minds associated with the formless realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by seeing the path and by cultivation.

If one sees that a perfected disciple of the Blessed One who has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm possesses various unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm that take as their object what is to be abandoned by cultivation.
This is called "the entity is not yet abandoned and the object is not yet abandoned.

Regarding that which has an entity not yet abandoned but an object already abandoned: this refers to those unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, and these minds take as their objects [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, those unobscured-neutral minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm take as their object that which is to be abandoned by seeing suffering, its origin, and its cessation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, then any unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by vision.
This is called "the entity has not been abandoned while the object has already been abandoned.

Regarding that which has an entity not yet abandoned and an object already abandoned, as well as an object not yet abandoned: this refers to those minds associated with the formless realm that are unobscured-neutral, when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, and these minds take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the factors to be abandoned by cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛtacitta*) associated with the formless realm take as their objects those things to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, then all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm take as their objects those states to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation.
This is called "the entity is not yet abandoned while the object is already abandoned" and "the object is not yet abandoned.
Now, if the object is not yet abandoned, is its entity also not yet abandoned?
He replied:
Thus it is said.
*The Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School*, Fascicle Eight.
*The Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Fascicle Nine.
Composed by the Arhat Devaśarman; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Four:

The Aggregate of Object-Conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya-skandha*), Part Four of the Uddāna Verses. There are ten types of mind: namely, wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, unwholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and unobscured-neutral mind; wholesome mind bound to the form realm, obscured-neutral mind, and unobscured-neutral mind; and wholesome mind bound to the formless realm, obscured-neutral mind, and unobscured-neutral mind.
Regarding the various wholesome minds bound to the desire realm: if their substance has been severed, has their object also been severed?
Conversely, if their object has been severed, has their substance also been severed?

Furthermore, regarding all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*): if their substance (*svabhāva*) has been severed, have their objects (*ālambana*) also been severed?
Conversely, if their objects have been severed, has their substance also been severed?
Regarding all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-citta*): if their substance has been severed, is their object (*ālambana*) also severed?

There are cases where both the substance and the object have been severed; cases where the substance has been severed but the object has not; cases where the substance has been severed and the object is both severed and not severed; and cases where the substance has been severed such that it cannot be distinguished whether this mind’s object has been severed or not.

Regarding "the entity has been severed and the object-condition has been severed": this refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm; their various wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those things bound to the desire realm.

For one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those things bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm, or both those bound to the desire realm and those bound to the form realm.

For one who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) take as their objects those things bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), those bound to the formless realm, those bound to both the desire and form realms, those bound to both the desire and formless realms, those bound to both the form and formless realms, and those bound to the desire, form, and formless realms.
This is called "the entity is already abandoned and the object is already abandoned.

Regarding that which has its entity already abandoned but whose object is not yet abandoned: it refers to one who has already become detached from the greed of the desire realm but has not yet become detached from the greed of the form realm, and for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; such a person’s various wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those bound to the form realm, those bound to the formless realm, or both those bound to the form realm and the formless realm.

When one has already abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, those wholesome minds bound to the desire realm that take as their object that which is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are said to have their substance already severed while their objects are not yet severed.

Regarding those whose intrinsic nature has been severed, whose objects have been severed, and whose objects have not yet been severed: this refers to wholesome minds bound to the desire realm belonging to one who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm; such minds take as their objects those bound to the desire realm and the form realm, those bound to the desire realm and the formless realm, and those bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

Having already abandoned craving for the form realm but not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those things bound to the desire realm and the formless realm, those bound to the form realm and the formless realm, and those bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
This is called "the entity has been abandoned, while the object-condition is both abandoned and not yet abandoned.

Regarding those cases where the entity has been abandoned but it cannot be distinguished whether the object-condition of this mind is abandoned or not yet abandoned: this refers to one who has already become detached from the greed of the desire realm but has not yet become detached from the greed of the form realm; for such a person, various wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.

Having already abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) take as their object that which is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
Having already abandoned craving for the formless realm, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.
This is called "the entity having been severed, such that it cannot be distinguished whether the object-condition of this mind has been severed or not.
Even if the object-condition has been severed, has its entity also been severed?

Either the object of focus has been severed and its substance has been severed; or the object of focus has been severed but its substance has not been severed; or both the object of focus has been severed and the object of focus has not been severed, yet its substance has been severed; or both the object of focus has been severed and the object of focus has not been severed, yet its substance has not been severed.

Regarding those whose objects of perception have been severed and whose substance has been severed: this refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm; their various wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is bound to the desire realm.

For one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects things bound to the desire realm, things bound to the form realm, or things bound to both the desire realm and the form realm.

For one who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) take as their objects those bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), those bound to the formless realm, those bound to both the desire and form realms, those bound to both the desire and formless realms, those bound to both the form and formless realms, and those bound to all three—the desire, form, and formless realms.
This is called "the object of cognition has been abandoned and its substance has been abandoned.

Regarding "the object of cognition has been abandoned but its substance has not been abandoned": this refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm; when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm that take as their object what is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origination.

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origination, and cessation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, then those wholesome minds bound to the desire realm that take as their object what is to be abandoned by vision are said to have their objects already abandoned while their own substance is not yet abandoned.

Regarding those whose objects have been abandoned as well as those whose objects have not yet been abandoned, but whose intrinsic nature has already been abandoned: this refers to the wholesome minds bound to the desire realm belonging to one who has already become detached from the greed of the desire realm but has not yet become detached from the greed of the form realm; these minds take as their objects that which is bound to the desire realm and bound to the form realm, that which is bound to the desire realm and bound to the formless realm, and that which is bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

Having already abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but not yet having abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) take as their objects those things bound to the desire realm and the formless realm, those bound to the form realm and the formless realm, and those bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
This is called that whose objects of cognition (*ālambana*) are both abandoned and un-abandoned, yet whose substance (*svabhāva*) is already abandoned.

Regarding that whose objects of cognition are both abandoned and un-abandoned, yet whose substance is not yet abandoned: it refers to wholesome minds bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) belonging to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; these [minds] take as their objects those things to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

If one observes a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision but has not yet abandoned the craving of the desire realm, then those wholesome minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects that which is to be abandoned by both vision and cultivation.
This is called "that which has its objects already abandoned and that which has its objects not yet abandoned, while its own substance is not yet abandoned."
Regarding all unwholesome minds: when their substance has been severed, is their object also severed?

There are cases where both the substance and the object have been severed; cases where the substance has been severed but the object has not; cases where the substance has been severed and the object is both severed and not severed; and cases where the substance has been severed but it cannot be distinguished whether this mind’s object has been severed or not.

Regarding "the entity has been abandoned and the object has been abandoned": this refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; their unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering take as their objects those things abandoned through the vision of suffering.

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination take as their object those [states] abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination.
Unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering take as their object those [states] abandoned through the vision of suffering.
An unwholesome mind abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-heya) takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of the origin.

When the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) has arisen but the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) has not yet arisen, various unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha) and the vision of the origin take as their objects that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of the origin, and the vision of cessation.
Unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering take as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of origination take as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination;
unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of cessation take as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation.

If one observes a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision but has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), their unwholesome minds to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) take as their object that which is to be abandoned by vision.

If they have already abandoned desire for the realm of desire but have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), their unwholesome minds take as their object that which is bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

For one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, all unwholesome minds take as their objects that which is bound to the desire realm and that which is bound to the form realm.

For one who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm, all unwholesome minds take as their objects that which is bound to the desire realm, that which is bound to the form realm, that which is bound to the formless realm, and that which is bound to both the form and formless realms.
This is called "the entity has been abandoned and the object has been abandoned.

Regarding that which is "the entity has been abandoned but the object has not been abandoned": it refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; their unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering take as their objects those things abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination take as their object that which is to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination take as their object that which is to be abandoned through the vision of the path and through cultivation.

If one considers a perfected disciple of the Blessed One who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm: their unwholesome minds to be abandoned by insight take as their object that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.

If they have already abandoned craving for the desire realm but have not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen: their unwholesome minds take as their object what is bound to the form realm, what is bound to the formless realm, or what is bound to both the form and formless realms.

When one has already abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all unwholesome minds take that which is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as their object.
This is called "the entity is already severed, but the object is not yet severed."

Regarding those whose intrinsic nature has been abandoned, whose objects have been abandoned, and whose objects have not yet been abandoned: this refers to unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in one who has not yet detached from the greed of the desire realm, for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; these minds take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

When the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination take as their objects those factors abandoned through the vision of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected right view has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), their unwholesome minds abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) take as their objects those things abandoned through both insight and cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Having already abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) but not yet abandoned desire for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), their unwholesome minds take as their objects those things bound to the realm of form and the formless realm.
This is called "the entity is already abandoned, while the object of focus is both already abandoned and not yet abandoned.

Regarding that which has its entity already abandoned but cannot be distinguished as to whether its object of focus is already abandoned or not yet abandoned: this refers to an unwholesome mind abandoned through the vision of cessation, belonging to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, whose knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has arisen but whose knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; such a mind takes as its object that which is not [to be] abandoned.

If one sees a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision but has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, their unwholesome minds to be abandoned by insight take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.

If they have already abandoned craving for the desire realm but have not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, their unwholesome minds likewise take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.
For one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, all unwholesome minds take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.
For one who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm, all unwholesome minds take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.
This is called "the entity having already been severed, such that it cannot be distinguished whether the object of this mind has been severed or not.
If the object has been severed, has its entity also been severed?

Either the object of focus has been severed and its substance has been severed; or the object of focus has been severed but its substance has not been severed; or both the object of focus has been severed and the object of focus has not been severed, yet its substance has been severed; or both the object of focus has been severed and the object of focus has not been severed, yet its substance has not been severed.

Regarding those whose objects of cognition have been abandoned and whose entities have been abandoned: this refers to one who has not yet abandoned the craving of the desire realm, for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; their unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering take as their objects those things abandoned through the vision of suffering.

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination take as their object those [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination;
unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering take as their object those [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering.
An unwholesome mind abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of the origin.

When the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) has arisen but the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) has not yet arisen, various unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha) and the origin take as their objects that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering, the origin, and cessation.
An unwholesome mind abandoned through the vision of suffering takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
an unwholesome mind abandoned through the vision of origination takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination;
an unwholesome mind abandoned through the vision of cessation takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation.

If one sees a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision but has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire, their unwholesome minds to be abandoned by vision take as their object that which is to be abandoned by vision.

If they have already abandoned desire for the realm of desire but have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of form, their unwholesome minds take as their object that which is bound to the realm of desire.

For one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, unwholesome states of mind take as their object that which is bound to the desire realm and that which is bound to the form realm.

For one who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm, unwholesome states of mind take as their object that which is bound to the desire realm, that which is bound to the form realm, that which is bound to the formless realm, and that which is bound to both the form and formless realms.
This is called that whose object-condition (*ālambana*) has been abandoned and whose substance (*svabhāva*) has also been abandoned.

Regarding that whose object-condition has been abandoned but whose substance has not yet been abandoned: this refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; it concerns unwholesome minds to be abandoned by the vision of origin, which take as their object those things to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
This is called "that whose object has been abandoned but whose substance has not yet been abandoned.

Regarding "that whose object has been abandoned and that whose object has not yet been abandoned, but whose substance has already been abandoned": this refers to one who has not yet abandoned the craving of the desire realm, for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; [in such a state], all unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering take as their objects those things abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation.

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination take as their objects those factors abandoned through the vision of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation.

When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all unwholesome minds abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation.

If one considers a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision but has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm: their unwholesome minds abandoned through vision take as objects those states abandoned through both vision and cultivation.

If they have already abandoned craving for the form realm but have not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm: their unwholesome minds take as objects those states bound to the form realm and the formless realm.
This is called that whose object has been abandoned and whose object has not been abandoned, yet whose substance has been abandoned;

and that whose object has been abandoned and whose object has not been abandoned, yet whose substance has not been abandoned. Regarding the latter: it refers to the unwholesome minds associated with views to be abandoned by seeing the origin (samudaya), belonging to one who has not yet abandoned desire for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, and which take as their objects those things to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
This is called: "the object-condition is both abandoned and not abandoned, while its substance is not abandoned.
Regarding those obscured-unspecified minds bound to the desire realm, if their substance has been abandoned, has their object-condition also been abandoned?

Either the entity has been abandoned and the object of cognition has been abandoned; or the entity has been abandoned and the object of cognition has not been abandoned; or the entity has been abandoned and both the object of cognition has been abandoned and the object of cognition has not been abandoned.

Regarding "the entity itself has been abandoned and the object-condition has been abandoned": this refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm; when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is to be abandoned by seeing suffering.

When the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those things to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origination.

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those things to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origination, and cessation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, their various obscured-unspecified minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is to be abandoned by vision.

Having already abandoned craving for the desire realm but not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is bound to the desire realm.

Having already abandoned craving for the form realm but not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is bound to the desire realm.

When one has already abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), those obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛtacitta*) bound to the desire realm that take objects bound to the desire realm as their cognitive objects are said to have "the entity already abandoned and the object already abandoned."

Regarding those whose substance has been severed but whose objects have not yet been severed: this refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm; when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects [the truths of] origin, cessation, and the path, as well as [factors] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those states to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, by the vision of the path, and by cultivation.

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those states to be abandoned by the vision of the path and by cultivation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire, their various obscured-unspecified minds bound to the realm of desire take as their object that which is to be abandoned through cultivation.
This is called "the entity has been abandoned, but the object has not been abandoned.

Regarding those cases where the entity has been abandoned and the object has been abandoned, as well as where the object has not been abandoned: this refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; their various obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds associated with the desire realm take as objects the [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those factors abandoned through seeing suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation.

When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, their various desire-realm-bound obscured-unspecified minds take as their object that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.
This is called "the entity is already abandoned and the object-condition is already abandoned" as well as "the object-condition is not yet abandoned.
Now, if the object-condition is already abandoned, is its entity also already abandoned?
It is said:
Thus it is.

Regarding those unobscured-neutral minds bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-avṛtāvyākṛta-citta*), if their substance has been abandoned, have their objects (*ālambana*) also been abandoned?
It is said:
It is so. If an object of cognition has been severed, is its substance also severed?

There are cases where the object has been severed and its substance is also severed; there are cases where the object has been severed but its substance is not yet severed; and there are cases where both the object and the non-object have been severed, yet its substance remains unsevered.

Regarding those whose objects of perception have been severed and whose substance has been severed: this refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm; their various unobscured-neutral minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is bound to the desire realm.

For one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the desire realm take objects within the desire realm.
For one who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm, all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the desire realm take objects within the desire realm.
This is called "the object of cognition has been abandoned and its substance has been abandoned.

Regarding "the object of cognition has been abandoned but its substance has not been abandoned": this refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm; when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds associated with the desire realm that take as their object what is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*darśana-prahātavya*).

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origination.

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds bound to the desire realm take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origination, and cessation.

If one sees that a perfected disciple of the Blessed One who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm possesses various unobscured-neutral minds bound to the desire realm that take as their object what is to be abandoned by seeing.
This is called "the object of cognition has been abandoned, but its substance has not been abandoned.

Regarding that which is "the object of cognition has been abandoned and the object of cognition has not been abandoned, yet its substance has not been abandoned": it refers to those whose craving for the desire realm has not yet been relinquished; when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, their various unobscured-neutral minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the desire realm take as their objects the [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those things to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those things to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

If one considers a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision but has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, their various unobscured-neutral minds bound to the desire realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by vision and cultivation.
This is called "that whose object has been abandoned as well as that whose object has not been abandoned, yet whose substance has not been abandoned.
Regarding wholesome minds bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), if their substance has already been abandoned, has their object also been abandoned?

Either its substance is already abandoned and its object is already abandoned; or its substance is already abandoned and its object is not yet abandoned; or its substance is already abandoned and both its object is already abandoned and its object is not yet abandoned; or its substance is already abandoned and it cannot be distinguished whether this mind’s object is already abandoned or not yet abandoned.

Regarding "the entity has been severed and the object has been severed": this refers to one who is already free from craving for the form realm but not yet free from craving for the formless realm; their various wholesome minds associated with the form realm take as objects those things associated with the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.

For one who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all wholesome minds bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) take as their objects those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those bound to the form realm, those bound to the formless realm; those bound to both the desire and form realms; those bound to both the desire and formless realms; those bound to both the form and formless realms; and those bound to all three—the desire, form, and formless realms.
This is called "the entity is already abandoned and the object is already abandoned.

Regarding that which is "the entity is already abandoned but the object is not yet abandoned": it refers to a wholesome mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) belonging to one who has already become detached from the greed of the form realm, but for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, taking as its object that which is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is called "the entity has been severed while the object has not yet been severed.

Regarding that which is "the entity has been severed and the object has been severed" as well as "the object has not yet been severed": it refers to those who have already abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but have not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and whose various wholesome minds bound to the form realm take as their objects things bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), things bound to the formless realm, things bound to both the form realm and the formless realm, or things bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
This is called "the entity is already abandoned, while the object is both abandoned and not yet abandoned.

Regarding that which has its entity already abandoned but cannot be distinguished as to whether its object is abandoned or not yet abandoned: this refers to those who have already abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but have not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); their various wholesome minds bound to the form realm take as their objects that which is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).

When one has already abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all wholesome minds bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) take as their object that which is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
This is called "the entity is already abandoned, yet it cannot be distinguished whether the objects of this mind are abandoned or unabandoned."
If an object of cognition has been abandoned, has its substance also been abandoned?
Is it the case that when the object of cognition has been abandoned, its substance has also been abandoned;
or is it the case that when the object of cognition has been abandoned, its substance has not yet been abandoned?

Either that which has its object already severed and its object not yet severed has its substance already severed; or that which has its object already severed and its object not yet severed has its substance not yet severed.

Regarding those whose objects of perception have been abandoned and whose substance has been abandoned: this refers to one who has already become detached from the greed of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but has not yet become detached from the greed of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). For such a person, all wholesome minds bound to the form realm take as their objects those bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm, or both those bound to the desire realm and the form realm.

For one who has already become detached from craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all wholesome minds bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) take as their objects those things bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those bound to the form realm, those bound to the formless realm; those bound to both the desire and form realms; those bound to both the desire and formless realms; those bound to both the form and formless realms; and those bound to all three—the desire, form, and formless realms.
This is called "the object of cognition has been abandoned and its substance has also been abandoned.

Regarding "the object of cognition has been abandoned but its substance has not yet been abandoned": this refers to one who has already become detached from the craving of the desire realm but has not yet become detached from the craving of the form realm; while the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, various wholesome minds bound to the form realm take that which is bound to the desire realm as their object.

For one who has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the realm of form take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds associated with the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) take as their object those factors to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds associated with the form realm take as their object those factors to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form, then any wholesome mind bound to the realm of form that takes as its object what is to be abandoned by vision is called "that which has its object already abandoned, but whose substance is not yet abandoned."

Regarding those whose objects of cognition have been abandoned and whose objects of cognition have not yet been abandoned, yet whose essential nature has already been abandoned: this refers to wholesome minds bound to the form realm belonging to one who has already become detached from the greed of the form realm but has not yet become detached from the greed of the formless realm; such minds take as their objects that which is bound to the desire realm or the formless realm, that which is bound to the form realm or the formless realm, or that which is bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
This is called that whose object has been abandoned and whose object has not been abandoned, yet whose substance has been abandoned;

and that whose object has been abandoned and whose object has not been abandoned, yet whose substance has not been abandoned. This refers to the various wholesome minds associated with the form realm belonging to one who has already become detached from the greed of the desire realm but has not yet become detached from the greed of the form realm, which take as their objects those things bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm, those bound to the desire realm and the formless realm, or those bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

For one who has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds bound to the realm of form take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of origin has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds associated with the form realm take as their objects those things to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, then any wholesome mind bound to the form realm takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by both seeing and cultivation.
This is called "the object is already abandoned and the object is not yet abandoned, while its substance is not yet abandoned."

Regarding all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*): if their substance (*svabhāva*) has been abandoned, have their objects (*ālambana*) also been abandoned?

There are four possibilities: (1) both the substance and the object have been abandoned; (2) the substance has been abandoned but the object has not been abandoned; (3) both the substance and the object have been abandoned as well as the object not having been abandoned; or (4) the substance has been abandoned, yet it cannot be distinguished whether this mind’s object has been abandoned or not.

Regarding "the entity has been abandoned and the object has been abandoned": this refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; such a person possesses obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, which take as their objects those [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin take as their object those [factors] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin.
The obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of suffering takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
the obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of origination takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origination take as their objects those factors to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origination, and cessation.
The obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of suffering takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
the obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of origination takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination.
The obscured-unspecified mind to be abandoned by the vision of cessation takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned the craving for the realm of form, then all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the realm of form that are to be abandoned by vision take as their objects that which is to be abandoned by vision.

Having already abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but not yet having abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the form realm take as their object that which is bound to the form realm.

Having already abandoned craving for the formless realm, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the form realm take as their object that which is bound to the form realm, that which is bound to the formless realm, and that which is bound to both the form realm and the formless realm.
This is called "the entity is already abandoned and the object is already abandoned.

Regarding that which has its entity already abandoned but whose object is not yet abandoned: this refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), where the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; [in such a state], the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering take as their objects those things to be abandoned by the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) associated with the vision of suffering and origin—which are to be abandoned by vision—and which take as their object the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds of the form realm associated with the views to be abandoned by the seeing of suffering and the seeing of origination take as their objects the truths of the path and those factors to be abandoned by cultivation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form, their obscured-unspecified mind associated with the realm of form that is to be abandoned by insight takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.

When one has already abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the form realm take as their object that which is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is called "the entity is already severed, but the object is not yet severed."

Regarding those whose intrinsic nature has been abandoned, whose objects have been abandoned, and whose objects have not yet been abandoned: this refers to the obscured-unspecified minds associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, belonging to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; these minds take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned by cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, there are obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin; these take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛta-avyākṛta-citta*) associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, their obscured-unspecified minds associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned by insight take as their objects those things to be abandoned by both insight and cultivation.

Having already abandoned craving for the form realm but not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the form realm take as their objects those things bound to the form realm and the formless realm.
This is called "the entity has been abandoned, but the object of cognition is both abandoned and not abandoned.

Regarding that which has its entity abandoned yet cannot be distinguished as to whether its object of cognition is abandoned or not abandoned: this refers to the obscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), belonging to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, for whom the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; such a mind takes as its object that which is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form, their obscured-unspecified mind associated with the realm of form—which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path—takes as its object that which is not to be abandoned.

For one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the form realm take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.
For one who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the form realm take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.
This is called having its substance already severed, such that one cannot distinguish whether the object of this mind has been severed or not.
Even if the object has been severed, has its substance also been severed?

Either the object of focus has been severed and its substance has been severed; or the object of focus has been severed but its substance has not been severed; or both the object of focus has been severed and the object of focus has not been severed, yet its substance has been severed; or both the object of focus has been severed and the object of focus has not been severed, yet its substance has not been severed.

Regarding "the object of cognition has been abandoned and its substance has been abandoned": this refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; in such a person, the obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned by seeing suffering take as their object those [factors] to be abandoned by seeing suffering.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛta-avyākṛta-citta*) bound to the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin take as their object those [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin.
The obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of suffering takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
the obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of origination takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of origin take as their objects those states to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, and the vision of cessation.
The obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of suffering takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
the obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of origination takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination.
The obscured-unspecified mind to be abandoned by the vision of cessation takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned the craving for the realm of form, then all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the realm of form that are to be abandoned by vision take as their objects that which is to be abandoned by vision.
