Having already abandoned craving for the form realm but not yet having abandoned craving for the formless realm, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the form realm take as their object that which is bound to the form realm.

Having already abandoned craving for the formless realm, all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the form realm take as their object that which is bound to the form realm, that which is bound to the formless realm, or both that which is bound to the form realm and that which is bound to the formless realm.
This is called "the object of focus has been abandoned and its substance has been abandoned.

Regarding "the object of focus has been abandoned but its substance has not been abandoned," it refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, any obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind associated with the form realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of origin, which takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
This is called "that whose object has been abandoned but whose substance has not yet been abandoned.

Regarding "that whose object has been abandoned as well as that whose object has not yet been abandoned, but whose substance has been abandoned": this refers to one who has not yet abandoned attachment to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; it concerns the obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, which take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, there are obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛta-avyākṛta-citta*) associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin; these take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

If one considers a perfected disciple of the Blessed One who has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form, their obscured-unspecified mind associated with the realm of form—which is to be abandoned by insight—takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by both insight and cultivation, [the latter] having already abandoned craving for the realm of form.

For one who has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), those obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) take as their objects both what is bound to the form realm and what is bound to the formless realm.
This is called "that which is already abandoned with respect to its object, and that which is not yet abandoned with respect to its object, but whose substance is already abandoned."

Regarding those whose objects have been abandoned, as well as those whose objects have not yet been abandoned, yet whose own substance has not been abandoned: this refers to the obscured-unspecified minds associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of origin, belonging to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; these minds take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned by cultivation.
This is called "the object of focus has been abandoned, but its substance has not been abandoned, and the object of focus has not been abandoned.

Regarding all unobscured-neutral minds bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-avṛtāvyākṛtacitta*), if their substance has already been abandoned, has their object of focus also been abandoned?
He said: "It is so. If that which is the object of focus has been severed, is its substance also severed?"

Either the object of cognition has been severed and its substance has been severed; or the object of cognition has been severed but its substance has not yet been severed; or both the object of cognition has been severed and the object of cognition has not yet been severed, while its substance has not yet been severed.

Regarding those whose objects of perception have been severed and whose essence has been severed: this refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm; their various unobscured-neutral minds associated with the form realm take as their objects those things associated with the desire realm or those associated with the form realm.

For one who has already become detached from craving for the formless realm, all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the form realm take as their object that which is associated with the desire realm or that which is associated with the form realm.
This is called "the object of cognition having been abandoned and its substance having been abandoned."

Regarding those whose objects of perception have been severed but whose substance has not yet been severed: this refers to the various unobscured-neutral minds associated with the form realm that take objects within the desire realm, by one who has already become detached from the greed of the desire realm but has not yet become detached from the greed of the form realm; and the various unobscured-neutral minds associated with the form realm that take as their object what is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, by one who has not yet become detached from the greed of the form realm, for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the form realm take as their object those factors to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the form realm take as their object those factors to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form, their various unobscured-neutral minds bound to the realm of form take as their object that which is to be abandoned by vision.
This is called "the object of cognition has been abandoned, but its substance has not been abandoned.

Regarding that which has both its object abandoned and its object not abandoned, yet its substance has not been abandoned: it refers to the non-obscured, neutral minds associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) for one who has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; these minds take as their objects those things to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the form realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds bound to the form realm take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned by cultivation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form, their unobscured-neutral minds bound to the realm of form take as their objects those states to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
This is called that whose object-condition (*ālambana*) has been abandoned as well as that whose object-condition has not been abandoned, yet whose substance (*svabhāva*) has not been abandoned.
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Fascicle Nine. *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Fascicle Ten.
Composed by the Arhat Devaśarman;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Uddāna Verse: The Fourth Aggregate on Object-Conditions (ālambana-pratyaya), Part Five. Regarding all wholesome minds associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): if their substance has been severed, have their objects also been severed?
It is so. If an object-condition (*ālambana*) has been severed, is its substance (*svabhāva*) also severed?

There are cases where the object-condition has been severed and its substance is also severed; there are cases where the object-condition has been severed but its substance is not yet severed; and there are cases where both the object-condition and the [remaining] object-conditions have not been severed and its substance is not yet severed.

Regarding those whose objects have been abandoned and whose substance has been abandoned: this refers to the wholesome minds associated with the formless realm that belong to one who has already become detached from the craving of the formless realm, and which take as their objects those things associated with the form realm or those associated with the formless realm.
This is called that whose object has been abandoned and whose substance has also been abandoned.

Regarding that whose object has been abandoned but whose substance has not been abandoned: it refers to wholesome minds bound to the formless realm that take as their object the realm of form, by one who has already become detached from the greed of the form realm but has not yet become detached from the greed of the formless realm.

When the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds associated with the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds associated with the formless realm take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśalacitta*) take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation.

Furthermore, for a disciple of the Blessed One who is perfected in vision but has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, all wholesome minds associated with the formless realm take as their object that which is to be abandoned by vision.
This is called "the object of focus has been abandoned, but its substance has not yet been abandoned.

Regarding "the object of focus has been abandoned and the object of focus has not yet been abandoned, while its substance has not yet been abandoned": this refers to wholesome minds associated with the formless realm when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; these minds take as their objects the truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of origin has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds associated with the formless realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all wholesome minds associated with the formless realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, then their wholesome minds associated with the formless realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by vision and cultivation.
This is called "the object of focus has been abandoned, yet the entity itself has not been abandoned, and the object of focus has not been abandoned.
Regarding those obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm: if their entity has already been abandoned, has their object of focus also been abandoned?

Either its substance is already abandoned and its object is already abandoned; or its substance is already abandoned and its object is not yet abandoned; or its substance is already abandoned and both its object is already abandoned and its object is not yet abandoned; or its substance is already abandoned such that it cannot be distinguished whether this mind’s object is abandoned or not yet abandoned.

Regarding "the entity has already been abandoned and the object has already been abandoned": this refers to when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; at that time, the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by seeing suffering take as their objects those [factors] to be abandoned by seeing suffering.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin take as their object those [factors] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin.
The obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of suffering takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
the obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of origination takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, there are obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, which take as their objects those things to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, its origin, and cessation.
The obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of suffering takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
the obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of origination takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination.
The obscured-unspecified mind to be abandoned by the vision of cessation takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned the craving for the formless realm, then all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by vision take as their objects that which is to be abandoned by vision.
When one has already abandoned craving for the formless realm, those obscured-unspecified minds bound to the formless realm take as their object that which is bound to the formless realm;
this is called "the entity is already severed and the object is already severed."

Regarding those whose substance has been severed but whose objects have not yet been severed: this refers to cases where the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of origination (samudaya-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen; in such instances, the obscured-unspecified minds (nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta) associated with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering take as their objects those states to be abandoned by the vision of origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin take as their objects those states to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, the obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin take as their objects both the path to be abandoned through vision and that to be abandoned through cultivation.

If one sees that a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision, but has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, possesses obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by insight and take as their object that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.
This is called "the entity is already abandoned while the object is not yet abandoned.

Regarding that which has both its entity and its object abandoned, as well as that which has its entity abandoned but its object not yet abandoned: this refers to the obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; these minds take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛta-avyākṛta-citta*) belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin take as their objects [the truths of] suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of origin take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned through cultivation.

If one considers a perfected disciple of the Blessed One who has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, their obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by insight have as their objects those states to be abandoned by both insight and cultivation.
This is called "the entity is already abandoned, while the object is both abandoned and not yet abandoned.

Regarding those cases where the entity is already abandoned but one cannot distinguish whether the object of that mind is abandoned or not yet abandoned: this refers to when one has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the *nirodha-anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge of cessation) has already arisen, but the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge of the path) has not yet arisen; at that time, the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation take as their objects those things that are not to be abandoned.

If one considers a perfected disciple of the Blessed One who has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, their obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm—which are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path—take as their object that which is not to be abandoned.

When one has already become detached from craving for the formless realm, all obscured-unspecified minds (nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta) bound to the formless realm take as their object that which is not to be abandoned (aprahātavya).
This is called "the entity itself is already abandoned, yet it cannot be distinguished whether the objects of this mind are already abandoned or not."
If an object-condition (*ālambana*) has been abandoned, is its substance (*svabhāva*) also abandoned?

There are four possibilities: either the object-condition has been abandoned and its substance has been abandoned; or the object-condition has been abandoned but its substance has not been abandoned; or both the object-condition and the non-object-condition have been abandoned and its substance has been abandoned; or both the object-condition and the non-object-condition have been abandoned but its substance has not been abandoned.

Regarding "the object of cognition has been abandoned and its substance has been abandoned": this refers to when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; at that time, the obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, take as their object those [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin take as their objects those [factors] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin.
The obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of suffering takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
the obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of origination takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, its origin, and cessation.
The obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of suffering takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
the obscured-unspecified mind abandoned through the vision of origination takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination.
The obscured-unspecified mind to be abandoned by the vision of cessation takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, then all obscured-unspecified minds bound to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by vision take as their objects that which is to be abandoned by vision.

When one has already become free from craving for the formless realm, those obscured-unspecified minds bound to the formless realm that take as their object what is bound to the formless realm are said to have both their objects and their substance already abandoned.

Regarding those whose objects have been abandoned but whose essence has not yet been abandoned: this refers to the obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), which take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), at a time when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.
This is called "the object of focus has been abandoned, but its substance has not yet been abandoned.

Regarding "the object of focus has been abandoned as well as the object of focus has not been abandoned, yet its substance has been abandoned": this refers to when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; at that time, the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which are to be abandoned by seeing suffering, take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, there are obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin; these take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned through cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen, all obscured-unspecified minds (nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta) belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

If one considers a perfected disciple of the Blessed One who has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, their obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by insight take as their objects those states to be abandoned by both insight and cultivation.
This is called that whose object has been abandoned and whose object has not been abandoned, yet whose substance has been abandoned;

and that whose object has been abandoned and whose object has not been abandoned, yet whose substance has not been abandoned. This refers to the obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which is to be abandoned by the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), at a time when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, and which takes as its objects the truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
This is called: "the object of focus has been abandoned and the object of focus has not been abandoned, yet its substance has not been abandoned.
Regarding all unobscured-neutral minds bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), if their substance has already been abandoned, has their object of focus also been abandoned?
He said: "It is so. If that which is the object of focus has been severed, is its substance also severed?"

Either the object of focus has been severed and its substance has been severed; or the object of focus has been severed but its substance has not been severed; or both the object of focus and the non-object of focus have been severed, yet its substance has not been severed.

Regarding those whose objects of perception have been severed and whose substance has been severed: this refers to the unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm that take as their object the formless realm, [in a person] who has already become detached from craving for the formless realm.
This is called "the object of cognition has been abandoned and its substance has been abandoned.

Regarding "the object of cognition has been abandoned but its substance has not been abandoned": it refers to those unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, and these minds take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds bound to the formless realm take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of origin.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, its origin, and its cessation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, then any unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by vision.
This is called "the object of cognition has been abandoned, but its substance has not yet been abandoned.

Regarding that which has both its object of cognition abandoned and its object of cognition not yet abandoned, while its substance has not yet been abandoned: it refers to those unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; these minds take as their objects the truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, as well as those factors to be abandoned through cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of origin has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.

When the subsequent knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, all unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm take as their objects those factors to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation.

If a disciple of the Blessed One who has perfected vision has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, their various unobscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm take as their objects those states to be abandoned by both vision and cultivation.
This is called "the object of cognition has been abandoned, yet the object of cognition has not been abandoned, and its substance has not been abandoned.
There are fifteen such states of mind: namely, five minds bound to the desire realm, five minds bound to the form realm, and five minds bound to the formless realm.
What are the five types of minds associated with the desire realm?

They are: the mind associated with the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, the mind to be abandoned by the vision of the origin, the mind to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, the mind to be abandoned by the vision of the path, and the mind to be abandoned by cultivation.
Just as there are five minds bound to the desire realm, so too are there five minds bound to the form realm and five minds bound to the formless realm.
Thus, these fifteen minds may be past, future, or present.

Regarding all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with the desire realm that were abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in past minds: if they increase in accordance with (*anuśerate*) this mind, are they capable of taking it as an object (*ālambaka*)?

If it is that which takes [an object] as its cognitive support (*ālambana*), is it also that which increases in accordance with it (*anuśerate*)? As it is for the past, so it is for the future and the present.

As it is for the mind abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), so it is for the minds abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, the path, and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
As it is with those bound to the desire realm, so it is with those bound to the form realm and the formless realm.

Regarding all past latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the mind associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*): if they increase in accordance with (*anuśerate*) this mind, are they able to take it as an object (*ālambaka*)?

Either that which increases through association is not an object-condition, or that which is an object-condition does not increase through association; or that which increases through association is also an object-condition, or that which neither increases through association nor is an object-condition.
That which is increased by association but is not an object-condition refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are associated with this mind and have not yet been abandoned.
That which is an object-condition but is not increased by association refers to those latent dispositions that take this mind as their object and have already been abandoned.

That which is both an object of increase (*anuśayana*) and an object of cognition (*ālambana*) refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have not yet been abandoned and can take this mind as their object.

That which is neither an object of increase nor an object of cognition refers to those latent dispositions associated with this mind that have already been abandoned, as well as other objects, other latent dispositions, or universal latent dispositions belonging to a different realm (*dhātu*).
As it is with the past, so it is with the future.

Regarding all present latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), if they increase in accordance with this mind, are they able to take it as an object (*ālambana*)?

Either that which increases through association is not an object of cognition, or that which is an object of cognition does not increase through association; or that which increases through association is also an object of cognition, or that which neither increases through association nor is an object of cognition.
That which is increased by association but is not an object-condition refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are associated with this mind.
That which is an object-condition but is not increased by association refers to those latent dispositions that take this mind as their object but have already been abandoned.

That which is both increased by association (*anuśayita*) and is also an object-condition (*ālambana*) refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have not yet been abandoned and can take this mind as their object.

That which is neither increased by association nor is an object-condition refers to those latent dispositions that are objects of other [minds], or other latent dispositions, or universal latent dispositions belonging to a different realm (*dhātu*).

Just as it is with the mind associated with the desire realm that is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), so it is with minds abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as defiled minds abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Regarding all past non-defiled minds associated with the desire realm that are abandoned through cultivation, if the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to them increase in accordance with this mind, are they able to take it as an object?
If the various latent dispositions (anuśaya) are both that which they increase through association and that which they take as an object,

or if they are that which they take as an object but not that which they increase through association— this refers to those latent dispositions that have taken this mind as an object but have already been abandoned.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future and the present.
As it is with those bound to the desire realm, so it is with those bound to the form realm and the formless realm.
There are fifteen minds: namely, five minds bound to the desire realm, five minds bound to the form realm, and five minds bound to the formless realm.
What are the five types of consciousness associated with the desire realm?

They are: the consciousness associated with the desire realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, and the consciousnesses associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of the origin, the cessation, and the path, as well as through cultivation.
Just as there are five types of consciousness associated with the desire realm, so it is for those associated with the form realm and the formless realm.
Regarding these fifteen states of mind— whether past, future, or present—

if there are latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and which belong to those past minds, do they not increase in accordance with (*anuśerate*) this [present] mind, and are they not its objects of cognition (*ālambana*)?
Is it not the case that what is not a capable object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is also not subject to increase through association (*anuśayana*)?
As it is with the past, so it is with the future and the present.

As it is with the mind abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), so it is with the minds abandoned by the vision of origin, cessation, the path, and those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
As it is with those bound to the desire realm, so it is with those bound to the form realm and the formless realm.

Regarding all past latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), if they do not increase in accordance with this mind, are they not its objects of cognition (*ālambana*)?

Either it is not that which increases through association and yet is not incapable of taking [it] as an object; or it is not capable of taking [it] as an object and yet does not increase through association; or it is both not that which increases through association and incapable of taking [it] as an object; or it is neither not increasing through association nor incapable of taking [it] as an object.

"Not increasing by way of association, yet not being unable to take it as an object" refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have already been abandoned with respect to this mind as their object.
"Not being able to take it as an object, yet not not increasing by way of association" refers to those latent dispositions that are associated with this mind and have not yet been abandoned.

Regarding that which neither increases through association nor acts as an object-condition: this refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are associated with this mind but have already been abandoned; or other objects of perception; or other latent dispositions; or universal latent dispositions belonging to a different realm.

Regarding "neither not increasing [the defilements] nor unable to take it as an object": this refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take this mind as their object and have not yet been abandoned.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future.

Are all latent dispositions belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and which exist within a present mind, such that they neither increase in relation to this mind nor are able to take it as an object?

Either it is not that which increases through association and yet is not incapable of taking [it] as an object; or it is not capable of taking [it] as an object and yet does not increase through association; or it is neither that which increases through association nor capable of taking [it] as an object; or it is neither not increasing through association nor incapable of taking [it] as an object.

"Not increasing by way of being associated, yet not incapable of taking it as an object" refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have already been abandoned with respect to this mind and take it as their object.
"Not capable of taking it as an object, yet not non-increasing" refers to those latent dispositions that are associated with this mind.

Regarding that which neither increases through association nor acts as an object-condition: this refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are other objects, other latent dispositions, or universal latent dispositions belonging to a different realm.
"Not non-increasing and not unable to take as object" refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have not yet been abandoned with respect to this mind.

This is the case, for example, for a mind in the desire realm associated with the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*); the same applies to minds associated with the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as to defiled minds abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Regarding all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with the past desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and belong to non-defiled minds: do they not either increase in accordance with this mind (*anuśerate*), or are they not able to take it as an object (*ālambana*)?

If the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are neither capable of taking [this mind] as an object (*ālambana*) nor do they increase therein (*anuśerate), or if they do not increase therein but are not incapable of taking it as an object—this refers to those latent dispositions that have taken this mind as their object but have already been abandoned.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future and the present.
As it is for those bound to the desire realm, so it is for those bound to the form realm and the formless realm.
There are fifteen states of mind: namely, five states of mind bound to the desire realm, five bound to the form realm, and five bound to the formless realm.
What are the five types of mind bound to the desire realm? They are:

the mind bound to the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; and the minds bound to the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through cultivation.
As with the five types of mind bound to the desire realm, so it is for the five types of mind bound to the form realm and the formless realm.
Can a mind belonging to the desire realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering discern phenomena belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering?
Can it discern the four types of phenomena to be abandoned within its own stage?
Can one discern the five types of factors associated with the form realm and the formless realm that are to be abandoned?

As it is with the mind associated with the desire realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, so it is with the minds associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of the origin, the cessation, the path, and through cultivation.
Just as it is with the five types of mind bound to the desire realm, so it is with the five types of mind bound to the form realm and the five types of mind bound to the formless realm.
Can a mind bound to the desire realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering discern phenomena bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering?
It is said: it is that which is capable of discerning.

That is to say, either grasping at it as a self, or grasping at it as belonging to a self, or grasping at it as annihilated, or grasping at it as eternal; or denying suffering, or grasping at it as venerable, or grasping at it as superior, or grasping at it as supreme, or grasping at it as foremost; or grasping at it as pure, or grasping at it as liberation, or grasping at it as escape; or whatever confusion, doubt, or hesitation there may be; or greed, hatred, pride, or delusion; or any discernment induced by improper mental application.
"Can one also discern the four kinds of phenomena to be abandoned within one's own stage?
He replied:
"One can discern them."

That is to say: either grasping at it as a self, or grasping at it as belonging to a self; or grasping at it as annihilated, or grasping at it as eternal; or denying the existence of suffering; or grasping at it as venerable, or grasping at it as supreme, or grasping at it as preeminent, or grasping at it as foremost; or grasping at it as pure, or grasping at it as liberation, or grasping at it as transcendence; or whatever confusion, doubt, or hesitation there may be; or lack of knowledge, obscurity, or delusion; or any discernment that is not in accordance with reality.
"Can one also discern the five kinds of factors to be abandoned that are associated with the form realm and the formless realm?
Answer: One can discern them."

That is to say: either denying the existence of suffering; or grasping at it as venerable, or grasping at it as supreme, or grasping at it as excellent, or grasping at it as foremost, or grasping at it as pure, or grasping at it as liberation, or grasping at it as transcendence; or being deluded, or doubtful, or hesitant; or lacking wisdom, or being in darkness, or being ignorant; or any discernment that is improperly induced.

Can a mind belonging to the desire realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin [of suffering] discern phenomena belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of the origin?
Answer: It can discern them.

That is to say: either denying the cause, or grasping it as venerable, or grasping it as superior, or grasping it as excellent, or grasping it as foremost; or being deluded, or doubtful, or hesitant; or having greed, or hatred, or pride, or ignorance; or any discrimination induced by improper mental application.
Can one also discern the four types of abandoned phenomena belonging to one’s own level, as well as the five types of abandoned phenomena pertaining to the form realm and the formless realm?
Answer: One can discern them.

That is to say: either denying the cause, or grasping it as venerable, or grasping it as supreme, or grasping it as excellent, or grasping it as foremost; or being deluded, or doubting, or hesitating; or lacking wisdom, or being in darkness, or being ignorant; or any discernment that is not brought about by correct reasoning.
Can a mind belonging to the desire realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation discern phenomena belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation?
Answer: It can discern them.

That is to say: either grasping at something as venerable, or grasping at it as superior, or grasping at it as foremost, or grasping at it as the best; or [grasping] through greed, hatred, pride, or delusion; or any discernment that is not brought about by correct reasoning.
"Can one also discern phenomena that are unconditioned by the realms?
Answer: One can discern them."
That is to say: either denying cessation, or discerning with doubt, or discerning with delusion, or discerning as induced by improper reflection;
such discernment, and other forms of non-discernment.
Can the various minds bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing discern phenomena bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing?
Answer: They can discern them.

That is to say: either grasping [it] as venerable, or grasping it as superior, or grasping it as excellent, or grasping it as foremost, or grasping it as pure, or grasping it as liberation, or grasping it as renunciation; or, through greed, hatred, pride, or delusion, there is a discrimination induced by improper mental application.
"Can one also discern phenomena that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
He replied:
"One can discern them."
That is to say, it is either the denial of the Path, or discernment characterized by doubt, or discernment characterized by delusion, or discernment induced by improper mental application.
Such discernment is what is meant here; other forms of discernment are not.
Can the minds of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation discern phenomena of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: They can discern them.

That is to say: whether it be greed, hatred, pride, or delusion; whether it be coarse, suffering, or an obstruction; whether it be like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, or like an affliction; whether it be impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; whether it be regarded as a cause, as an origin, as an arising, or as a condition; whether there be a cause, an origination, such a possibility, or such a fact; whether it be a discernment induced by correct reasoning, a discernment induced by incorrect reasoning, or a discernment induced neither by correct nor by incorrect reasoning.
Can one also discern the four kinds of phenomena to be abandoned within one's own stage?
Answer: One can discern them.

Whether as coarse, or as suffering, or as an obstruction; whether as like a disease, or like an abscess, or like an arrow, or as affliction and harm; whether as impermanent, or as suffering, or as empty, or as non-self; whether regarding causes as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; whether there is a cause, or an origination, or this possibility, or this fact; whether it is a discernment induced in accordance with reality, or a discernment neither induced in accordance with reality nor not induced in accordance with reality.
"Can one also discern the four types of dharmas associated with the form realm and the formless realm that are to be abandoned?
Answer: One can discern them."

That is to say: whether it be coarse, or painful, or an obstruction; or like a disease, or like an abscess, or like an arrow, or a source of affliction and harm; or impermanent, or suffering, or empty, or non-self; or regarding the cause as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; or that which has a cause, or that which has an origination, or that which has such a possibility, or that which has such a reality; or that which is discerned in accordance with reason.
Can one also discern those phenomena associated with the form realm and the formless realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation?
It is said:
one can discern them.

That is to say: whether as coarse, or painful, or an obstruction; or as calm, or sublime, or renunciation; or as like a disease, or like an abscess, or like an arrow, or like an affliction; or as impermanent, or suffering, or empty, or non-self; or regarding the cause as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; or as having a cause, or having an origination, or having such a possibility, or having such a reality; or as being discerned in accordance with reason.
"Can one also discern phenomena that are unconditioned (aniyata)?
He replied:
"One can discern them."

That is to say: regarding cessation, one discerns it as cessation, as peace, as excellence, and as renunciation; regarding the path, one discerns it as the path, as suchness, as practice, and as emergence; or [one discerns] impermanence, emptiness, or non-self; or that there is a cause, that there is an arising, that there is this possibility, or that there is this fact; or whatever is discerned as being drawn forth in accordance with reality.

Can a mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) discern phenomena associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering?
Answer: It can discern them.

That is to say: clinging to it as a self, or clinging to it as belonging to a self; clinging to it as annihilated, or clinging to it as eternal; denying suffering; or clinging to it as venerable, or clinging to it as supreme, or clinging to it as preeminent, or clinging to it as foremost; or clinging to it as pure, or clinging to it as liberation, or clinging to it as renunciation; or being deluded, or doubtful, or hesitant; or being characterized by greed, pride, or delusion; or any discernment induced by improper mental application.
"Can one also discern the four kinds of phenomena to be abandoned within one's own stage?
He replied:
"One can discern them."

That is to say: clinging to it as a self, or clinging to it as belonging to a self; clinging to it as annihilated, or clinging to it as eternal; denying suffering; or clinging to it as venerable, or clinging to it as supreme, or clinging to it as preeminent, or clinging to it as foremost; or clinging to it as pure, or clinging to it as liberation, or clinging to it as renunciation; or being confused, or doubtful, or hesitant; or lacking wisdom, or being in darkness, or being deluded; or any discernment that is improperly induced.
"Can one also discern the five kinds of phenomena associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned?
Answer: One can discern them."

That is to say: either denying the existence of suffering; or grasping at it as venerable, or as supreme, or as excellent, or as foremost, or as pure, or as liberation, or as transcendence; or being deluded, or doubtful, or hesitant; or lacking wisdom, or being in darkness, or being ignorant; or any discernment that is not brought about by correct reasoning.
Having distinguished them in this way, there are others that are not so distinguished.

Can a mind belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), bound by views and to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), distinguish phenomena belonging to the form realm that are bound by views and to be abandoned through the vision of the origin?
It is said:
it is able to discern.

That is to say, either denying the cause, or grasping it as venerable, or grasping it as superior, or grasping it as excellent, or grasping it as foremost; whether it be delusion, doubt, or hesitation; or greed, pride, or ignorance; or any discernment induced by improper mental application.
Can one also discern the four types of phenomena belonging to one’s own level and the five types of phenomena bound to the formless realm that are to be abandoned?
He replied: "One can discern them. That is to say:

either denying the cause, or grasping [them] as venerable, or grasping [them] as superior, or grasping [them] as excellent, or grasping [them] as foremost; or being deluded, or doubting, or hesitating; or lacking wisdom, or being in darkness, or being ignorant; or discerning in a manner not brought about by correct reasoning."
Having distinguished these in such a manner, others are not so distinguished.
Can a mind belonging to the form realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation distinguish phenomena belonging to the form realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation?
It is said:
It is able to discern.

That is to say, it either clings to [something] as honorable, or clings to it as superior, or clings to it as excellent, or clings to it as foremost; whether it be greed, pride, or delusion, it is a discernment induced by what is not in accordance with reality.
"Can one also discern phenomena that are unconditioned by the realms?
Answer: One can discern them."
That is to say: either the denial of cessation, or discernment accompanied by doubt, or discernment accompanied by delusion, or discernment induced by improper reflection;
such discernment, as well as other forms of non-discernment.

Can the minds associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) discern phenomena associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing?
Answer: They can discern them.

That is to say, it is the conceptualization that [something] is venerable, or superior, or supreme, or foremost, or pure, or liberated, or a means of transcendence; whether it be through greed, pride, or delusion, it is a discernment induced by improper mental application.
"Can one also discern phenomena that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
He replied:
"One can discern them."
That is to say: either the denial of the path, or discernment accompanied by doubt, or discernment accompanied by delusion, or discernment induced by improper mental application.
Such is discernment; that which is other than this is non-discernment.
Can the minds associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation discern phenomena associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: They can discern them.

That is to say: whether it be greed, pride, or delusion; whether it be coarse, suffering, or an obstruction; whether it be calm, sublime, or renunciation; whether it be like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, or like an affliction; whether it be impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; whether it be regarded as a cause, as an origin, as arising, or as a condition; whether there be a cause, an origination, such a possibility, or such a fact; whether it be a discernment induced by correct reasoning, a discernment induced by incorrect reasoning, or a discernment induced neither by correct nor by incorrect reasoning.
Can one also discern the five types of phenomena bound to the desire realm and the four types of phenomena belonging to one's own level that are to be abandoned?
Answer: One can discern them.

That is to say: whether it be coarse, or painful, or an obstruction; or like a disease, or like an ulcer, or like an arrow, or a source of affliction and harm; or impermanent, or suffering, or empty, or non-self; or regarding the cause as a cause, as an origin, as arising, or as a condition; or that there is a cause, that there is an origination, that there is such a possibility, or that there is such a fact; or that which is discerned as being drawn forth in accordance with reality.
Can one also discern the four kinds of phenomena associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned?
Answer: One can discern them.

That is to say: whether it be coarse, or painful, or an obstruction; or like a disease, like an abscess, or like an arrow, or a source of affliction and harm; or impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; or regarding the cause as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; or that which has a cause, that which has an origination, that for which there is a possibility, or that for which there is a reality; or that which is discerned in accordance with reason.
"Can it also discern the factors associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: It can discern them."

That is to say: as coarse, as painful, as an obstruction; as calm, as sublime, as renunciation; as like a disease, as like an ulcer, as like an arrow, as an affliction; as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, as non-self; or regarding the cause as cause, as origin, as arising, as condition; or as having a cause, as having an origination, as being possible, as being factual; or as discerned in accordance with reality.
"Can one also discern phenomena that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
He replied:
'One can discern them.'"

That is to say: regarding cessation, one discerns it as cessation, as peace, as sublime, and as renunciation; regarding the path, one discerns it as the path, as suchness, as practice, and as emergence; or [one discerns] impermanence, emptiness, or non-self; or that there is a cause, that there is an arising, that there is this possibility, or that there is this fact; or that which is induced by correct reasoning.

Can a mind belonging to the formless realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering discern phenomena belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering?
Answer: It can discern them.

That is to say: clinging to it as a self, or clinging to it as belonging to a self; clinging to it as annihilated, or clinging to it as eternal; denying the existence of suffering; or clinging to it as venerable, or clinging to it as superior, or clinging to it as supreme, or clinging to it as foremost; or clinging to it as pure, or clinging to it as liberation, or clinging to it as deliverance; or being confused, or doubtful, or hesitant; or being characterized by craving, pride, or delusion; or any discernment that is improperly induced.
Can one also discern the four kinds of phenomena to be abandoned within one's own stage?
Answer: One can discern them.

That is to say: grasping at it as a self, or grasping at it as belonging to a self; grasping at it as annihilated, or grasping at it as eternal; denying suffering; grasping at it as venerable, or grasping at it as supreme, or grasping at it as excellent, or grasping at it as foremost; or grasping at it as pure, or grasping at it as liberation, or grasping at it as transcendence; or being deluded, or doubtful, or hesitant; or any discernment induced by improper mental application.
Thus it is discerned, while others are not so discerned.

Can a mind belonging to the formless realm, bound by the fetters of the formless realm and to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering], discern phenomena belonging to the formless realm that are bound by the fetters of the formless realm and to be abandoned through the vision of the origin?
It is said:
It is that which is able to discern.

This refers to either denying causes, or grasping [something] as venerable, or grasping it as superior, or grasping it as excellent, or grasping it as foremost; or being deluded, or doubtful, or hesitant; or having greed, or pride, or ignorance; or any discernment induced by improper mental application.
Can one also discern the four kinds of phenomena to be abandoned within one's own stage?
Answer: One can discern them.

That is to say: either denying the cause; or clinging to it as venerable, or clinging to it as supreme, or clinging to it as excellent, or clinging to it as foremost; or being deluded, or doubting, or hesitating; or lacking wisdom, or being in darkness, or being ignorant; or any discernment that is improperly induced.
Having distinguished these in this way, others are not so distinguished.

Can a mind belonging to the formless realm, bound by the fetters and to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, distinguish phenomena belonging to the formless realm that are bound by the fetters and to be abandoned through the vision of cessation?
It is said:
it is able to discern.

That is to say, either grasping [it] as honorable, or grasping it as superior, or grasping it as excellent, or grasping it as foremost; whether it be greed, pride, or delusion, it is a discernment induced by what is not in accordance with reality.
"Can one also discern phenomena that are unconditioned?
He replied,
"One can discern them."
That is to say: either the denial of cessation, or discernment accompanied by doubt, or discernment accompanied by delusion, or discernment induced by improper reflection;
such discernment, and other forms of non-discernment.
Can the minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the path of vision discern phenomena associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the path of vision?
Answer: They can discern them.

That is to say, it is the conceptualization that regards something as venerable, or superior, or excellent, or foremost, or pure, or liberated, or a means of transcendence; whether it be through craving, pride, or delusion, it is a discrimination induced by improper mental application.
"Can one also discern phenomena that are unconditioned by the realms?
Answer: One can discern them."
That is to say, it refers to either the denial of the Path, or discernment characterized by doubt, or discernment characterized by delusion, or discernment induced by improper mental application;
such is discernment, while other forms are non-discernment.

Can the various minds associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation discern phenomena associated with the formless realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: They can discern them.

That is to say: whether it be greed, pride, or delusion; whether it be coarse, suffering, or an obstruction; whether it be calm, sublime, or renunciation; whether it be like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, or like an affliction; whether it be impermanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; whether it be regarded as a cause, as an origin, as arising, or as a condition; whether there be a cause, an origination, such a possibility, or such a fact; whether it be a discernment induced by correct reasoning, a discernment induced by incorrect reasoning, or a discernment induced by neither correct nor incorrect reasoning.
Can one also discern the four kinds of phenomena to be abandoned within one's own stage?
Answer: One can discern them.

That is to say: whether as coarse, or as suffering, or as an obstruction; or as like a disease, or like an abscess, or like an arrow, or as affliction and harm; or as impermanent, or as suffering, or as empty, or as non-self; or regarding the cause as cause, as origin, as arising, or as condition; or as having a cause, or having an origination, or having this possibility, or having this fact; or as discernment induced in accordance with reality, or as discernment neither induced in accordance with reality nor not induced in accordance with reality.
"Is it also able to discern the five kinds of dharmas bound to the realm of form that are to be abandoned?
Answer: It is able to discern them."
That is to say: if [a phenomenon] is coarse, or suffering, or an obstruction, and is discerned as it is induced by correct reasoning, can it also discern phenomena that are unconditioned?
He replied:
It is the discernment that understands:

regarding cessation as cessation, as peace, as excellence, and as liberation; regarding the path as the path, as suchness, as practice, and as emergence; or as impermanent, as empty, or as non-self; or as having a cause, as having an origin, as having this possibility, or as being this fact—discerning in accordance with reality.
Thus they are discerned, while others are not so discerned.
There are fifteen types of mind: namely, five minds bound to the desire realm, five minds bound to the form realm, and five minds bound to the formless realm.
What are the five types of mind bound to the desire realm?

They are: the mind bound to the desire realm abandoned through the vision of suffering, and the minds bound to the desire realm abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation.
As it is with the five types of mind bound to the desire realm, so it is with the five types of mind bound to the form realm and the formless realm.

Regarding those minds bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), if they are able to discern phenomena bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are present as latent increases (*anuśerate*) therein?
If one can discern other dharmas, how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are there that increase therein?

This continues up to the mind belonging to the formless realm, abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which, if it can discern dharmas belonging to the formless realm abandoned through cultivation, how many underlying tendencies are there that increase therein?
If one can discern other dharmas, how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase therein?

Regarding a mind bound to the desire realm that is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), if it can discern dharmas bound to the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering, all underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of suffering and the pervasive underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) increase therein.

If one can discern the remaining dharmas, herein there are likewise all latent dispositions (anuśaya) bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, as well as the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin; these are what increase by way of association.

Regarding all minds bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), if they can discern phenomena bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of the origin, then within these [minds], all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of the origin, as well as the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), are those that increase through association.

If one can discern the remaining phenomena within this context, there are also all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), which increase in accordance with them.

Regarding all minds bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), if they can discern phenomena bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, then within these [minds], there are the outflow-bound (*āsrava-ālambana*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions which increase through association.

If one can discern those phenomena that are not bound [to any realm], within these there are all latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation that are bound to the desire realm, as well as universal latent dispositions; these are what increase in accordance with them.

Regarding all minds bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*), if they can discern phenomena bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing, then among these there are outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) objects-conditioned (*ālambana*) proclivities (*anuśaya*) and universal (*sarvatraga*) proclivities bound to the desire realm that are subject to increase (*anuśerate*).

If one is able to discern those phenomena that are not bound, within this state there are all latent dispositions (anuśaya) bound to the desire realm to be abandoned by the path of vision, as well as the universal latent dispositions, which are what increase through association.

Regarding all minds bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), if they can discern phenomena bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation, then within these [minds], all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*), are those that increase by way of being associated with them.

If one is able to discern the remaining dharmas, within these there are all latent dispositions (anuśaya) bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the universal latent dispositions; these are what increase [in association] with them.
As it is with the mind bound to the desire realm, so it is with the minds bound to the form realm and the formless realm.
There are fifteen minds: namely, five minds bound to the desire realm, five minds bound to the form realm, and five minds bound to the formless realm.
What are the five types of mind bound to the desire realm?

They are: the mind bound to the desire realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, and the minds bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as by cultivation.
As it is with the five types of mind bound to the desire realm, so it is with the five types of mind bound to the form realm and the formless realm.
These fifteen states of mind are either wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, or unobscured-neutral.

Regarding the wholesome mind of the desire realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are present as latent increases within the consciousness that takes this [wholesome mind] as its object?

Regarding all unwholesome minds, obscured-unspecified minds, and non-obscured-unspecified minds bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*): how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are augmented by these cognitions that take them as objects?

As it is with the mind abandoned through the vision of suffering, so it is with the minds abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation.
As it is for those bound to the desire realm, so it is for those bound to the form realm and the formless realm.

Regarding all minds bound to the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), there are none that are wholesome or unobscured-neutral; nor is there any consciousness capable of taking such minds as its object, for they are exclusively unwholesome or obscured-neutral.

In this cognizing consciousness, there are the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three categories of the desire realm, as well as the universal latent dispositions belonging to the form realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation; these are what increase by way of being associated with it.

Among all minds bound to the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering], there are none that are wholesome, obscured-unspecified, or unobscured-unspecified; nor is there any consciousness capable of taking such a mind as its object, for they are exclusively unwholesome.

This cognizing consciousness is subject to the increase of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three categories of the desire realm, as well as the universal latent dispositions belonging to the form realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation.

Among the various minds bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, there are none that are wholesome, obscured-neutral, or unobscured-neutral; nor is there any consciousness capable of taking such a mind as its object—there is only the unwholesome.

In this cognizing consciousness, there are the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the three categories belonging to the desire realm, as well as the outflow-conditions (sāsrava-ālambana) latent dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of cessation belonging to the desire realm, the universal latent dispositions belonging to the form realm, and the latent dispositions to be abandoned by cultivation; these are what increase through association.

Among the various minds bound to the desire realm that are abandoned by the path of seeing, there are none that are wholesome, obscured-neutral, or unobscured-neutral; nor is there any consciousness capable of taking such minds as its object—there is only the unwholesome.

This cognizing consciousness is subject to the increase of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three categories of the desire realm, the outflow-conditions (sāsrava) latent dispositions to be abandoned by the path of vision (darśana-mārga) within the desire realm, the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) belonging to the form realm, and the latent dispositions to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya). These are what increase [in association] with it.

Regarding all minds bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation, there are none that are obscured-unspecified; nor is there any consciousness capable of taking such a mind as its object. There are, however, minds that are wholesome, unwholesome, or unobscured-unspecified.
