This cognizing consciousness is subject to the increase of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three categories of the desire realm, as well as the universal latent dispositions belonging to the form realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation.

All minds bound to the form realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering are neither wholesome, unwholesome, nor unobscured-neutral; furthermore, there is no consciousness capable of taking such a mind as its object, for there is only the obscured-neutral.

This cognizing consciousness is subject to the increase of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the desire realm and the form realm belonging to the three categories, the universal latent dispositions associated with the formless realm, and the latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation.

Regarding all minds associated with the form realm that are abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering], there is neither wholesome, unwholesome, nor unobscured-neutral [mind]; furthermore, there is no consciousness capable of taking such a mind as its object, for there is only the obscured-neutral.

This cognizing consciousness is subject to increase through the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the desire realm and the form realm belonging to the three categories, the universal latent dispositions associated with the formless realm, and the latent dispositions to be abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding all minds associated with the form realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), there are none that are wholesome, unwholesome, or undefiled-neutral; nor is there any consciousness capable of taking such a mind as its object, for there is only the obscured-neutral (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*).

This cognizing consciousness is subject to increase by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the desire realm and the three categories associated with the form realm; the contaminated-object latent dispositions associated with the form realm to be abandoned through the vision of cessation; the universal latent dispositions associated with the formless realm; and the latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation. These are what increase within it.

The various minds of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) bound by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) that are to be abandoned are neither wholesome, unwholesome, nor unobscured-neutral; furthermore, there is no consciousness capable of taking these minds as its object, for there is only the obscured-neutral.

This cognizing consciousness is subject to the increase of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the desire realm and the three categories belonging to the form realm; the outflow-conditions (sāsrava-ālambana) latent dispositions to be abandoned by the path of vision belonging to the form realm; the universal latent dispositions belonging to the formless realm; and the latent dispositions to be abandoned by cultivation. These are what increase in association with it.

Among the minds associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there are none that are unwholesome (*akuśala*). Furthermore, there is no consciousness capable of taking such a mind as its object; rather, there are wholesome (*kuśala*), obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), and unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) [minds].

This cognizing consciousness is subject to the increase of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three categories of the desire realm and the form realm, the universal latent dispositions belonging to the formless realm, and the latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation.

The various minds of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) associated with the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) are neither wholesome, unwholesome, nor unobscured-neutral; furthermore, there is no consciousness that can take these minds as its object, for there exists only the obscured-neutral [consciousness].
Regarding this cognizing consciousness, there are latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and the three categories that increase in accordance with it.

As for all minds bound to the formless realm that are abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya), they are neither wholesome, unwholesome, nor unobscured-neutral; furthermore, there is no consciousness capable of taking these minds as its object, but only that which is obscured-neutral.
Regarding this cognizing consciousness, there are latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and the three categories that increase in accordance with it.

As for all minds of the formless realm associated with the cessation of views (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), they are neither wholesome, unwholesome, nor unobscured-neutral; furthermore, there is no consciousness capable of taking these minds as its object, but only that which is obscured-neutral (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*).

This cognizing consciousness is subject to increase by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and the three categories, as well as the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) objects-of-perception latent dispositions belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation. These are what it increases.

The various minds of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) bound by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) that are to be abandoned are neither wholesome, unwholesome, nor unobscured-neutral; furthermore, there is no consciousness capable of taking these minds as its object, for there exists only the obscured-neutral.

This cognizing consciousness is subject to increase by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and the three categories, as well as the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) object-conditioned latent dispositions of the formless realm that are to be abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga). These are what it is increased by.

Among the minds associated with the formless realm that are abandoned through cultivation, there are none that are unwholesome, nor is there any consciousness capable of taking such a mind as its object; rather, they are wholesome, obscured-unspecified, or unobscured-unspecified.
Regarding this cognizing consciousness, there are latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and the three categories that increase in accordance with it.
*Sarvāstivāda-vijñānakāya-śāstra*, Fascicle Ten;
*Abhidharma-vijñānakāya-śāstra*, Fascicle Eleven.
Composed by the Arhat Devaśarman;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
In the first section on the Aggregate of the Miscellaneous, first are the defiled [dharmas], followed by those that are cognizable, matter, feeling, perception, and the world.
The immediate condition increases the severance of wholesome roots and defilements; through the division of views, conditions, and elements, there is subsequent discernment.
There are six groups of consciousness, namely: eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
The five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) can only give rise to defilement and cannot be free from it;
the group of mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna-kāya*) can both give rise to defilement and be free from it.

The minds of those in the hell realm (*naraka-gati*), the animal realm (*tiryagyoni-gati*), the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*), those who have severed their roots of goodness (*samucchinna-kuśala-mūla*), those fixed in wrongness (*mithyātva-niyata*), those in Uttarakuru, and non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) can only give rise to defilement and cannot be free from it.
The minds of sentient beings in the indeterminate class, the fixed-in-rightness class, Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, and Aparagoyānī can both give rise to defilement and become free from defilement.

The minds of beings in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahma-world heavens, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, and the Bṛhatphala Heaven—excluding those of the non-percipient beings—as well as the minds of beings in the intermediate state and in the formless realms, are likewise capable of becoming defiled and are likewise capable of being freed from defilement.

The minds of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) are capable only of abandoning defilement; they are not capable of giving rise to defilement.

The minds of those who have attained through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those who have attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and those who have realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*) are capable both of giving rise to defilement and of abandoning defilement.
The minds of those liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*) and those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*) are neither capable of producing defilement nor capable of abandoning defilement.
Some say that these two are also capable of abandoning defilement, speaking from the perspective of remote separation (*dūrabhāga*).
There are six groups of consciousness, namely: eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
All material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are cognized by these six consciousnesses; however, only material phenomena are cognized by the five [sensory] consciousnesses.
All formless phenomena (*arūpadharma*) are cognized by a single consciousness; only formless phenomena are not cognized by consciousness.
All visible phenomena (*sanidarśanadharma*) are cognized by two consciousnesses; only visible phenomena are cognized by a single consciousness.
All non-visible phenomena (*anidarśana*) are cognized by the five consciousnesses; only non-visible phenomena are cognized by four consciousnesses.
All resistant phenomena (*sapratigha*) are cognized by the six consciousnesses; only resistant phenomena are cognized by the five consciousnesses.
All non-obstructive dharmas are cognized by a single consciousness; only non-obstructive dharmas are not cognized by consciousness.
All contaminated dharmas are cognized by the six consciousnesses; only contaminated dharmas are cognized by the five [sensory] consciousnesses.
All untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena are cognized by a single consciousness; only untainted phenomena are not cognized by consciousness.
All conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena are cognized by the six consciousnesses; only conditioned phenomena are cognized by the five [sensory] consciousnesses.
All unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are cognized by a single consciousness; however, only unconditioned phenomena themselves are not cognized by consciousness.
There are six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*), namely: eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.

With the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises. If various blue forms are accompanied by what is agreeable and pleasant, one discerns this blue as being accompanied by what is agreeable and pleasant; through contact, feeling, perception, and volition, this blue form proceeds as being accompanied by what is agreeable and pleasant. By means of this, one is able to nourish the sense faculties and augment the primary elements.

With the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises. If various blue forms are disagreeable and accompanied by suffering, the discernment of these blue forms as disagreeable and accompanied by suffering, and the contact, feeling, perception, and volition regarding these blue forms, turn into something disagreeable and accompanied by suffering; by this, one is able to diminish the sense faculties and destroy the primary elements.

With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises. If a certain blue form is neither agreeable nor disagreeable, and is accompanied by neither suffering nor pleasure, then the discernment of this blue is neither agreeable nor disagreeable, and is accompanied by neither suffering nor pleasure. Contact, feeling, perception, and volition regarding this blue form proceed as neither agreeable nor disagreeable, and are accompanied by neither suffering nor pleasure. Consequently, the faculties are neither nourished nor impaired; the great elements are likewise neither increased nor destroyed.
As it is with blue, so it is with yellow, red, and white.
As it is with visual consciousness, so it is with auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses.

With the mind and mental objects as conditions, mental consciousness arises; if there are various phenomena associated with what is agreeable and pleasant, one discerns these phenomena as associated with what is agreeable and pleasant, and contact, feeling, perception, and volition proceed in association with what is agreeable and pleasant. By this, one is able to nourish the sense faculties and increase the primary elements.

With the mind and mental objects as conditions, mental consciousness arises. If there are various phenomena that are disagreeable to the mind and accompanied by suffering, and one discriminates these phenomena as being disagreeable to the mind and accompanied by suffering, then contact, feeling, perception, and volition—all these factors operate in a manner that is disagreeable to the mind and accompanied by suffering; by this, the sense faculties are diminished and the primary elements are destroyed.

With the mind and mental objects as conditions, mental consciousness arises. If there are mental objects that are neither agreeable nor disagreeable, and are accompanied by neither suffering nor pleasure, the discernment of these objects is neither agreeable nor disagreeable, and is accompanied by neither suffering nor pleasure. Contact, feeling, perception, and volition associated with these phenomena proceed in a manner that is neither agreeable nor disagreeable, and are accompanied by neither suffering nor pleasure. Consequently, these faculties are neither nourished nor impaired; the primary elements likewise neither increase nor deteriorate.

There are some forms that possess color but lack shape; there are some forms that possess shape but lack color; there are some forms that possess both color and shape; and there are some forms that possess neither color nor shape.

Those that have manifestation but no shape refer to the single category of manifest color: blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, light, brightness, darkness, and space; these are just like those [colors]—blue, yellow, red, and white.
That which has form but no manifestation refers to bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*).
That which has both manifestation and form refers to those material phenomena (*rūpa*) that possess both manifestation and form.
That which has neither manifestation nor form refers to those material phenomena that possess neither manifestation nor form.
Is there such a case where this mind is bound by these fetters and this karma is performed, and yet this very mind and this very karma are themselves the fruit of those fetters?
He replied: "There is."
Just as a mind bound to the desire realm and karma bound to the desire realm result in fruits bound to the desire realm;
so too do minds and karma bound to the form and formless realms result in fruits bound to the form and formless realms.
Is there a case where this mind and this karma are bound by this bond, yet this mind and this karma are not the fruit of this bond?
He replied: "There is."
Just as one on the path of the form realm manifests transformations in the desire realm, performing deeds of the desire realm and speaking the language of the desire realm;
so too does one on the path of the form or formless realms sever the fetters and realize their cessation.
If all feelings are past, have all these feelings already ceased?
It is said:
If all feelings are past, all these feelings have already ceased.
If a feeling has already ceased, is this feeling not of the past? That is to say, it refers to a feeling that has arisen within this present life and subsequently ceased.
As for all feelings of the future, are all such feelings yet to arise?
It is said:
Regarding those sensations that are future, all such sensations have not yet arisen.
Or, there may be sensations that have not yet arisen which are not "future," namely, those sensations within this present life that are certain to arise.
If all sensations are present, are all these sensations manifest?
It is said:
If all sensations are manifest, all these sensations are present.

Or there are feelings that are experienced in the present, yet these feelings are not manifest; that is to say, feelings within this life that have already arisen and ceased, as well as feelings within this life that are certain to arise. There are six types of mind:

the mind associated with the desire realm to be abandoned by insight, the mind associated with the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation; the mind associated with the form realm to be abandoned by insight, the mind associated with the form realm to be abandoned by cultivation; and the mind associated with the formless realm to be abandoned by insight, the mind associated with the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation.
Is there any mind bound to the desire realm that is abandoned by insight which is determined to take only wholesome phenomena as its object?
Or only unwholesome phenomena? Or only obscured-neutral phenomena?
Do they take only non-obscured, neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena as their objects?
As it is with the mind abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), so it is with the mind abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
As it is for those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), so it is for those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Is there any mind bound to the desire realm that is abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) which is determined to take only wholesome phenomena as its object?
It is said:
Yes; namely, those minds associated with the outflows-toward-the-ineffable (*anāsrava-ālambana-anuśaya*) that are abandoned through insight into cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).
Is there any mind bound to the desire realm that is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) which is determined to take only unwholesome phenomena as its object?
It is said:

Yes. This refers to those minds associated with the non-universal (*asarvatraga*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned by insight into the origin (*samudaya*) of suffering, as well as those minds associated with the outflow-bound (*sāsrava*) latent dispositions abandoned by insight into cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).

Is there any mind belonging to the desire realm that is abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) which necessarily takes only obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas or unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas as its object? He replied: No.
Is there any mind bound to the desire realm that is abandoned through cultivation which is determinately directed only toward wholesome phenomena?
It is said:
There is; namely, those minds associated with the emptiness-of-emptiness and the wishlessness-of-wishlessness that are bound to the desire realm.
Is there any mind belonging to the desire realm that is abandoned through cultivation and which is determined to take only unwholesome dharmas or obscured-neutral dharmas as its object? Answer: No.
Is there a mind bound to the desire realm that is abandoned through cultivation and which definitely takes only non-obscured-neutral phenomena as its object?
Answer: Yes;
namely, the three groups of consciousness bound to the desire realm, and those minds bound to the desire realm that are associated with the signless and the signless-less.
Is there any mind associated with the form realm that is abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) which is determined to take only wholesome phenomena as its object?
Answer: Yes;
namely, those minds associated with the outflows-toward-the-ineffable (*anāsrava-ālambana-anuśaya*) that are abandoned through insight into cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).
Is there any mind bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) that is abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and which necessarily takes only unwholesome phenomena as its object? Answer: No.

Is there any mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) that is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and which necessarily takes only obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena as its object?

Answer: There is. Specifically, it refers to those minds associated with the non-universal (*asarvatraga*) proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through seeing suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) within the form realm, as well as those minds associated with the outflow-bound (*sāsrava-ālambana*) proclivities abandoned through seeing cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) within the form realm.

Is there any mind belonging to the realm of form that is abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and which necessarily takes only non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena as its object? Answer: No.
Is there a mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) which necessarily takes only wholesome phenomena as its object?
Answer: Yes;
namely, those minds associated with the emptiness-of-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) and the wishlessness-of-wishlessness (*apraṇihitāpraṇihita*) that are bound to the form realm.

Is there any mind belonging to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which necessarily takes only unwholesome (*akuśala*) phenomena or obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena as its object? Answer: No.

Is there a mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) which necessarily takes only non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena as its object?
Answer: Yes;
namely, one group of consciousnesses (*vijñānakāya*) bound to the form realm, and all minds associated with the signless-of-the-signless (*animittānimitta*) samādhi that are bound to the form realm.
Is there any mind associated with the formless realm that is abandoned through insight and which necessarily takes only wholesome phenomena as its object?
Answer: There is;

namely, those minds associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object and are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path within the formless realm.
Is there any mind bound to the formless realm that is to be abandoned by insight and which exclusively takes unwholesome phenomena as its object? Answer: No.

Is there any mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that is abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and which necessarily takes only obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena as its object?
Answer: There is.

Namely, those minds associated with the non-universal (*asarvatraga*) proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through insight into suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) within the formless realm, as well as those minds associated with the tainted-object (*sāsravālambana*) proclivities abandoned through insight into cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga*) within the formless realm.

Is there any mind connected with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and which necessarily takes only non-obscured neutral phenomena (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-dharma*) as its object? Answer: No.
Is there any mind associated with the formless realm that is to be abandoned through cultivation which is determined to take only wholesome phenomena as its object?
It is said:
Yes; namely, those minds associated with the formless realm that are linked with the emptiness-of-emptiness and the wishlessness-of-wishlessness.

Is there any mind belonging to the formless realm that is abandoned through cultivation, which is determined to take only unwholesome phenomena or obscured-neutral phenomena as its object? Answer: No.

Is there any mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and which definitely takes only non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena as its object?
It is said:
Yes; namely, those minds associated with the signless-of-the-signless (*animittānimitta*) that belong to the formless realm.

Are there any phenomena that are mundane, with outflows, conforming to grasping, and included within the aggregates of grasping; which arise from internal origination and through discernment; which are sublime, wholesome, and bound to the desire realm; and which exist only for noble ones and not at all for foolish ordinary worldlings?
He said: Yes;
it refers to the various conventional knowledges (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) at the final stage following the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) pertaining to the desire realm.

He said: Yes;

Are there any phenomena that are mundane, with outflows (*sāsrava*), conforming to grasping, and included within the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*), which arise internally through their own deliberation and so forth, belong to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), exist only for noble ones (*ārya*), and are not shared by any foolish ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)?

up to how many minds arise immediately after a mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Immediately after a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, nine minds arise.
An unwholesome mind and a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the desire realm give rise, as their immediate antecedents, to four minds;
a mind that is unobscured-unspecified gives rise, as its immediate antecedent, to seven minds.

a obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) and an unobscured-unspecified mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) arise immediately after six minds.
A wholesome mind associated with the formless realm arises immediately after nine minds;

A mind of training (śaikṣa) arises immediately after five minds;

Regarding the unobscured-unspecified mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the formless realm, it is said to act as a condition by way of the single dominant condition alone.

The mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-citta) acts as a condition for the mind of one beyond training by way of the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya). Thus it is said to be able to serve as a condition.

Regarding a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, it is said to function as a condition by way of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Regarding an unwholesome mind, it is said to function as a condition by way of the object condition and the dominant condition.

Regarding the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is said that they can act as conditions by way of the single predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

Regarding the wholesome minds (*kuśalacitta*) bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is said that they can act as conditions by way of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), and the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

Regarding the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the form realm, it is said to act as a condition by way of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Regarding the unobscured-unspecified mind associated with the form realm, it is said to act as a condition by way of the single dominant condition alone.

Regarding the wholesome mind associated with the formless realm, it is said to act as a condition by way of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Regarding the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the formless realm, it is said to act as a condition by way of the object-condition and the dominant condition.
Regarding the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm, it is said to act as a condition by virtue of one predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Regarding the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*), it is said to act as a condition by virtue of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the predominant condition.
What is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*)?
It refers to the case where, with the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; this visual consciousness takes the eye as its dominant condition.

It is likewise for visible forms, the ear and sounds and auditory consciousness, the nose and odors and olfactory consciousness, the tongue and tastes and gustatory consciousness, the body and tangibles and tactile consciousness, and the mind and mental phenomena and mental consciousness.

Whether these are associated dharmas or co-existent dharmas, whether they are material or immaterial, visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—all such dharmas serve as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), with the sole exception of their own nature (*svabhāva*).

In this way, with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as conditions, mental consciousness arises. This mental consciousness takes the mind as its predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and it also takes as its predominant conditions the mental objects (*dharma*), the eye and visible forms along with visual consciousness, the ear and sounds along with auditory consciousness, the nose and odors along with olfactory consciousness, the tongue and tastes along with gustatory consciousness, the body and tangibles along with tactile consciousness, as well as all associated factors (*samprayukta-dharma*) and co-existent factors (*sahabhū-dharma*). Whether they are material or immaterial, visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant, outflowing (*āsrava*) or non-outflowing, conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned—all such phenomena serve as predominant conditions, with the sole exception of their own nature (*svabhāva*).
This is called the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Regarding those who sever their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), how do they sever them?
By what mode of activity (*ākāra*) are they severed?

That is to say, there is one who kills his mother, kills his father, kills an arhat, causes a schism in the Saṃgha, and with a violent and evil mind draws the blood of a Tathāgata; such a person is able to sever their roots of goodness.
Regarding those who intentionally take the life of their mother, how do they kill her?
By what mode of action do they kill her?

It is as follows: there is someone possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion, whose nature is fierce and sharp; because of that fierce and sharp greed, hatred, and delusion, he is addicted to gambling, fond of wine, and given over to lust; he delights in evil friends and evil companions, and becomes habituated to various forms of heedlessness.
His mother, with single-minded resolve, restrained and forbade him, saying:
"My son, my son!

From now on, do not again take pleasure in gambling, nor indulge in wine, nor be addicted to lust; do not favor evil friends or evil companions, and do not habitually practice any of the various forms of heedlessness."
"You must not now go to the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.
You must not now fall into the various evil places or be born in the various evil destinies.
Because his mother was so intent on restraining and forbidding him, he gave rise to fierce anger toward her; unable to endure it and lacking faith, he uttered these words of grievance:
“Alas, what bitter poison!
How can my mother restrain me from my beloved companions—those friends and associates of gambling, wine, and lust?
If she again performs such harmful acts toward me, I shall certainly take her life.”
In this way, it is able to be severed.

However, at another time, the anger he had previously aroused becomes further intensified, hardened, and inflamed through his lack of forbearance and lack of faith; because that aroused anger, lack of forbearance, and lack of faith become successively more intense, firm, and blazing, he again gives rise at a later time to such an entanglement of anger that is to be abandoned through cultivation.
Because he is bound by this entanglement of hatred, he deliberately initiates the intent to take his mother’s life.
Due to such types of physical action, verbal action, and mental volition—characterized by seeking, wishing, and striving—he is said to possess "wrongness."

By this, one abandons what was previously accomplished—the designations, conceptualizations, and conventional expressions that abide in the indeterminate group and the indeterminate lineage—and by this, one acquires what was previously unaccomplished: the designations, conceptualizations, and conventional expressions that abide in the wrongly fixed group and the wrongly fixed lineage. One thereby acquires the five types of persons, the mixed class, the associated class, and the evil homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga), as well as the acquisition of state, the acquisition of object, and the acquisition of birthplace—namely: killing one’s mother, killing one’s father, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and with a malicious and wrathful mind, drawing the blood of a Tathāgata.
Regarding those who intentionally take the life of their mother, they harm her in such a manner.
This mode of harming is as described for killing one's mother; it is the same for killing one's father.
As for those who take the lives of Śrāvakas and Arhats, how do they harm them?
What is the mode of action that causes harm?

It refers to a certain person who, regarding the robes and alms bowl of a śrāvaka arhat, or any single requisite for the life of a śramaṇa acquired in accordance with the Dharma, gives rise to extreme craving and attachment, binding their mind to it without relinquishing it.
He reflects thus: "I must now, according to my capacity, steal from him by stealth.
If, because of this, he should inflict harm upon me—binding, imprisoning, demoting, rebuking, reviling, or causing me to fall into a lowly and ignoble station—I shall certainly take his life."
In this way, they are able to sever [doubt].
Furthermore, it is like a śrāvaka arhat who, amidst a great assembly, elucidates, establishes, clarifies, and reveals his own discourse, while refuting and obstructing the discourse of others.
Among them, there were certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who harbored views of malice and hostility and propounded doctrines of enmity; they uttered these words of resentment:
"Alas! What bitter poison!"

How is it that such a person, though merely a nominal śramaṇa, when amidst a great assembly, elucidates, establishes, and reveals his own discourse, while refuting and obstructing the discourse of others?
"If anyone should again perform such harmful acts against me, I shall certainly destroy their life-force.
Thinking thus, he is able to sever [the connection].
At another time, the anger, intolerance, and lack of faith that he had previously aroused become even more intense, firm, and blazing.

Due to the arising of anger, intolerance, and lack of faith—which become progressively more intense, firm, and blazing—one subsequently gives rise to such fetters of anger that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
Because they are bound by this entanglement of hatred, they intentionally bring about the death of a śrāvaka arhat.

Due to such types of bodily action, verbal action, and mental volition characterized by seeking and wishing, they are said to possess "wrong nature" (*mithyātva*). Consequently, they abandon all previously accomplished designations, conceptual identifications, and conventional expressions, and come to abide in the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) and the indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*).

By this, they acquire for the first time those designations, conceptualizations, and conventional expressions that were previously unestablished; they abide in the category of the wrongly fixed and the lineage of the wrongly fixed.

They acquire five types of persons, belonging to a mixed class and a class of companions, sharing an evil commonality of destiny, and attaining their state, their object, and their place of birth—namely: killing one's mother, killing one's father, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and with a malicious and wrathful mind, drawing blood from the body of a Tathāgata.
Regarding those who take the life of a śrāvaka arhat, they harm them in such a manner; this is the mode of harming.
Regarding those who cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha of the Tathāgata’s śrāvaka disciples, how do they cause that schism?
What is the mode of refutation?

It is as follows: suppose there is someone who perceives what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and perceives what is not the Vinaya as the Vinaya; yet they do not conceal this perception, do not conceal this acceptance, and do not conceal such a delight in wisdom, insight, and vision.

He instructs, exhorts, and advises the harmonious Saṃgha of the Tathāgata’s śrāvaka disciples, causing them to joyfully practice, study, and uphold [the teachings], saying: "This is the True Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this is the teaching of the Great Teacher:
'O Venerable Ones!'"

Regarding this True Dharma, this Vinaya, and the teaching of the Great Master, you should now grant your approval, accept it with patience, and clarify it; you should rise and take up the voting tally.

If one who takes up the voting tally as the fifth by means of that body were to be the minimum number of persons required, then although it is said that they can "break" the harmonious Saṃgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples, they cannot produce the offense of dwelling for an eon (*kalpa*).

Furthermore, suppose there is someone who perceives what is not Dharma as Dharma, and what is not Vinaya as Vinaya; yet they do not conceal this perception, do not conceal this acceptance, and do not conceal such a delight in wisdom, insight, and vision.

Regarding the harmonious Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s śrāvaka disciples whom he instructs and exhorts, causing them to joyfully practice, study, and uphold [the teachings], [someone] says: "It is not the True Dharma; it is not the Vinaya; it is not the teaching of the Great Master:
'O Venerable One!'"
Regarding this which is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Great Master, you should now approve, tolerate, and manifest it; you should rise and take up the voting tally.

If one who raises the tally as the fifth by including that person’s own body were to be the minimum number of individuals required, then even if they were said to be able to split the harmonious Saṃgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples, they could not produce the offense of dwelling for an eon.

Furthermore, suppose there is someone who perceives what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and perceives what is not the Vinaya as the Vinaya; he conceals this perception, conceals this acceptance, and conceals such a delight in wisdom, insight, and vision.

He instructs and exhorts the harmonious Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s śrāvaka disciples, causing them to joyfully practice, train, and uphold [the teachings], saying: "This is the True Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this is the teaching of the Great Master:
'O Venerable Ones!'"

Regarding this True Dharma, this Vinaya, and this teaching of the Great Master, you should now grant your approval, accept it with patience, and clarify it; you should rise and take up the voting tally.

If one who takes up the voting tally makes that person the fifth, then at the very least, these number of individuals should be said to be capable of breaking the harmonious Saṃgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples, and they shall also incur the offense that remains for an eon.

Furthermore, suppose there is someone who perceives as Dharma what is Dharma and perceives as Vinaya what is Vinaya; yet they conceal this perception, conceal this acceptance, and conceal such a joyful wisdom-insight, while instructing and exhorting the harmonious Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s śrāvaka disciples, causing them to joyfully train in, study, and uphold [their own views], saying: "O Venerable Ones! This is not the True Dharma, it is not the Vinaya, it is not the teaching of the Great Master.
"Venerable Ones! [he says].
Regarding this which is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Great Master, you should now approve, tolerate, and manifest it; you should rise and take up the voting tally.

If that person, as the fifth, were to take up the voting tally, then at the very least, such a number of individuals should be said to be capable of breaking the harmonious Saṃgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples, and they would also incur the offense that persists for an eon.

Due to such types of bodily action, vocal action, and mental intentions characterized by seeking and aspiring, these are termed "wrong nature" (*mithyātva*). By means of this, one abandons all previously accomplished designations, conceptual identifications, and conventional expressions, and comes to abide in the indeterminate group and the indeterminate lineage.

By this, one acquires for the first time those previously unaccomplished designations, conceptualizations, and conventional expressions; one abides in the group of the wrongly fixed and the lineage of the wrongly fixed.

One acquires the five types of persons, the category of the mixed, the category of the associated, and the acquisition of an evil commonality of lot, the acquisition of place, the acquisition of object, and the acquisition of the place of birth—namely: killing one’s mother, killing one’s father, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and with a violent and malicious mind, drawing blood from the Tathāgata.
Regarding those who disrupt the harmonious Saṃgha of the Tathāgata’s śrāvaka disciples: in what manner do they disrupt it? It is by means of this mode of action that they disrupt it.
Regarding those with violent and malicious intent who shed the blood of a Tathāgata: in what way do they shed it?
What is its mode of activity?
It is as follows: when the Tathāgata is amidst the great assembly, he illuminates, designates, establishes, and reveals his own discourse, while he refutes and obstructs the discourse of others.
Among them, there are certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who harbor views of malice and propound doctrines of malice, uttering these words of resentment:
"Alas, what bitter poison!"

How is it that such a person, though merely a nominal śramaṇa, when standing amidst the great assembly, illuminates, establishes, and elucidates his own discourse, while refuting and obstructing the discourse of others?
"If anyone else should again perform such harmful acts against me, I shall certainly destroy their life-force.
Thinking thus, he was able to sever [the connection].
At another time, the anger, intolerance, and lack of faith that had arisen within him became even more fierce, firm, and intense.

Due to the anger that has arisen—which is characterized by intolerance, lack of faith, and is mutually intense, firm, and blazing—one subsequently gives rise to such an outburst of hatred (*dveṣa-paryavasthāna*) that must be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Because he was thus entangled by the fetter of hatred, he gave rise to a deliberate thought:
"I shall now certainly take the life of the Tathāgata.
However, it is the natural law for all Tathāgatas that no one can take their life; there is only the possibility of drawing the blood of a Tathāgata through the arousal of a violent and evil mind.

By means of such types of bodily action, vocal action, and mental volitions characterized by seeking and aspiring, this is called "wrongness" (*mithyātva*). Consequently, one abandons all previously accomplished designations, conceptual identifications, and conventional expressions, and comes to abide in the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) and the indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*).

By this, one acquires for the first time those designations, conceptualizations, provisional establishments, and verbal expressions that were previously unattained; one abides in the category of those fixed in error and the lineage of those fixed in error.

One acquires the five types of *pudgalas* and the categories of associates and companions of a mixed nature: an evil *nikāyasabhāga*, the acquisition of place, the acquisition of object, and the acquisition of the locus of birth—namely, killing one's mother, killing one's father, killing an *arhat*, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and with a malicious and wrathful mind, drawing blood from the Tathāgata.
Those who, with a violent and malevolent mind, shed the blood of a Tathāgata—thus they emerge; thus this mode of emergence emerges.
