2. Uddāna Verses: Miscellaneous Aggregate, Part Five, Section Two. Regarding those who sever the roots of goodness: how do they sever them?
What are the modes of abandonment?
For example, there is one who intentionally takes the life of his mother or his father and subsequently feels no remorse or regret.
Conversely, there is another who intentionally takes the life of his mother or his father and subsequently feels remorse and regret.

These two kinds of people follow various śramaṇas or brahmins, such as the Ukkalakas or their like, who hold the view of non-existence and establish the doctrine of non-existence; they claim there is no cause and no action, asserting that all various wholesome and unwholesome karmas are annihilated and destroyed.
He went frequently to inquire:
"What is wholesome? What is unwholesome?"
What constitutes an offense?
What constitutes no offense?
By performing what actions does one achieve what is good and avoid what is evil?

Because he has approached, attended upon, and made offerings to such a teacher, he does not give rise to shame or regret for the transgressions he has committed that have not yet arisen, and he swiftly eliminates the shame and regret for those already arisen, saying:
"Killing is foolish and deluded; it is empty and without fruit, devoid of purpose, without origination, without flavor, and without benefit."
There is no killing, nor is there any karmic maturation resulting from killing.

Likewise, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong view—all these are foolish and delusory, devoid of fruit; they are meaningless, without origin, without flavor, and without benefit.
"There is no wrong view, nor is there any maturation resulting from wrong view.
He develops a deep attachment to, acceptance of, and advocacy for this matter.

Because he develops such deep attachment, acceptance, and advocacy for this matter, it is said that this person treads upon the left-hand path—namely, wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.

Because he thus treads upon the left-hand path, his three roots of goodness gradually diminish, become faint, and become interrupted; his three unwholesome roots gradually increase, becoming fierce, sharp, and blazing.
His three types of sublime conduct gradually diminish, become faint, and become interrupted; his three types of evil conduct gradually increase, becoming fierce, sharp, and blazing.
The ten paths of wholesome action gradually diminish, become faint, and become interrupted; the ten paths of unwholesome action gradually increase, becoming fierce, sharp, and blazing.
The Eightfold Noble Path on the right gradually diminishes, becoming thin and fragmented; the eightfold wrong path on the left gradually increases, becoming fierce, sharp, and blazing.

Because they further increase killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong view, they dwell frequently in a state of non-quiescence and frequently in a state of non-restraint.

Although for a short time they may give rise to weak and inferior wholesome states of mind and mental factors accompanied by right view, various evil and unwholesome dharmas nevertheless largely manifest and predominantly reside within their left-hand category.

It is like when the summer heat has passed and the autumn coolness arrives; at the hour of midnight, clouds gather thickly and it becomes pitch black, when a thunderclap and a flash of lightning momentarily emit light, allowing one to briefly behold various forms before they swiftly vanish once more.

Thus, that person dwells frequently in a state of non-quiescence and frequently in a state of non-restraint; although for a brief time they give rise to weak and inferior wholesome states of mind and mental factors accompanied by right view, nevertheless, various evil and unwholesome dharmas predominantly manifest, and they mostly abide on the side of error.
Furthermore, it is like a person at the end of spring or the beginning of summer, distressed by heat and thirst and tormented by hot winds, who enters a cool pond to bathe in its clear, cold water.
Having bathed and drunk, he quickly emerges; all the coarse droplets on his body have fallen away, and only minute droplets remain within his pores.

Thus, that person dwells frequently in a state of non-quiescence and frequently in a state of non-restraint; although for a brief time they may give rise to weak and inferior wholesome states of mind and mental factors accompanied by right view, nevertheless, various evil and unwholesome dharmas largely manifest, and they mostly abide on the side of error.

At a later time, they will also be able to harm the lives of those who are noble and eminent; yet, they feel no sense of shame or remorse, ultimately repudiating the ripening of the fruits of all virtuous and non-virtuous karma.

Because they harm the lives of those who are most venerable and superior without any sense of shame or remorse, and because they ultimately repudiate all the ripening results of wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions, it is said that such persons have severed all roots of virtue belonging to the three realms—namely, those bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

It should be known that such a person is unable to reconnect any of their wholesome roots within this present life; they will certainly reconnect those wholesome roots either at the time of death in hell or at the time of birth there.
Question:
If one kills such a *pudgala*, and if one kills an ant egg or a legless ant, which carries the greater offense?
Answer:
If the entanglements are equal, the maturation (vipāka) is also equal.
Furthermore, some say that the offense incurred by killing ant eggs or ants with broken legs is greater than that incurred by killing such a person (pudgala).
Why is this? Because while ant eggs and ants with broken legs do not sever their roots of goodness, such types of *pudgalas* do sever their roots of goodness.
By means of such types of bodily action, vocal action, mental intention, aspiration, vow, and practice, these are termed "wrong nature" (*mithyātva*).
Consequently, they abandon all previously accomplished designations, conceptual identifications, and conventional expressions, and abide within the indeterminate group and the indeterminate lineage.

By this, one acquires for the first time those designations, conceptualizations, and conventional verbal expressions that were previously unestablished; one abides in the category of those fixed in error and the lineage of those fixed in error.

One acquires the five types of persons, the mixed class, and the class of associates, as well as an evil commonality of destiny, the acquisition of place, the acquisition of object, and the acquisition of the place of birth—namely: killing one’s mother, killing one’s father, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and with a malicious and wrathful mind, drawing blood from the body of a Tathāgata.
Regarding those who sever the roots of virtue, they sever them in this manner; that is, they sever them through these modes of activity.

Specifically, there is a certain class of persons (*pudgala*) for whom, due to the manifestation of various defiled minds bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), their roots of virtue are either relinquished and not acquired, or acquired and not relinquished, or both relinquished and acquired, or neither relinquished nor acquired.
"Abandoning without obtaining" refers to the time when the roots of goodness are severed;

as well as when an ordinary person who has already become detached from the greed of the desire realm falls away due to the fetters of the desire realm, thereby abandoning all roots of goodness associated with the form and formless realms without obtaining them again.

An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm, upon falling away due to the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm, relinquishes the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) associated with the form realm and does not regain them.

A trainee (*śaikṣa*) who has already abandoned craving for the form realm, upon falling away due to the entanglements of the desire realm, relinquishes the roots of goodness associated with the formless realm and does not regain them.
This is called "abandoning but not attaining.
Regarding "attaining but not abandoning," this refers to when the continuum of the mind is deluded while the roots of goodness remain.

Regarding "both abandoning and attaining," this refers to when one dies in the formless realm and is born into the desire realm; at that time, one abandons the roots of goodness associated with the formless realm and attains the roots of goodness associated with the desire realm.

When one passes away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one abandons the wholesome roots associated with the form realm and acquires the wholesome roots associated with the desire realm.

When Arhats fall away due to the fetters of the desire realm, they abandon the wholesome roots associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as well as those of the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and acquire the wholesome roots of one in training (*śaikṣa*); thus, they fall from the mind of one beyond training and abide in the mind of one in training.
This is called both relinquishing and obtaining.
As for neither relinquishing nor obtaining, it refers to one who does not sever the roots of goodness and, passing away from the desire realm, is reborn again in the desire realm.
This is called "neither relinquishing nor attaining.

Furthermore, there is a class of persons (*pudgala*) for whom, because various defiled minds bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) manifest, their roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) are either relinquished without being attained, or both relinquished and attained, or neither relinquished nor attained.

Regarding "abandoning but not obtaining": this refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already become detached from the craving of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), yet, through a lapse due to the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) of the form realm, they abandon the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) pertaining to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and do not obtain them again.
When one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm, one abandons the wholesome roots associated with the desire realm but does not acquire them.
This is called "abandoning but not acquiring.

As for "both abandoning and acquiring," it refers to when one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm; at that time, one abandons the wholesome roots associated with the formless realm and acquires the wholesome roots associated with the form realm.

When Arhats fall away due to the fetters of the form realm, they relinquish the wholesome roots associated with the formless realm and those of the state beyond training (aśaikṣa), and acquire the wholesome roots of one in training (śaikṣa); they fall away from the mind of one beyond training and abide in the mind of one in training.
This is called both relinquishing and obtaining.
That which is neither relinquished nor obtained refers to one who passes away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is reborn again in the form realm.
This is called neither relinquishing nor obtaining.

Furthermore, there is a class of individuals who, because of the manifestation of various defiled minds associated with the formless realm, either abandon their roots of goodness without acquiring them, or both abandon and acquire them, or neither abandon nor fail to acquire them.

"Abandoning but not obtaining" refers to one who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm; such a person abandons the wholesome roots associated with the desire realm and the form realm, yet does not obtain them again.

When one passes away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one abandons the wholesome roots associated with the form realm and does not acquire them again.
This is called "abandoning and not acquiring. Regarding "both abandoning and acquiring":

this refers to an Arhat who falls away due to the entanglements of the formless realm; he abandons the wholesome roots of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and acquires the wholesome roots of one in training (*śaikṣa*), falling from the mind of one beyond training and abiding in the mind of one in training.
This is called both relinquishing and obtaining.
As for neither relinquishing nor obtaining, it refers to passing away from the formless realm and being reborn again in the formless realm.
This is called neither relinquishing nor obtaining.

Furthermore, there are the twelve bases (āyatana), namely: the eye base and the form base; the ear base and the sound base; the nose base and the odor base; the tongue base and the taste base; the body base and the tangible base; and the mind base and the mental-object base.
What is the eye-base?
It refers to those eye-bases that have seen forms, are seeing forms, or will see forms, as well as other remaining [eye-bases] of the same class (sabhāga).
What is the eye-base of the same class (*sabhāga*)?
It refers to the eye-base of the same class, whether past, future, or present.
What is the past eye-base of the same class?
This refers to those eye bases that have ceased after not seeing forms.
What is the future "homogeneous" (sabhāga) eye base?
It refers to those eye bases which either will certainly not arise in the future, or which, though they will arise, will cease without seeing forms.
What is the present eye-base of the same class (*sabhāga*)?
It refers to those eye-bases that have ceased without having seen visible forms.
What is the form-base (*rūpāyatana*)?

This refers to those bases of form which have been seen by the eye, are being seen by the eye, or will be seen by the eye; or else, it refers to other "partially homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) bases of form.
What are these partially homogeneous bases of form?
This refers to the sense-base of form that is "of the same class" (sabhāga), whether past, future, or present.
What is the past sense-base of form that is of the same class?
It refers to those sense-bases of form that have already been seen by the eye and have ceased.
What is the sphere of form that is future and of its own kind (*sabhāga*)?
It refers to those spheres of form which either will certainly not arise in the future, or which, though they will arise, will be destroyed before being seen by the eye.
What is the present *sabhāga* (homogeneous) form-base (*rūpāyatana*)?
It refers to those form-bases that are not currently being seen by the eye and have not yet ceased.
As it is with the eye-base and the form-base, so it is with the ear-base and sound-base, the nose-base and odor-base, the tongue-base and taste-base, and the body-base and tangible-base.
What is the sense base of the mind (manāyatana)?

It refers to all instances of the sense base of the mind that have already cognized dharmas, are currently cognizing dharmas, or will cognize dharmas, as well as other instances of the sense base of the mind that are of the same class (tatsabhāga).
What is the sphere of mind that is "of similar lot" (*sabhāga*)?

It refers to those spheres of mind that exist in the future and are destined never to arise; there is no such sphere of mind of similar lot in the past or present, nor is there any such sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) of similar lot.

Regarding the past eye and visible forms, there are two propositions: namely, that the past eye either has already seen a visible form—without seeing it now or seeing it in the future—or has not already seen it, does not see it now, and will not see it in the future.

Regarding the future eye and visible forms, there are three propositions: namely, that the future eye with respect to visible forms is either (1) neither already seen, nor being seen now, nor to be seen; or (2) neither already seen nor being seen now, but to be seen; or (3) neither already seen nor being seen now, and either to be seen or not to be seen.

Regarding the present eye in relation to forms, there are twelve propositions: namely, the present eye may have already seen a form, but does not see it now and will not see it; or it may see it now, but has not already seen it and will not see it; or it may see it in the future, but has not already seen it and does not see it now; or it may have already seen it and sees it now, but will not see it [in the future]; or it may have already seen it and will see it, but does not see it now; or it may see it now and will see it, but has not already seen it; or it may have already seen it, but neither sees it now nor will see it; or it may see it now, but neither has already seen it nor will see it; or it may neither have already seen it nor see it now, but will see it; or it may neither have already seen it nor see it now, but will not see it; or it may have already seen it and sees it now, but will not see it; or it may have already seen it and sees it now, and will see it; or it may neither have already seen it nor see it now nor will see it.
Does the eye serve as a condition for that which is intermediate, or does it serve as a condition for that which is superior?
What kind of condition is this, such that it conditions the inferior eye?
It is said: Yes; namely, the intermediate and the superior.
Is it the case that the eye serves as a condition for the first [moment], yet is not this same condition?
Why is it not this condition? It is because it consists of the primary elements (mahābhūta) produced by karma.
He said: "There are;
namely, the inferior, the middling, and the superior.
As it is with the eye, so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, and body."
Is the mind that serves as a condition for the middle [mind] also a condition for the superior [mind]?
And what kind of condition is this mind that serves as a condition for the inferior mind?
He replied:
There are, namely those of the middle and upper stages.
Is there perhaps an intention that takes the first stage as its object but for which this [first stage] is not the object-condition? Why is it not the object-condition?
This refers to karma and afflictions.
It is said:
they exist, namely as inferior, middling, and superior.

There are eighteen elements (dhātus), namely: the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
If the eye-element has been abandoned and fully understood, is the form-element likewise?
And if the form-element has been abandoned and fully understood, is the eye-element likewise?
Is it the case that when the eye-element has been abandoned and fully understood, this also applies up to the mind-consciousness-element?
And conversely, if the mind-consciousness-element has been abandoned and fully understood, is the eye-element also thus?
If the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) has been abandoned and fully known, is the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) likewise?
Conversely, if the mental-consciousness-element has been abandoned and fully known, is the dharma-element likewise?
Is it the case that when the eye-element has been abandoned and fully understood, the form-element is likewise?
He replied: "It is so."
If the form element (*rūpadhātu*) has already been abandoned and fully understood, is it also the same for the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*)?
He replied: "It is so."

As it is with the visual faculty (cakṣurdhātu) in relation to the visible-object faculty (rūpadhātu), so it is in relation to the auditory faculty, the audible-object faculty, the olfactory faculty, the gustatory faculty, the tactile faculty, and the tangible-object faculty.
Is it the case that when the visual faculty has been abandoned and fully understood, the visual-consciousness faculty (cakṣurvijñānadhātu) is likewise abandoned and fully understood?
It is said:
If the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) has been abandoned and fully known, the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) is likewise.

Or, the eye-consciousness-element has been abandoned and fully known, but not the eye-element; this refers to one who has already become free from craving for the Brahma-world but is not yet free from craving for the higher realms.

As it is with the visual faculty (*cakṣur-dhātu*) in relation to the visual consciousness element (*cakṣur-vijñāna-dhātu*), so it is in relation to the auditory consciousness element (*śrotra-vijñāna-dhātu*) and the body consciousness element (*kāya-vijñāna-dhātu*).
Is it possible that when the visual faculty has been abandoned and fully known, the olfactory element (*gandha-dhātu*) is likewise [abandoned and fully known]?
It is said:
If the eye-element has been abandoned and fully understood, the nose-element is likewise.

Or, the nose-element may have been abandoned and fully understood while the eye-element has not; this refers to one who has already become detached from the greed of the desire realm but has not yet become detached from the greed of the higher realms.

As it is with the visual faculty (*cakṣurdhātu*) in relation to the olfactory object (*gandhadhātu*), so it is in relation to the gustatory object (*rasadhātu*), the olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), and the gustatory consciousness (*jihvāvijñānadhātu*).
Is it possible that when the visual faculty has been abandoned and fully known, the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) is likewise [abandoned and fully known]?
It is said:
If the mind-element (*manodhātu*) has been abandoned and fully known, the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is likewise.

Or, the eye-element may have been abandoned and fully known while the mind-element has not; this refers to one who has already detached from the greed of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but has not yet detached from the greed of the higher realms.

As it is with the visual faculty (*cakṣurdhātu*) in relation to the mental faculty (*manodhātu*), so it is in relation to the dharma-faculty (*dharmadhātu*) and the mental-consciousness faculty (*manovijñānadhātu*).

As the visual faculty has been explained in detail, so too should the form-faculty (*rūpadhātu*), auditory faculty (*śrotradhātu*), auditory-object faculty (*śabdadhātu*), olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇadhātu*), gustatory faculty (*jihvādhātu*), tactile faculty (*kāyadhātu*), and tangible-object faculty (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) be explained in detail.
Is it the case that when the eye-consciousness element has been abandoned and fully understood, the ear-consciousness element is likewise?
He replied: "It is so."
If the ear-consciousness element has been abandoned and fully understood, is the eye-consciousness element also thus? It is said: Yes.
Just as it is with respect to the ear-consciousness element, so it is with respect to the body-consciousness element.
Is it possible that when the eye-consciousness element has been abandoned and fully known, the fragrance element is likewise [abandoned and fully known]?
It is said:
If the eye-consciousness element has been abandoned and fully understood, the fragrance element is likewise so.

Or, the fragrance element may have been abandoned and fully understood while the eye-consciousness element has not; this refers to one who has already become detached from the desire realm but is not yet detached from the greed of the Brahma-world.

As it is with the visual consciousness element in relation to the odor element, so it is in relation to the taste element, the olfactory consciousness element, and the gustatory consciousness element.
Is it the case that when the visual consciousness element has been abandoned and fully known, the mental element (*manodhātu*) is likewise?
It is said:
If the mind-element (*manodhātu*) has been abandoned and fully understood, the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) is likewise.

Or, the eye-consciousness-element may have been abandoned and fully understood while the mind-element has not; this refers to one who has already become free from craving for the Brahma-world but is not yet free from craving for the higher realms.
As it is with the visual consciousness element in relation to the mental element, so it is in relation to the mental-object element and the mental-consciousness element.
Just as this has been explained in detail for the visual consciousness element, so too should it be explained in detail for the auditory consciousness element and the tactile consciousness element.
If the odor-element has been abandoned and fully understood, is the taste-element likewise?
He replied: "It is so."
If the taste element (*rasadhātu*) has been abandoned and fully understood, is the odor element (*gandhadhātu*) likewise?
He replied: "It is so."
As it is with the odor element in relation to the taste element, so it is in relation to the nose-consciousness element and the tongue-consciousness element.
Is it the case that when the odor element has been abandoned and fully understood, the mind element is likewise [abandoned and fully understood]?
It is said:
If the mind-element (*manodhātu*) has been abandoned and fully understood, the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*) is likewise.

Or, the odor-element may have been abandoned and fully understood while the mind-element has not; this refers to one who has already become detached from the greed of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but has not yet become detached from the greed of the higher realms.
As it is with the fragrance element in relation to the mind element, so it is in relation to the mental-object element and the mental-consciousness element.
As the fragrance element has been explained in detail, so too should the taste element, the nose-consciousness element, and the tongue-consciousness element be explained in detail.
Is it the case that when the mind-element (*manodhātu*) has been abandoned and fully understood, the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) is likewise?
He replied: "It is so."
If the dharma-element has been abandoned and fully understood, is the mind-element likewise? It is said: Yes.
As it is with the mental faculty element (*manodhātu*) in relation to the dharma element (*dharmadhātu*), so it is in relation to the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
Is it the case that when the dharma element has been abandoned and fully known, the mental consciousness element is likewise abandoned and fully known?
He said: "It is so.
If the consciousness element has been abandoned and fully understood, is it the same for the dharma element?"
It is said:

Thus there are twelve types of mind, namely: the wholesome mind, the unwholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the non-obscured-unspecified mind bound to the desire realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the non-obscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the non-obscured-unspecified mind bound to the formless realm; as well as the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Thus, these twelve types of consciousness may be past, future, or present.
Regarding the past wholesome consciousness associated with the desire realm, there are four propositions:

namely, that which has already cognized but does not cognize now nor will cognize; that which has already cognized and will cognize but does not cognize now; that which has already cognized and cognizes now but will not cognize; and that which has already cognized, cognizes now, and will cognize.
Those who have already discerned, but do not discern now nor will discern in the future, are the noble *pudgalas* born and growing in the realms of form and formlessness.

Those who have already discerned and will discern in the future, but do not discern now, are *pudgalas* whose roots of virtue have been severed, as well as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born and growing in the realms of form and formlessness.

"Having already cognized and currently cognizing, but not to be cognized in the future" refers to those non-returners (anāgāmin) born and raised in the desire realm who have entered the realms of form or formlessness and abide in their final wholesome mind.

"Having already discerned, currently discerning, and about to discern" refers to those born and growing in the desire realm who have not severed their roots of goodness and abide in their natural state.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future.
Regarding the four propositions concerning the wholesome mind bound to the desire realm that has never been previously attained:

it may be that which was not already cognized, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized in the future; or, it may be that which was not already cognized, is not being cognized now, but will be cognized in the future; or, it may be that which was not already cognized, is not being cognized now, and either will be cognized in the future or will not be cognized in the future; or, it may be that which is being cognized now and will be cognized in the future, but was not already cognized.
"Not previously cognized, not presently cognized, and not to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained and will not be attained in the future.
"Not previously cognized, not presently cognized, but to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained but will certainly be attained in the future.
That which has not been cognized, is not being cognized, or will either be or will not be cognized, refers to that which was previously never attained, or will be attained, or will not be attained.
Regarding "presently discerning and to-be-discerned, but not already-discerned," this refers to that which has never been attained before and is now manifest for the first time.
There are three possibilities for a wholesome mind associated with the desire realm in the present:

(1) it has already been discerned, is presently discerning, but will not be discerned in the future; (2) it has not already been discerned, is presently discerning, and will be discerned in the future; or (3) it has already been discerned, is presently discerning, and will be discerned in the future.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, but not to be discerned in the future" refers to those non-returners born and raised in the desire realm who have entered the form or formless realms and abide in their final wholesome mind.
"Neither previously discerned, nor being discerned now, nor to be discerned in the future" refers to that which has never been attained before and now manifests for the first time.
"Previously discerned, being discerned now, and to be discerned in the future" refers to that which was previously attained and now manifests in the present.

Regarding past unwholesome mental states, there are seven propositions: (1) that which has already been cognized, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized in the future; (2) that which has already been cognized, is not being cognized now, but will be cognized in the future; (3) that which has already been cognized, is not being cognized now, and may or may not be cognized in the future; (4) that which has already been cognized, is being cognized now, but will not be cognized in the future; (5) that which has already been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future; (6) that which has already been cognized, is being cognized now, and may or may not be cognized in the future; (7) that which has already been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future.

"Having already discerned, neither discerning now nor to be discerned in the future" refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm and will certainly not fall away from that state of freedom from craving.

"Having already discerned, not discerning now, but to be discerned in the future" refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm but will certainly fall away from that state of freedom from craving.

Regarding "that which has already been cognized, but is not being cognized now, nor will it be cognized, or will not be cognized": this refers to one who has already become free from craving for the desire realm, and from that state of freedom from craving, either will or will not fall away.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, but not to be discerned in the future" refers to one who dwells in the state free from sensual desire and attachment, attains freedom from sensual desire and attachment within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and will certainly not fall away from that freedom from sensual desire and attachment.

"Having already discerned, currently discerning, and will discern" refers to one who dwells in the state of freedom from sensual desire, attains freedom from sensual desire during the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), yet is certain to fall away from that freedom from sensual desire.

Regarding "already discerned, presently discerning, or will discern, or will not discern": this refers to one who dwells having abandoned sensual desire, attaining the abandonment of sensual desire within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and from that state of abandonment of sensual desire, either being subject to falling away or not being subject to falling away.
"Having cognized, cognizing now, and will cognize" refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm and abides in their natural state.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future.
Regarding the present unwholesome mind, there is one phrase:
namely, that which has already been cognized, is being cognized, and will be cognized—referring to the unwholesome mind that is currently manifest.
Regarding the past desire-realm-bound obscured-neutral mind, there are seven phrases:

Either it has been cognized, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized; or it has been cognized, is not being cognized now, but will be cognized; or it has been cognized, is not being cognized now, and either will be cognized or will not be cognized; or it has been cognized, is being cognized now, but will not be cognized; or it has been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized; or it has been cognized, is being cognized now, and either will be cognized or will not be cognized; or it has been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized.

Regarding that which has already been discerned, is not being discerned now, and will not be discerned in the future: this refers to ordinary beings who have already abandoned craving for the desire realm and will certainly not fall away from that state of abandonment;

as well as noble ones who have not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm but have already produced the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering at the conclusion of the clear observation (*abhisamaya*).

"Those who have already discerned, but do not discern now, and will not discern in the future" refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already abandoned craving for the desire realm and are certain to fall away from that state of freedom from craving.

Regarding "that which has already been discerned, but is not being discerned now, nor will it be discerned, or will not be discerned": this refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm, and who may or may not fall away from that abandonment of craving for the desire realm.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, but not to be discerned in the future" refers to those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who abide in the state of being free from sensual desire, attaining freedom from sensual desire within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and who will certainly not fall away from that freedom from sensual desire;

as well as noble ones (*ārya*) who have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*), in whom the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) at the conclusion of the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) has not yet arisen.

"Having already discerned, currently discerning, and about to discern" refers to those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who abide in the state of being free from sensual desire; while in the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), they attain freedom from sensual desire, yet they are certain to fall away from that freedom from sensual desire.

"Having already discerned, currently discerning, or will discern—or will not discern"—refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who abide in the state of being free from sensual desire; while in the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*), they attain freedom from sensual desire, and from that freedom from sensual desire, they may either fall away or not fall away.

"Having cognized, currently cognizing, and will cognize" refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm and abides in their natural state (*svabhāvasthā*).
As it is with the past, so it is with the future.

Regarding the obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) in the present, there is one phrase: "that which has already discerned, is now discerning, and will discern," namely, when the obscured-unspecified mind bound to the desire realm is manifest in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding past unobscured-neutral minds bound to the desire realm, there are four permutations:

(1) those that have already been cognized, but are not being cognized now, nor will they be cognized in the future; (2) those that have already been cognized, but are not being cognized now, yet will be cognized in the future; (3) those that have already been cognized and are being cognized now, but will not be cognized in the future; and (4) those that have already been cognized, are being cognized now, and will also be cognized in the future.
"Those who have already cognized, but do not cognize now, nor will cognize in the future" refers to noble persons (ārya-pudgala) born and dwelling in the formless realm.
"Those who have already cognized, do not cognize now, but will cognize in the future" refers to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) born and dwelling in the formless realm.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, but not to be discerned in the future" refers to those non-returners (anāgāmin) born in the desire realm or the form realm who are proceeding toward the formless realm and abide in their final moment of consciousness.
"Having already discerned, currently discerning, and about to discern" refers to those born and raised in the desire realm or the form realm who abide in their natural state (*svabhāva-avasthā*).
As it is with the past, so it is with the future.
Regarding the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the desire realm that has never before been attained, there are four permutations:

(1) that which has not already been cognized, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized in the future; (2) that which has not already been cognized, is not being cognized now, but will be cognized in the future; (3) that which has not already been cognized, is not being cognized now, but may or may not be cognized in the future; and (4) that which has not already been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future.
"Neither previously discerned, nor presently discerned, nor to be discerned in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained and will not be attained in the future.
"Neither previously discerned nor presently discerned, but to be discerned in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained but will certainly be attained in the future.
"Neither previously cognized, nor being cognized now, nor to be cognized, or not to be cognized" refers to that which was never previously attained, or will be attained, or will not be attained.
Regarding "not previously cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future," this refers to that which has never been attained before and is now manifesting for the first time.
There are three propositions concerning the present non-obscured, indeterminate mind associated with the desire realm:

(1) it has been cognized, is being cognized now, but will not be cognized in the future; (2) it has not been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future; or (3) it has been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, but not to be discerned in the future" refers to those non-returners (anāgāmin) born in the desire realm or the form realm who are proceeding toward the formless realm, abiding in their final unobscured-neutral mind.
"Not previously cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future" refers to that which has never been attained before and is now appearing for the first time.
"Previously cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was previously attained and is now appearing in the present.
Regarding past wholesome minds associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), there are four propositions:

(1) those that have already been cognized, but are not being cognized now, nor will they be cognized in the future; (2) those that have already been cognized, but are not being cognized now, yet will be cognized in the future; (3) those that have already been cognized and are being cognized now, but will not be cognized in the future; and (4) those that have already been cognized, are being cognized now, and will also be cognized in the future.
"Those who have already discerned, but do not discern now, nor will discern in the future" refers to noble *pudgalas* born and raised in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

"Those who have already discerned, but do not discern now, yet will discern in the future" refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born and raised in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who have not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm, as well as those born and raised in the formless realm.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, but not to be discerned in the future" refers to those non-returners (*anāgāmin*) born in the desire realm or the form realm who are proceeding toward the formless realm and abide in their final moment of consciousness.

"Having already discerned, currently discerning, and will discern" refers to one born and raised in the desire realm who has attained a wholesome mind of the form realm and abides in its natural state, as well as one born and raised in the form realm who abides in its natural state.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future.
Regarding the four propositions concerning the wholesome mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that has not yet been attained:

it may be such that it has not already been cognized, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized; or it may be such that it has not already been cognized, is not being cognized now, but will be cognized; or it may be such that it has not already been cognized, is not being cognized now, but may either be cognized or not be cognized in the future; or it may be such that it has not already been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized.
"Neither previously cognized, nor presently cognized, nor to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained and will not be attained in the future.
"Neither previously cognized nor presently cognized, but to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained but will certainly be attained.

"Neither previously cognized, nor currently being cognized, nor to be cognized, or not to be cognized" refers to that which was never previously attained, or will be attained, or will not be attained.
Regarding "not previously cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future": this refers to that which has never been attained before and is now appearing for the first time.
There are three propositions concerning the presently occurring wholesome mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*):

either it has been cognized, is being cognized now, but will not be cognized in the future; or it has not been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future; or it has been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, but not to be discerned in the future" refers to those non-returners born in the form realm who are proceeding toward the formless realm and abide in their final wholesome mind.
"Not previously cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained and is now appearing for the first time.
"Previously cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was previously attained and is now appearing in the present.
Regarding past minds associated with the form realm that are obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), there are seven propositions:

1. That which has already been cognized, but is not being cognized now, nor will it be cognized; 2. That which has already been cognized, but is not being cognized now, yet will be cognized; 3. That which has already been cognized, but is not being cognized now, and may or may not be cognized [in the future]; 4. That which has already been cognized and is being cognized now, but will not be cognized [further]; 5. That which has already been cognized and is being cognized now, and will be cognized; 6. That which has already been cognized and is being cognized now, and may or may not be cognized [further]; 7. That which has already been cognized and is being cognized now, and will be cognized.

"Already cognized, not being cognized now, and not to be cognized in the future" refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and will certainly not fall away from that abandonment of craving for the form realm.

"Already cognized, not being cognized now, but to be cognized in the future" refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm but will certainly fall away from that abandonment of craving for the form realm.

"Having already discerned, but not discerning now, nor will it be discerned, or will not be discerned" refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and from that state of abandonment, may either fall away or not fall away.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, and not to be discerned in the future" refers to one who dwells having abandoned craving for form, attains the abandonment of craving for form within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and will certainly not fall away from that abandonment of craving for form.

"Having already discerned, currently discerning, and about to discern" refers to one who dwells having abandoned desire for the form realm (*rūparāga*), attains the abandonment of desire for the form realm during the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*), yet is certain to fall away from that abandonment of desire for the form realm.

"Having already discerned, currently discerning, or will discern—or will not discern"—refers to one who dwells having abandoned craving for form (*rūpa-rāga*), attaining that abandonment of craving for form within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and from that abandonment of craving for form, either being subject to falling away or not being subject to falling away.
"Having already discerned, currently discerning, and about to discern" refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and abides in their natural state.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future.
Regarding the mind associated with the form realm that is obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), there is one phrase:

namely, "that which has already discerned, is currently discerning, and will discern," referring to the moment when the mind associated with the form realm that is obscured and indeterminate is manifest in the present.
Regarding past minds associated with the form realm that are unobscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), there are four permutations:

(1) those already cognized, not being cognized now, and not to be cognized in the future; (2) those already cognized, not being cognized now, but to be cognized in the future; (3) those already cognized, being cognized now, but not to be cognized in the future; and (4) those already cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future.

Those who have already cognized [an object], but do not cognize it now, nor will cognize it in the future, are the noble persons (*ārya-pudgala*) born and raised in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Those who have already cognized [an object], do not cognize it now, but will cognize it in the future, are those born and raised in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who have not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, as well as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born and raised in the formless realm.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, but not to be discerned in the future" refers to those non-returners (*anāgāmin*) born in the desire realm or the form realm who are proceeding toward the formless realm and abide in their final moment of consciousness.

"Having already discerned, currently discerning, and will discern" refers to those born and raised in the desire realm who have already abandoned craving for the desire realm, as well as those born and raised in the form realm who abide in their natural state.

As it is with the past, so it is with the future. Regarding the mind that is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and never before attained (*apūrva-labdha*), there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*):

1. It has not been cognized (*na vijñāta*) previously, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized in the future; 2. It has not been cognized previously, is not being cognized now, but will be cognized in the future; 3. It has not been cognized previously, is not being cognized now, but may be cognized in the future or may not be cognized in the future; 4. It has not been cognized previously, but is being cognized now and will be cognized in the future.
"Neither previously discerned, nor presently discerned, nor to be discerned in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained and will not be attained in the future.
"Neither previously discerned, nor presently discerned, but to be discerned in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained but will certainly be attained in the future.

"Neither already cognized, nor being cognized now, nor to be cognized in the future, nor not to be cognized" refers to that which was previously never attained, or may be attained, or may not be attained.
Regarding "not previously cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future": this refers to that which was never previously attained and is now appearing for the first time.
There are three propositions concerning the present unobscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*):

either it has been cognized, is being cognized now, but will not be cognized in the future; or it has not been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future; or it has been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, but not to be discerned in the future" refers to those non-returners born in the form realm who are proceeding toward the formless realm and abide in their final unobscured-neutral mind.
"Not previously cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained and is now appearing for the first time.
"Previously cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was previously attained and is now appearing before one.
Regarding past wholesome minds associated with the formless realm, there are two cases:
either they have been cognized but are not being cognized now and will be cognized, or they have been cognized, are being cognized now, and will be cognized.
"Those that have been cognized, but are not being cognized now, nor will be cognized" refers to those who have not yet attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
"Those that have been cognized, are being cognized now, and will be cognized" refers to those who have already attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future.
Regarding the four propositions concerning the wholesome mind associated with the formless realm that has not yet been attained:

it may be that which was not already cognized, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized; or it may be that which was not already cognized, is not being cognized now, but will be cognized; or it may be that which was not already cognized, is not being cognized now, but may either be cognized or not be cognized; or it may be that which was not already cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized.
"Neither previously discerned, nor presently discerned, nor to be discerned in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained and will not be attained in the future.
"Neither previously discerned, nor presently discerned, but to be discerned in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained but will certainly be attained.

"Neither previously cognized, nor being cognized now, nor to be cognized in the future, or not to be cognized" refers to that which was never previously attained, or will be attained, or will not be attained.
Regarding "not already cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future," this refers to that which was previously never attained and is now appearing for the first time.
Regarding wholesome states of mind associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) in the present, there are two cases:
either they are not already cognized, are being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future; or they have already been cognized, are being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future.
"Not previously cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained and now manifests for the first time.
"Previously cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was previously attained and is now manifesting.
Regarding past minds associated with the formless realm that are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), there are seven cases:

(1) those already cognized, not being cognized now, and not to be cognized in the future; (2) those already cognized, not being cognized now, but to be cognized in the future; (3) those already cognized, not being cognized now, and either to be cognized or not to be cognized in the future; (4) those already cognized, being cognized now, and not to be cognized in the future; (5) those already cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future; (6) those already cognized, being cognized now, and either to be cognized or not to be cognized in the future; (7) those already cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future.

"Having already discerned, not discerning now, and not to be discerned in the future" refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm and will certainly not fall away from that state of having abandoned craving for the formless realm.

"Having already discerned, but not discerning now, nor to be discerned in the future" refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm, yet is certain to fall away from that abandonment of craving for the formless realm.

"Having already discerned, but not discerning now, nor discerning in the future, nor not discerning in the future" refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm, and from that state of abandonment, either will fall away or will not fall away.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, and not to be discerned in the future" refers to one who dwells having abandoned craving for the formless realm, attaining that abandonment of craving for the formless realm within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and from which abandonment of craving for the formless realm they shall never fall away.

Regarding "has already discerned, is now discerning, or will discern—or will not discern"—this refers to one who dwells having abandoned craving for the formless realm, attains abandonment of craving for the formless realm during the path of immediate succession, and from that abandonment of craving for the formless realm, either may fall away or may not fall away.
"Having cognized, currently cognizing, and will cognize" refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm and abides in their natural state.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future.
Regarding the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the formless realm, there is one phrase:
"that which has already discerned, is now discerning, and will discern," namely, when the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the formless realm is currently manifest.
Regarding past minds of the formless realm that are unobscured-neutral, there is one case:
namely, that which has already been cognized, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized in the future—referring to a resultant mind that has already ceased.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future.
Regarding the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm that has not yet been attained, there are three propositions:

either it was not previously cognized, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized in the future; or it was not previously cognized, is not being cognized now, but will be cognized in the future; or it was not previously cognized, is not being cognized now, and may or may not be cognized in the future.
"Neither previously cognized, nor presently cognized, nor to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained and will not be attained in the future.
"Neither previously cognized nor presently cognized, but to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained but will certainly be attained in the future.

"Neither previously cognized, nor being cognized now, nor to be cognized in the future, or not to be cognized" refers to that which was never previously attained, or will be attained, or will not be attained.
Regarding the present mind of the formless realm that is unobscured and indeterminate, there is one case:

namely, that which has not already been cognized, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized in the future; this refers to when the resultant mind (vipāka-citta) is manifesting in the present.
There are seven propositions regarding the mind that has been previously cultivated (*pūrvābhyasta-citta*):

(1) that which has already been cognized, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized in the future; (2) that which has already been cognized, is not being cognized now, but will be cognized in the future; (3) that which has already been cognized, is not being cognized now, and may or may not be cognized in the future; (4) that which has already been cognized, is being cognized now, and will not be cognized in the future; (5) that which has already been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future; (6) that which has already been cognized, is being cognized now, and may or may not be cognized in the future; (7) that which has already been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future.
"Already discerned, not being discerned now, and not to be discerned in the future" refers to an Arhat who will certainly not fall away from the fruit of Arhatship.
"Already discerned, not being discerned now, but to be discerned in the future" refers to an Arhat who will certainly fall away from the fruit of Arhatship.
"Having already discerned, but not discerning now, nor will discern, or will not discern" refers to an Arhat who, from the fruit of Arhatship, will either fall away or will not fall away.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, and not to be discerned in the future" refers to one who abides in the fruit of arhatship, attains the fruit of arhatship within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and shall certainly never fall away from that fruit of arhatship.

"Having discerned, currently discerning, and will discern" refers to one who dwells in the fruit of arhatship, attains the fruit of arhatship within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and is certain to fall away from that fruit of arhatship.

Regarding "having already discerned, currently discerning, or will discern—or will not discern": this refers to one who abides in the fruit of arhatship, attains the fruit of arhatship within the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga), and from that fruit of arhatship, either will fall away or will not fall away.
"Having already discerned, currently discerning, and about to discern" refers to those in training (śaikṣa) who abide in their natural state.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future.
There are four propositions regarding the mind of training that has never before been attained:

Either it was not already cognized, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized; or it was not already cognized, is not being cognized now, but will be cognized; or it was not already cognized, is not being cognized now, and either will be cognized or will not be cognized; or it was not already cognized, but is being cognized now and will be cognized.
"Not previously cognized, not currently cognized, and not to be cognized" refers to that which was never previously attained and will not be attained in the future.
"Not previously cognized, not currently cognized, but to be cognized" refers to that which was never previously attained but will certainly be attained in the future.

"Neither previously cognized, nor being cognized now, nor to be cognized in the future, or not to be cognized" refers to that which was never previously attained, or will be attained, or will not be attained.
Regarding "not already cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future": this refers to that which was previously never attained and is now appearing for the first time.

There are eight propositions concerning the mind of one currently in training (*śaikṣa*): 1. Not already cognized, being cognized now, and not to be cognized in the future; 2. Not already cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future; 3. Not already cognized, being cognized now, and either to be cognized in the future or not to be cognized in the future; 4. Already cognized, being cognized now, and not to be cognized in the future; 5. Already cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future; 6. Already cognized, being cognized now, and either to be cognized in the future or not to be cognized in the future; 7. Not already cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future; 8. Already cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future.

Regarding "that which was not previously cognized, is being cognized now, but will not be cognized in the future": this refers to one who has not previously fallen away from the fruit of arhatship, who abides in the fruit of arhatship, and who attains the fruit of arhatship within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), such that they shall certainly never fall away from the fruit of arhatship.

"Neither already cognized, nor being cognized now, nor to be cognized in the future" refers to one who has not previously fallen away from the fruit of arhatship and dwells in that fruit; having attained the fruit of arhatship within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), they are certain to fall away from the fruit of arhatship.

Regarding "not already cognized, nor being cognized now, nor to be cognized, or not to be cognized": this refers to one who has not previously fallen away from the fruit of arhatship, who abides in the fruit of arhatship, and who attains the fruit of arhatship within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*); such a person may subsequently fall away from the fruit of arhatship or may not fall away from it.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, but not to be discerned in the future" refers to one who has previously fallen away from the fruit of arhatship, but while abiding in the fruit of arhatship during the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), attains the fruit of arhatship and will certainly never again fall away from that fruit of arhatship.

"Having already discerned, presently discerning, and about to discern" refers to one who has previously fallen away from the fruit of arhatship, yet while abiding in the fruit of arhatship, attains that fruit during the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and is destined to fall away from the fruit of arhatship.

Regarding "has already discerned, is now discerning, or will discern—or will not discern": this refers to one who has previously fallen away from the fruit of arhatship, yet while abiding in the fruit of arhatship, attains the fruit of arhatship within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and may subsequently fall away from that fruit of arhatship or may not fall away from it.
"Neither previously cognized, nor being cognized now, nor to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained and is for the first time manifesting before one.
"Previously cognized, being cognized now, and to be cognized in the future" refers to that which was already previously attained and is now manifesting before one.
Regarding past minds of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there are four permutations:

(1) that which has already been cognized, but is not being cognized now and will not be cognized in the future; (2) that which has already been cognized, is not being cognized now, but will be cognized in the future; (3) that which has already been cognized and is being cognized now, but will not be cognized in the future; and (4) that which has already been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future.

That which has already been discerned, is not being discerned now, and will not be discerned in the future refers to an Arhat of the fruit of liberation through time who has entered the state of immovability (*akopya*).
That which has already been discerned, is not being discerned now, but will be discerned in the future refers to an Arhat who has fallen away from the fruit of Arhatship.

"Having already discerned, currently discerning, but not to be discerned in the future" refers to an Arhat liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) who dwells in the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) leading to the state of immovability (*akopyadharman*).
"Having already discerned, currently discerning, and to be discerned in the future" refers to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who abide in their natural state.
As it was with the past, so it is with the future. Regarding the four propositions concerning the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣacitta*) that has never before been attained:

(1) it has not already been cognized, is not being cognized now, and will not be cognized in the future; (2) it has not already been cognized, is not being cognized now, but will be cognized in the future; (3) it has not already been cognized, is not being cognized now, and may either be cognized in the future or not be cognized in the future; (4) it has not already been cognized, is being cognized now, and will be cognized in the future.
"Neither previously discerned, nor presently discerned, nor to be discerned in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained and will not be attained in the future.
"Neither previously discerned nor presently discerned, but to be discerned in the future" refers to that which was never previously attained but will certainly be attained in the future.

"Neither previously cognized, nor being cognized now, nor to be cognized in the future, or not to be cognized" refers to that which was never previously attained, or will be attained, or will not be attained.
Regarding "neither previously cognized, nor presently cognizing, nor to be cognized": this refers to that which was never previously attained and now manifests for the first time.
There are three possibilities concerning the present mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):

either it has been previously cognized, is presently cognizing, but will not be cognized in the future; or it has not been previously cognized, is presently cognizing, and will be cognized in the future; or it has been previously cognized, is presently cognizing, and will be cognized in the future.

"Having already discerned, discerning now, but not to be discerned in the future" refers to an Arhat liberated by time (samaya-vimukta) who abides in the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) leading to the unshakable state (*akopya*).
"Neither having already discerned, nor discerning now, nor to be discerned in the future" refers to that which has never been attained before and is for the first time manifesting.
"Having cognized, cognizing now, and will cognize" refers to that which was previously acquired and is now present before one.
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Fascicle Twelve;
*Abhidharma-jñānakāya-pāda-śāstra*, Fascicle Thirteen.
Composed by the Arhat Devaśarman;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Initial attainment and non-attainment, as well as relinquishment and acquisition, And the two types of mind: that which has not yet been severed and that which has already been severed.
Regarding the two Brahma-worlds of the *pudgala*, there are twelve minds at the end of the stages of training (*śaikṣa*) and no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*).

These twelve minds are: the wholesome mind, the unwholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind belonging to the desire realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind belonging to the form realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind belonging to the formless realm; as well as the mind of one in training and the mind of one beyond training.
If one accomplishes a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, does one also accomplish an unwholesome mind?
Conversely, if one accomplishes an unwholesome mind, does one also accomplish this wholesome mind?
If one accomplishes a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, does one also accomplish an *aśaikṣa* (non-learner) mind?
Conversely, if one accomplishes an *aśaikṣa* mind, does one also accomplish this wholesome mind?
Furthermore, if one possesses a mind of training (śaikṣa-citta), does one also possess a mind beyond training (aśaikṣa-citta)?
Conversely, if one possesses a mind beyond training, does one also possess a mind of training?
If one accomplishes a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, does one also accomplish an unwholesome mind?

Or, one may accomplish a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm but not an unwholesome mind; or, one may accomplish an unwholesome mind but not this wholesome mind; or, one may accomplish both this wholesome mind and the unwholesome mind; or, one may accomplish neither this wholesome mind nor the unwholesome mind.

One who achieves a wholesome mind associated with the desire realm but not an unwholesome mind refers to a person (pudgala) born and raised in the desire realm who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm.
One who achieves an unwholesome mind but not this wholesome mind refers to a person whose roots of goodness have been severed.

Those who accomplish both this wholesome mind and the unwholesome mind are persons (pudgala) born and raised in the desire realm who have not severed their wholesome roots and have not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm.
Regarding those who neither possess this wholesome mind nor an unwholesome mind, these refer to individuals born and raised in the form and formless realms.
If one possesses a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, does one also possess a mind that is obscured and indeterminate (nivṛtāvyākṛta) bound to the desire realm?

Either one possesses a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm but does not possess a hindered-neutral mind bound to the desire realm; or one possesses a hindered-neutral mind bound to the desire realm but does not possess a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm; or one possesses both this wholesome mind and this hindered-neutral mind; or one possesses neither this wholesome mind nor this hindered-neutral mind.

Those who have accomplished a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm but not a mind that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) bound to the desire realm are: noble ones and ordinary beings born and raised in the desire realm who have already abandoned craving for the desire realm; as well as noble ones who have not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, in whom the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna) at the limit of clear observation (abhisamaya) has already arisen.

One who possesses a mind that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), but does not possess a mind that is wholesome (*kuśala*) and bound to the desire realm, refers to a person (*pudgala*) whose roots of virtue have been severed.

One who possesses both a mind that is wholesome and bound to the desire realm and a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the desire realm, refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born and raised in the desire realm who has not severed the roots of virtue and has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm; as well as a noble one (*ārya*) who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, in whom the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) at the limit of clear observation (*abhisamaya*) has not yet arisen.

Those who neither possess a wholesome mind associated with the desire realm nor a mind that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) associated with the desire realm are individuals born and raised in the form or formless realms.
If one accomplishes a wholesome mind associated with the desire realm, does one also accomplish an unobscured-neutral mind associated with the desire realm?
If one accomplishes a wholesome mind associated with the desire realm, one necessarily accomplishes an unobscured-neutral mind associated with the desire realm.

Or, one may possess an unobscured-neutral mind bound to the desire realm but not a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm; this refers to individuals who have severed their roots of virtue or those born and growing within the form realm.
If one accomplishes a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, does one also accomplish a wholesome mind bound to the form realm?

There may be cases where one accomplishes a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm but not a wholesome mind bound to the form realm; or where one accomplishes a wholesome mind bound to the form realm but not a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm; or where one accomplishes both a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm and a wholesome mind bound to the form realm; or where one accomplishes neither a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm nor a wholesome mind bound to the form realm.

One who has accomplished a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm but not a wholesome mind bound to the form realm refers to a person (pudgala) born and raised in the desire realm whose roots of goodness are uninterrupted but who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm.

One who possesses wholesome minds associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) but not wholesome minds associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) refers to a person (*pudgala*) born and raised in the form realm.

One who possesses both wholesome minds associated with the desire realm and wholesome minds associated with the form realm refers to a person born and raised in the desire realm who has already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm.

Those who neither possess a wholesome mind connected with the desire realm nor a wholesome mind connected with the form realm are those individuals who have severed their roots of goodness and those born and growing in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes a wholesome mind associated with the desire realm, does one also accomplish a mind that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) and associated with the form realm?
