There are four possibilities: one may accomplish a mind that is unobscured-neutral and bound to the desire realm but not a mind of training; one may accomplish a mind of training but not a mind that is unobscured-neutral and bound to the desire realm; one may accomplish both a mind that is unobscured-neutral and bound to the desire realm and a mind of training; or one may accomplish neither a mind that is unobscured-neutral and bound to the desire realm nor a mind of training.

Those who have attained a mind that is unobscured-neutral and bound to the desire realm, yet are not of the stage of training (śaikṣa), are: Arhats born and raised in the desire or form realms, as well as all ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).

One who possesses a mind in training (*śaikṣa-citta*) but not a non-obscured neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the desire realm refers to a person in training (*śaikṣa-pudgala*) born and raised in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
One who possesses both a mind bound to the desire realm and a mind in training refers to a person in training born and raised in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Those who neither possess a mind associated with the desire realm that is unobscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), nor possess a mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*), are those Arhats born and dwelling in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as well as all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
If one accomplishes a mind that is unobscured-neutral and bound to the desire realm, does one also accomplish a mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?

Or, one may accomplish a mind that is unobscured-neutral and bound to the desire realm without accomplishing a mind of one beyond training; thus, the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are explained in detail.

Those who accomplish a mind that is unobscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta) bound to the desire realm, yet are not of the state beyond training (aśaikṣa), are those in training (śaikṣa) born and raised in the desire or form realms, as well as all ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).

One who possesses the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣacitta*) but not the non-obscured neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛtacitta*) bound to the desire realm refers to Arhats born and growing in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

One who possesses both the non-obscured neutral mind bound to the desire realm and the mind of one beyond training refers to Arhats born and growing in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Those who neither possess the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the desire realm nor the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are those in training (śaikṣa) born and growing in the formless realm, as well as all ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).

If one accomplishes a wholesome mind bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-citta*), does one also accomplish a mind that is obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the realm of form?

Or, one may accomplish a wholesome mind bound to the realm of form without accomplishing a mind that is obscured and indeterminate bound to the realm of form; thus, the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are explained in detail.

One who accomplishes wholesome minds associated with the form realm but not obscured-unspecified minds associated with the form realm refers to a person (pudgala) born and raised in the desire realm or the form realm who has already become detached from craving for the form realm.

One who has accomplished a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the form realm, but not a mind that is wholesome and bound to the form realm, refers to a person born and raised in the desire realm who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm.

One who accomplishes both a wholesome mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-citta*) and an obscured-unspecified mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) refers to: (1) a person born and raised in the desire realm who has already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm but has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm; and (2) a person born and raised in the form realm who has not yet abandoned craving for that [form realm].

Those who neither possess a wholesome mind associated with the form realm nor a mind that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) associated with the form realm are individuals born and growing in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes a wholesome mind associated with the form realm, does one also accomplish an unobscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm?
If one accomplishes an unobscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm, one necessarily accomplishes a wholesome mind associated with the form realm.

Or, one may possess a wholesome mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-citta*) but not a non-obscured neutral mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*); this refers to a person (*pudgala*) born and raised in the desire realm who has not yet abandoned desire for the desire realm but has already attained a wholesome mind associated with the form realm.
If one accomplishes a wholesome mind bound to the form realm, does one also accomplish a wholesome mind of the formless realm?
Or, one may accomplish a wholesome mind bound to the form realm but not a wholesome mind bound to the formless realm; thus, the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are explained in detail.

One who has achieved a wholesome mind associated with the form realm but not a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm refers to: a person born and raised in the desire realm who has already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm but has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm; and a person born and raised in the form realm who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm.
One who possesses wholesome states associated with the formless realm but not wholesome states associated with the form realm refers to a person born and raised in the formless realm.

One who possesses both wholesome states associated with the form realm and wholesome states associated with the formless realm refers to a person born and raised in either the desire realm or the form realm who has already attained wholesome states of the formless realm.

One who neither possesses a wholesome mind associated with the form realm nor a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm refers to a person born and raised in the desire realm who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm.

If one accomplishes a wholesome mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-citta*), does one also accomplish a mind that is obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?

Or, one may accomplish a wholesome mind bound to the form realm without accomplishing a mind that is obscured-unneutral bound to the formless realm; thus, the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are explained in detail.

Those who achieve wholesome minds associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-citta*) but not obscured-neutral minds associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) are the various Arhats born and raised in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm.

Regarding those who have accomplished an obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) but not a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*) associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): this refers to those born and raised in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who have not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm, as well as those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born and raised in the formless realm.

Those who accomplish both wholesome minds connected with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and obscured-unspecified minds connected with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-āvṛtāvyākṛta*) are: those learners (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) born and raised in the desire realm who have already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm; as well as learners and ordinary persons born and raised in the form realm.
Those who neither possess a wholesome mind connected to the form realm nor an obscured-unspecified mind connected to the formless realm are the Arhats born and dwelling in the formless realm.

If one possesses a wholesome mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-citta*), one certainly does not possess a non-obscured neutral mind associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*).
If one possesses a non-obscured neutral mind associated with the formless realm, one certainly does not possess a wholesome mind associated with the form realm.
If one accomplishes a wholesome mind bound to the form realm, does one also accomplish a mind of training (*śaikṣa*)?
Or, one may accomplish a wholesome mind bound to the form realm without accomplishing a mind of training; thus, the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are explained in detail.

One who has accomplished a wholesome mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-citta*) but not a mind of training (*śaikṣa-citta*) refers to: an Arhat or any ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born and raised in the desire realm who has already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm; or an Arhat or any ordinary person born and raised in the form realm.
One who possesses a mind in training that is not associated with the form realm refers to a person in training (śaikṣa-pudgala) born and raised in the formless realm.
One who possesses both a mind associated with the form realm and a mind in training refers to a person in training born and raised in either the desire realm or the form realm.

Those who neither possess a wholesome mind associated with the form realm nor a mind of training (śaikṣa) are those born and raised in the desire realm who have not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm, as well as arhats and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) born and raised in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes a wholesome mind associated with the form realm, does one also accomplish a mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Or, one may accomplish a wholesome mind associated with the form realm without accomplishing a mind of one beyond training; thus, the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are explained in detail.

One who has accomplished a wholesome mind bound to the form realm, but not a mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), refers to those in training (śaikṣa) or ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) born and raised in the desire realm who have already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm, as well as those in training or ordinary persons born and raised in the form realm.
One who possesses an *aśaikṣa* mind but not a wholesome mind bound to the form realm refers to Arhats born and dwelling in the formless realm.
One who possesses both a wholesome mind bound to the form realm and an *aśaikṣa* mind refers to Arhats born and dwelling in the desire realm or the form realm.

Those who neither possess a wholesome mind associated with the form realm nor an aśaikṣa mind are: those born and raised in the desire realm who have not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm, as well as śaikṣas and ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) born and raised in the formless realm.

If one accomplishes a mind that is bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) and is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta), does one also accomplish a mind that is bound to the form realm and is unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta)?

Or, one may accomplish a mind bound to the form realm that is obscured-unspecified but not a mind bound to the form realm that is unobscured-unspecified; thus, the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are explained in detail.

One who achieves a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified, but not a mind associated with the form realm that is unobscured-unspecified, refers to a person born and raised in the desire realm who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm.

One who accomplishes a mind that is unobscured-neutral and bound to the form realm, but not a mind that is obscured-neutral and bound to the form realm, refers to a person (pudgala) born and raised in the desire realm or the form realm who has already abandoned craving for the form realm.

Regarding the accomplishment of both obscured-unspecified minds associated with the form realm and non-obscured-unspecified minds associated with the form realm: this refers to individuals who have been born and raised in the desire realm and have already abandoned craving for the desire realm but have not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, as well as individuals born and raised in the form realm who have not yet abandoned craving for that [form realm].

One who neither possesses a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the form realm, nor a mind that is unobscured-unspecified and bound to the form realm, refers to a person born and raised in the formless realm.

If one accomplishes a mind that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), does one also accomplish a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*) bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?

Or, one may accomplish a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the form realm, but not a wholesome mind bound to the formless realm; thus, the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are explained in detail.

One who has accomplished a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified, but not a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm, refers to a person (pudgala) born and raised in the desire realm or the form realm who has not yet attained a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm.

One who achieves a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm but not a mind that is obscured-unspecified and associated with the form realm refers to a person who has been born and grown in the desire realm or the form realm and has already abandoned craving for the form realm, as well as a person born and grown in the formless realm.

One who accomplishes both the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the form realm and the wholesome mind associated with the formless realm refers to a person (pudgala) born and raised in the desire realm or the form realm who has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm but has already attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm.
Regarding the statement "neither possessing a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the form realm, nor possessing a wholesome mind bound to the formless realm," there is no such case.
If one possesses a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the form realm, does one also possess a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the formless realm?

If one accomplishes a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-nivṛtāvyākṛtacitta*), one necessarily accomplishes a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-nivṛtāvyākṛtacitta*).

Alternatively, one may accomplish a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the formless realm without accomplishing a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the form realm; this refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) or ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already become detached from the craving of the form realm.

If one possesses a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the form realm, one certainly does not possess a mind that is unobscured-unspecified and bound to the formless realm, nor a mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

If one possesses a mind that is non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta) bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), or if one possesses a mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), one certainly does not possess a mind that is obscured and indeterminate (nivṛtāvyākṛta) bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu).
If one accomplishes a mind that is associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), does one also accomplish a mind of training (*śaikṣa*)?

Or, one may accomplish a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured and indeterminate without accomplishing a mind of training; thus, the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are explained in detail.

One who possesses a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), but does not possess a mind of training (*śaikṣa*), refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet abandoned craving for the form realm.

One who possesses a mind of training, but does not possess a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified, refers to those in training who have already abandoned craving for the form realm.

Those who possess both a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and a mind of training (*śaikṣa*) are those learners (*śaikṣa*) who have not yet abandoned craving for the form realm.

Those who possess neither a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified nor a mind of training are the arhats and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already abandoned craving for the form realm.

If one accomplishes a mind that is non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta) bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu), does one also accomplish a wholesome mind (kuśala-citta) bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?

Or, one may accomplish a mind that is non-obscured and indeterminate bound to the realm of form without accomplishing a wholesome mind bound to the formless realm; thus, the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are explained in detail.

One who has accomplished a mind associated with the form realm that is unobscured and neutral, but not a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm, refers to a person (pudgala) who has been born and grown in the desire realm, has already abandoned craving for the desire realm, but has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm; as well as a person who has been born and grown in the form realm and has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm.
One who accomplishes a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm but not an unobscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm refers to a person born and raised in the formless realm.

One who accomplishes both a mind associated with the form realm that is unobscured-neutral and a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm refers to a person (pudgala) who has been born and grown in the desire or form realms and has already attained a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm.

One who neither possesses a non-obscured neutral mind associated with the form realm nor a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm refers to a person born and raised in the desire realm who has not yet abandoned desire for the desire realm.

If one accomplishes a mind that is non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta) bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu), does one also accomplish a mind that is obscured and indeterminate (nivṛtāvyākṛta) bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?

Or, one may accomplish a mind that is non-obscured and indeterminate bound to the realm of form without accomplishing a mind that is obscured and indeterminate bound to the formless realm; thus, the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are explained in detail.

One who accomplishes a mind that is form-realm-bound, unobscured-neutral, but not a mind that is formless-realm-bound, obscured-neutral, refers to Arhats born and raised in the desire realm or the form realm.

One who achieves a mind associated with the formless realm that is obscured and indeterminate, but not a mind associated with the form realm that is unobscured and indeterminate, refers to those born and raised in the desire realm who have not yet abandoned desire for the desire realm, as well as those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) born and raised in the formless realm.

One who accomplishes both the non-obscured neutral mind associated with the form realm and the obscured neutral mind associated with the formless realm refers to those in training (śaikṣa) or ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) born and raised in the desire realm who have already abandoned craving for the desire realm, as well as those in training or ordinary worldlings born and raised in the form realm.

Those who neither possess a mind that is unobscured-neutral and bound to the form realm, nor a mind that is obscured-neutral and bound to the formless realm, are those Arhats born and growing within the formless realm.

If one possesses a mind that is non-obscured and neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu), one certainly does not possess a mind that is non-obscured and neutral bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
If one possesses a mind that is non-obscured and neutral bound to the formless realm, one certainly does not possess a mind that is non-obscured and neutral bound to the realm of form.
If one accomplishes a mind that is unobscured-neutral and bound to the form realm, does one also accomplish a mind of training (*śaikṣa*)?
Or, one may accomplish a mind that is unobscured-neutral and bound to the form realm without accomplishing a mind of training; thus, the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are explained in detail.

Regarding those who have accomplished an unobscured-neutral mind bound to the form realm, but not a mind of training (śaikṣa): this refers to Arhats and ordinary beings born and raised in the desire realm who have already abandoned craving for the desire realm; as well as Arhats and ordinary beings born and raised in the form realm.

Regarding those who have accomplished a mind of training that is not associated with the form realm and is non-obscured-neutral: this refers to those in training (śaikṣa) born and raised in the desire realm who have not yet abandoned desire for the desire realm, as well as persons in training born and raised in the formless realm.

Regarding the accomplishment of both an unobscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm and a mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*): this refers to those in training who have been born and raised in the desire realm and have already abandoned craving for the desire realm, as well as those persons in training who have been born and raised in the form realm.

Those who neither possess the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the desire realm nor the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) are: ordinary beings born and raised in the desire realm who have not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, as well as all Arhats and ordinary beings born and raised in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes a mind that is unobscured and neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) and bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-saṃprayukta), does one also accomplish a mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
Or, one may accomplish a mind bound to the realm of form that is unobscured and neutral, yet not a mind of one beyond training; thus, the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are explained in detail.

Regarding those who have achieved a mind associated with the form realm that is unobscured and neutral, but not a mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa): this refers to those in training (śaikṣa) or ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) born and raised in the desire realm who have already abandoned craving for the desire realm, as well as those in training or ordinary worldlings born and raised in the form realm.
One who possesses an *aśaikṣa* mind but not a non-obscured neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) bound to the form realm refers to Arhats born and growing in the formless realm.
One who possesses both a non-obscured neutral mind bound to the form realm and an *aśaikṣa* mind refers to Arhats born and growing in the desire realm or the form realm.

Those who neither possess a mind associated with the form realm that is non-obscured and neutral, nor an untrained (aśaikṣa) mind, are those born and raised in the desire realm who have not yet abandoned desire for the desire realm, as well as those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) born and raised in the formless realm.

Section Two: Udānavarga Verses. Chapter Six: Attainment of the Aggregates (II). If one attains a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm, does one also attain a mind that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) and associated with the formless realm?

Or, one may possess a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm but not a obscured-unspecified mind associated with the formless realm; this is explained in detail through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the case of possessing a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm but not an obscured-unspecified mind associated with the formless realm: this refers to an Arhat.

One who has accomplished a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the formless realm, but has not accomplished a wholesome mind bound to the formless realm, refers to those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) who have not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm.

Regarding the accomplishment of both wholesome minds associated with the formless realm and obscured-unspecified minds associated with the formless realm: this refers to those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) who have already attained a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm.

Regarding the statement, "One neither possesses a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm nor a mind that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) associated with the formless realm," such a case does not exist.
However, if one possesses a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm, does one also possess a non-obscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) mind associated with the formless realm?
If one accomplishes an unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm, one necessarily accomplishes a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm.

Alternatively, one may accomplish a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm without accomplishing an unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm; this refers to those born and raised in the desire realm or the form realm who have already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm, as well as those born and raised in the formless realm whose resultant ripening mind is not currently manifest.
If one accomplishes a wholesome mind bound to the formless realm, does one also accomplish a mind of training (śaikṣa)?
Or, one may accomplish a wholesome mind bound to the formless realm without accomplishing a mind of training; thus, the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are to be explained in detail.

One who has accomplished a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm but not a mind of training refers to an Arhat, as well as ordinary worldlings who have already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm.

One who possesses the mind of a trainee (*śaikṣa*) but does not possess a wholesome mind bound to the formless realm refers to those trainees who have not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm.
One who possesses both a wholesome mind bound to the formless realm and the mind of a trainee refers to those trainees who have already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm.

Those who neither possess the wholesome mind of the formless realm nor the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) are those ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who have not yet attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm.
If one possesses the wholesome mind of the formless realm, does one also possess the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
If one accomplishes the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣacitta), one necessarily accomplishes the wholesome mind associated with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśalacitta).

Alternatively, one may accomplish the wholesome mind associated with the formless realm without accomplishing the mind of one beyond training; this refers to those in training (śaikṣas) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjanas) who have already attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm.

If one accomplishes a mind that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), does one also accomplish a mind that is unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) and bound to the formless realm?

Or, one may accomplish a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the formless realm without accomplishing a mind that is unobscured-unspecified and bound to the formless realm; thus, the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are explained in detail.

One who accomplishes a mind that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), but does not accomplish a mind that is unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) and bound to the formless realm, refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) or ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) born and raised in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as well as those in training or ordinary worldlings born and raised in the formless realm, when a resultant-retribution mind (*vipākaphala-citta*) is not present before them.

One who does not possess the mind of a trainee (*śaikṣa*) but does not lack the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) refers to an Arhat.
One who does not possess the mind of one beyond training but does not lack the mind of a trainee refers to those who are still in training (*śaikṣas*).
Those who neither possess the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) nor the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
There is no such category as those who do not fail to possess the mind of one in training and yet also do not fail to possess the mind of one beyond training.

There are twelve types of mind: namely, the wholesome mind, the unwholesome mind, the obscured-neutral mind, and the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the desire realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-neutral mind, and the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-neutral mind, and the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm; as well as the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
If, when a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm is relinquished, it is no longer possessed and its non-possession is attained, is it the same for an unwholesome mind?
And if, when an unwholesome mind is relinquished, it is no longer possessed and its non-possession is attained, is it the same for a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm?
If one abandons the possession of a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm and does not attain it, is it the same for the mind of an Arhat (aśaikṣacitta)?
Conversely, if one abandons the possession of the mind of an Arhat and does not attain it, is it the same for the wholesome mind bound to the desire realm?
Furthermore, if the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) is abandoned such that it is no longer possessed but was previously possessed, is the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) likewise?
And if the mind of one beyond training is abandoned such that it is no longer possessed but was previously possessed, is the mind of one in training likewise?

If one abandons and achieves the possession of a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm while failing to achieve its possession, it is certainly not the case for an unwholesome mind or a mind obscured by defilements (nivṛtāvyākṛta) bound to the desire realm.

Regarding the case where one abandons the possession of and fails to acquire the wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, as well as the unobscured-neutral mind bound to the desire realm: this refers to when one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm.

If a wholesome mind bound to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) abandons its non-acquisition and attains its acquisition, is it the same for an unobscured-unspecified mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) bound to the form realm?

Or is it the case that a wholesome mind bound to the form realm abandons its non-acquisition and attains its acquisition while an unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm does not? These constitute the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), as explained in detail.

Regarding the case where one abandons the non-possession and attains the possession of a wholesome mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-citta*), but does not [attain] the non-possession and [abandon] the possession of an unobscured-neutral mind bound to the form realm: this refers to the initial manifestation of a wholesome mind of the form realm when practicing preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Regarding the case where one abandons the non-attainment and attains the attainment of the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm, but not the wholesome mind associated with the form realm: this refers to the time when one attains detachment from desire within the desire realm.

Regarding the case where one abandons and no longer possesses, but then newly acquires, a wholesome mind bound to the form realm, as well as a non-obscured neutral mind bound to the form realm: this refers to the time when one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm.

Regarding the statement that "there is neither the abandonment and non-accomplishment nor the acquisition and accomplishment of a wholesome mind bound to the form realm, nor of an unobscured-neutral mind bound to the form realm," this excludes the aforementioned characteristics.
If one abandons and ceases to possess a wholesome mind associated with the form realm while attaining it anew, it is certainly not a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm.
If one abandons and ceases to possess a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm while attaining it anew, it is certainly not a wholesome mind associated with the form realm.
From this point onward, nothing further exists.

If one abandons the possession of and achieves the non-possession of a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), is it the same for a mind associated with the form realm that is unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)?

Or, there may be the case where one abandons the non-accomplishment and achieves the accomplishment of a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), but does not [achieve the accomplishment] of a mind associated with the form realm that is unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); this is explained in detail through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding the case where one abandons the possession of and acquires the possession of a mind that is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), but does not [acquire] a mind that is bound to the form realm and non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*): this refers to when one who has already abandoned craving for the form realm falls back from that state of abandonment, as well as when one dies in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding the case where one abandons the non-accomplishment and achieves the accomplishment of the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm, but not the obscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm: this refers to the time when one attains detachment from desire within the desire realm.

Regarding the case where one abandons the non-accomplishment and achieves the accomplishment of the obscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm, as well as the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm: this refers to the time when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm.

Regarding the statement that one neither fails to achieve nor achieves the abandonment of the obscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm, nor the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm: this excludes the aforementioned characteristics.

If one abandons the possession of and achieves the non-possession of a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), it is certainly not a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm.

If one abandons the possession of and achieves the non-possession of a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm, it is certainly not a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified.

If one who was not previously endowed with, but now becomes endowed with, a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), is it also the case for a mind associated with the formless realm that is obscured and indeterminate?

Or, there may be the case where one abandons the possession of and achieves the non-possession of a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), but does not [achieve the non-possession of] a mind associated with the formless realm that is obscured-unspecified; this is explained in detail through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding the case where one abandons the non-attainment and achieves the attainment of the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*), but not that of the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*): this refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already abandoned craving for the form realm, at the time they fall back from that state of having abandoned craving for the form realm, as well as when passing away from the formless realm and being reborn in the desire realm.

Regarding the case where one abandons the possession of the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the formless realm and achieves its possession, but does not [achieve] the possession of the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the form realm: this refers to when an Arhat gives rise to the fetters of the formless realm and subsequently regresses.

Regarding the abandonment of the non-accomplishment and the attainment of the accomplishment of the obscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*), as well as the obscured-unspecified mind bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*): this refers to when an Arhat gives rise to the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm or the form realm and subsequently regresses.

Regarding the statement that one neither loses nor acquires the obscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm, nor the obscured-unspecified mind bound to the formless realm: this excludes the aforementioned characteristics.

If one abandons the non-attainment and attains the attainment of a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured and indeterminate, it is certainly not the case that this concerns a mind associated with the formless realm that is unobscured and indeterminate, nor an arhat’s mind.

If one abandons the non-obscured neutral mind associated with the formless realm and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), thereby achieving their acquisition rather than their possession, this is certainly not the case for the obscured neutral mind associated with the form realm.

If, when a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) is abandoned and no longer possessed while being newly acquired, the same applies to a mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*),

or if it is the case that a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified is abandoned and no longer possessed while being newly acquired but it is not a mind of one in training— these are explained in detail through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding the case where one who is not a learner (aśaikṣa) loses the possession and acquires the non-possession of a mind that is bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu), obscured and indeterminate (nivṛtāvyākṛta): this refers to a learner (śaikṣa) or an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who has already abandoned craving for the form realm, at the time they fall back from that abandonment; and when one dies in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and is reborn in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the form realm.

Regarding the case where the mind of training (śaikṣa-citta) achieves what was previously unachieved while the obscured-unspecified mind (nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta) bound to the form realm does not: this refers to when an Arhat gives rise to the entanglements (paryavasthāna) of the formless realm and subsequently regresses, as well as when one enters the path of vision (darśanamārga) through preparatory application (prayoga).

Regarding the case where one who is neither in training (*śaikṣa*) loses the possession of and acquires the non-possession of the obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*): this refers to when an Arhat gives rise to the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm or the form realm and subsequently regresses.

Regarding the statement that one neither fails to achieve nor achieves the relinquishing of a mind associated with the form realm that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), nor does one fail to achieve or achieve a mind of training (*śaikṣa*): this excludes the aforementioned characteristics.
If one relinquishes and achieves a mind associated with the form realm that is unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), it is certainly not a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm.

If a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is abandoned and no longer possessed while being newly attained, it is certainly not a non-obscured neutral mind (anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta) associated with the form realm (rūpadhātu);
from that point onward, there is nothing at all [of that latter kind].

If one abandons a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm and achieves its non-possession, it is certainly not a mind that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) and associated with the formless realm.
If one abandons an obscured-unspecified mind associated with the formless realm and achieves its non-possession, it is certainly not a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm.
From this point onward, nothing further exists.

If there is the relinquishing of non-possession and the attainment of possession of a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the formless realm, it is certainly not the case for a mind that is unobscured-unspecified and bound to the formless realm, nor for a mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

If one abandons and no longer possesses, while newly attaining, an unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm or a mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), it is certainly not the case that one simultaneously abandons and no longer possesses, while newly attaining, an obscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm.

If one who is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) achieves the acquisition and loses the non-acquisition of a mind that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), this necessarily applies to the mind of a trainee (*śaikṣa*).

Alternatively, there may be cases where one achieves the acquisition and loses the non-acquisition of the mind of a trainee, yet does not achieve the acquisition and lose the non-acquisition of the mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the formless realm; this refers to when one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) by means of preparatory cultivation (*prayoga*).

If one abandons what was not accomplished and accomplishes what was not previously accomplished regarding an unobscured-neutral mind bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*), it is certainly not a mind of training (*śaikṣa*) or a mind beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

If one abandons what was not accomplished and accomplishes what was not previously accomplished regarding a mind of training or a mind beyond training, it is certainly not an unobscured-neutral mind bound to the formless realm.

If there is the relinquishing of the unaccomplished and the accomplishment of the accomplished state of the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*), it is certainly not the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
If there is the relinquishing of the unaccomplished and the accomplishment of the accomplished state of the mind of one beyond training, it is certainly not the mind of one in training.

There are ten types of mind, namely: wholesome mind, unwholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and non-obscured-neutral mind bound to the desire realm; wholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and non-obscured-neutral mind bound to the form realm; and wholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and non-obscured-neutral mind bound to the formless realm.
If a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm has not been abandoned, does one possess that mind?
Conversely, if one possesses that mind, has it not been abandoned? This continues up to:
if an unobscured-neutral mind bound to the formless realm has not been abandoned, does one possess that mind?
If one possesses this mind, has this mind not been abandoned?
If a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm has not been abandoned, does one possess this mind?

Or, there may be cases where a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm has not been abandoned but one does not possess it; or where one possesses it but this mind has not been abandoned; or where this mind has not been abandoned and one also possesses it; or where neither this mind has been abandoned nor does one possess it.
One for whom this mind has not been severed but who does not possess it refers to one whose roots of goodness have already been severed.
One who possesses this mind but for whom it has not been severed refers to one born and raised in the desire realm who has already become detached from the greed of the desire realm.

Regarding "this mind has not been severed and one also possesses this mind": it refers to those born and raised in the desire realm who have not severed their roots of goodness and have not yet abandoned the craving of the desire realm.
Regarding "this mind has not been severed and one does not possess this mind": it refers to those born and raised in the form and formless realms.
If an unwholesome mind has not been abandoned, does one possess that mind? Answer: It is so.
If one has attained this mind, has this mind not yet been abandoned?
It is said: "It is so."
If an obscured-unspecified mind bound to the desire realm has not been abandoned, does one possess that mind? Answer: Yes.
If one has accomplished this mind, has this mind not yet been abandoned?
It is said: Yes.
If an unobscured-neutral mind bound to the desire realm has not been abandoned, does one possess that mind?
If this mind has not been abandoned, one necessarily possesses it.

Or, there may be cases where one possesses this mind but has not yet abandoned it; that is to say, those born and raised in the desire realm who have already detached from the greed of the desire realm, as well as those born and raised in the form realm.
If a wholesome mind associated with the form realm has not been abandoned, does one possess this mind?

Either the wholesome mind bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) has not been abandoned yet one does not possess it; or one possesses this mind yet this mind has not been abandoned; or this mind has not been abandoned and one also possesses it; or neither has this mind been abandoned nor does one possess it.

Regarding those for whom the wholesome mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) has not been abandoned but they do not possess this mind: this refers to those born and raised in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who have not yet attained the wholesome mind of the form realm.

Regarding those who possess this mind but for whom it has not been abandoned: this refers to those born and raised in either the desire or form realms who have already become detached from craving for the form realm.

Regarding "this mind has not been abandoned and one also possesses this mind": this refers to those born and raised in the desire realm who have already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm but have not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, as well as those born and raised in the form realm who have not yet abandoned craving for that [form realm].
That which is neither one whose mind has not been abandoned nor one who possesses that mind refers to those born and growing in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If a mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) has not been abandoned, does one possess that mind?
He said: "It is so.
If one achieves this mind, has this mind not yet been abandoned?"
He said: "It is so.
If an unobscured-neutral mind bound to the form realm has not been abandoned, does one possess that mind?"

Either there is an unobscured-neutral mind bound to the form realm that has not been abandoned yet one does not possess it; or one possesses this mind yet this mind has not been abandoned; or this mind has not been abandoned and one also possesses it; or neither this mind has been abandoned nor does one possess it.

Regarding those for whom the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) is not yet abandoned but is not possessed: this refers to those born and raised in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who have not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm.

Regarding those who possess this mind but for whom it is not the case that it is not yet abandoned: this refers to those born and raised in the desire realm or the form realm who have already abandoned craving for the form realm.

Regarding "this mind has not been abandoned and one is also possessed of this mind": this refers to those born and raised in the desire realm who have already abandoned craving for the desire realm but have not yet abandoned craving for the form realm; as well as those born and raised in the form realm who have not yet abandoned craving for that [form realm].
"Neither this mind has been severed nor is one possessed of this mind" refers to those born and growing in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm has not been severed, is one possessed of that mind?

Either the wholesome mind of the formless realm has not been severed yet one does not possess this mind; or one possesses this mind yet this mind has not been severed; or this mind has not been severed and one also possesses this mind; or neither has this mind been severed nor does one possess this mind.

Regarding those for whom the wholesome mind associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) has not been abandoned yet they do not possess this mind: this refers to those who have not yet attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm.
Regarding those who possess this mind but for whom it has not been abandoned: this refers to Arhats.
Regarding "this mind has not been abandoned and one also possesses this mind," this refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding "one has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm, yet this mind has neither been abandoned nor is it possessed," there is no such case.
If the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the formless realm has not been abandoned, does one possess that mind? Answer: It is so.
If one has attained this mind, has this mind not yet been severed? Answer: It is so.
If an unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) has not been abandoned, does one possess this mind?

Or, there may be cases where the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm has not been abandoned but one does not possess it; or where one possesses this mind but it has not been abandoned; or where this mind has not been abandoned and one also possesses it; or where neither this mind has been abandoned nor does one possess it.

Regarding those for whom the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm has not been abandoned yet they do not possess that mind: this refers to those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) for whom a resultant mind associated with the formless realm is not currently manifest.
"One who accomplishes this mind but has not yet abandoned it" refers to an Arhat when a resultant mind associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is currently manifest.

"One who has not yet abandoned this mind and also accomplishes this mind" refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) when a resultant mind associated with the formless realm is currently manifest.

That which is neither the non-cessation of this mind nor the possession of this mind refers to the case where an Arhat’s resultant mind associated with the formless realm does not manifest before him.

There are ten types of mind: namely, wholesome mind, unwholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and non-obscured-neutral mind associated with the desire realm; wholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and non-obscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm; and wholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and non-obscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm.
If a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm has been abandoned, is that mind not possessed?
Conversely, if that mind is not possessed, has it been abandoned?
And so on, until: if an unobscured-neutral mind bound to the formless realm has been abandoned, is that mind not possessed?
If one does not possess this mind, has this mind already been abandoned?
If a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm has been abandoned, does one not possess this mind?

Or, while the wholesome mind bound to the desire realm has been abandoned, one does not fail to possess it; or, while one fails to possess this mind, this mind has not been abandoned; or, this mind has been abandoned and one also fails to possess it; or, this mind has neither been abandoned nor does one fail to possess it.

Regarding "the wholesome mind bound to the desire realm has been severed, yet one is not non-possessed of this mind": this refers to those born and raised in the desire realm who have already become detached from the craving of the desire realm.
Regarding "one is not possessed of this mind, yet this mind has not been severed": this refers to those who have already severed their roots of goodness.
"Those for whom this mind has already been abandoned and they no longer possess it" refers to those born and raised in the form and formless realms.

"Neither those for whom this mind has been abandoned nor those who do not possess it" refers to those born and raised in the desire realm who have not severed their roots of goodness and have not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm.
If an unwholesome mind has already been abandoned, is one not possessed of that mind?
It is said: Yes.
If one does not achieve this mind, has this mind already been severed?
He replied: "It is so."
If the obscured-unspecified mind bound to the desire realm has been abandoned, is that mind no longer possessed? Answer: It is so.
If one does not accomplish this mind, has this mind already been severed?
He replied: "It is so."
If the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the desire realm has been abandoned, is that mind not possessed?
If the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the desire realm is not possessed, then that mind has certainly been abandoned.

Or, is it that this mind has already been abandoned, yet one is not non-possessed of this mind? This refers to those born and raised in the desire realm who have already become detached from the greed of the desire realm, as well as those born and raised in the form realm.
If a wholesome mind associated with the form realm has already been abandoned, is one then non-possessed of this mind?

Either the wholesome mind bound to the form realm has been abandoned but one is not non-possessed of this mind; or one is non-possessed of this mind but this mind has not been abandoned; or this mind has been abandoned and one is also non-possessed of this mind; or neither has this mind been abandoned nor is one non-possessed of this mind.

Regarding those for whom the wholesome mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) has been abandoned but they have not failed to attain this mind: this refers to those born and raised in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm who have already become detached from craving for the form realm.

Regarding those who have not attained this mind but for whom it has not been abandoned: this refers to those born and raised in the desire realm who have not yet attained the wholesome mind of the form realm.
Regarding "this mind has already been abandoned and one does not possess it": this refers to those born and growing up in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding "neither has this mind been abandoned nor is one non-possessing of it": this refers to those born and growing up in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who have already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm but have not yet abandoned craving for the form realm; as well as those born and growing up in the form realm who have not yet abandoned craving for that [form realm].
If the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the form realm has been abandoned, is one not possessed of this mind? Answer: It is so.
If one does not achieve this mind, has this mind already been severed?
He said: "It is so."
If a mind associated with the form realm that is unobscured and neutral has been abandoned, is this mind not possessed?

Or, is it the case that while a mind associated with the form realm that is unobscured and neutral has been abandoned, this mind is not yet non-possessed; or that while this mind is not possessed, this mind has not been abandoned; or that this mind has been abandoned and is also not possessed; or that this mind has neither been abandoned nor is it non-possessed?

Regarding those who have severed the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm but do not fail to possess it: this refers to those born and raised in the desire realm or the form realm who have already become detached from craving for the form realm.
"One who does not possess this mind and for whom this mind has not been abandoned" refers to those born and raised in the desire realm who have not yet abandoned the craving of the desire realm.
"One for whom this mind has already been abandoned and who also does not possess this mind" refers to those born and raised in the formless realm.

"Neither having this mind already abandoned nor not being possessed of it" refers to those born and raised in the desire realm who have already abandoned craving for the desire realm but have not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, as well as those born and raised in the form realm who have not yet abandoned craving for that [form realm].
If a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm has been severed, is that mind not possessed?
If a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm has been severed, it is certainly not the case that this mind is not possessed.
Or, one does not possess this mind, yet it is not the case that this mind has been abandoned; that is to say, one who has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If the obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind bound to the formless realm has been abandoned, does one not possess this mind?
He said: "It is so.
If this mind is not yet accomplished, has this mind already been severed?"
He said: "It is so.
If the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm has been abandoned, is one not possessed of this mind?"

Either the mind associated with the formless realm that is unobscured and indeterminate has been abandoned but one does not lack possession of it; or one lacks possession of this mind but this mind has not been abandoned; or this mind has been abandoned and one also lacks possession of it; or neither has this mind been abandoned nor does one lack possession of it.

Regarding those for whom the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm has been abandoned yet they have not failed to possess this mind: it refers to an Arhat when a resultant mind associated with the formless realm is currently manifest.

"One who does not possess this mind and for whom this mind has not been abandoned" refers to those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) for whom a resultant mind associated with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is not currently manifest.
"Having already abandoned this mind and not yet possessing it" refers to an Arhat for whom a resultant consciousness associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is not currently manifest.

"Neither having already abandoned this mind nor not possessing it" refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) or ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) for whom a resultant consciousness associated with the formless realm is currently manifest.

There are twelve types of mind: namely, the wholesome mind, the unwholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the desire realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the formless realm; as well as the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
If one possesses a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, how many of these twelve minds are possessed and how many are not?
This continues up to: if one possesses a mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), how many of these twelve minds are possessed and how many are not?

If one accomplishes a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, two minds are necessarily accomplished, one mind is necessarily not accomplished, and the remaining [minds] may or may not be accomplished.
If one accomplishes an unwholesome mind, four minds are necessarily accomplished, four minds are necessarily not accomplished, and the remaining ones may or may not be accomplished.

If one accomplishes a mind that is obscured-unspecified and bound to the desire realm, five minds are necessarily accomplished, four minds are necessarily not accomplished, and the remaining ones may or may not be accomplished.

If one accomplishes a mind that is unobscured and neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) and bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), this one mind is necessarily accomplished, while this one mind is necessarily not accomplished; as for the others, they may be either accomplished or not accomplished.

If one accomplishes a wholesome mind associated with the form realm, two minds are necessarily accomplished, one mind is necessarily not accomplished, and the remaining [minds] may or may not be accomplished.

If one accomplishes a mind that is bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu) and is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta), three minds are necessarily accomplished, two minds are necessarily not accomplished, and the remaining [minds] may or may not be accomplished.

If one accomplishes a mind that is bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu) and is non-obscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta), three minds are necessarily accomplished, three minds are necessarily not accomplished, and the remaining [minds] may or may not be accomplished.

If one accomplishes a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm, this one mind is necessarily accomplished, two minds are necessarily not accomplished, and the remaining [minds] may or may not be accomplished.

If one accomplishes a mind that is bound to the formless realm and is obscured-unspecified, this one mind is necessarily accomplished, this one mind is necessarily not accomplished, and the remainder may or may not be accomplished.

If one accomplishes an unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm, two minds are necessarily accomplished, seven minds are necessarily not accomplished, and the remaining minds may or may not be accomplished.
If one accomplishes the mind of a trainee (*śaikṣa*), two minds are necessarily accomplished, one mind is necessarily not accomplished, and the remainder may or may not be accomplished.
If one accomplishes the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), two minds are necessarily accomplished, five minds are necessarily not accomplished, and the remainder may or may not be accomplished.

There are twelve types of mind: namely, the wholesome mind, the unwholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the desire realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the formless realm; as well as the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
If one does not possess the wholesome mind associated with the desire realm, how many of these twelve minds are not possessed and how many are possessed? ...
[and so on] ... up to: if one does not possess the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), how many of these twelve minds are not possessed and how many are possessed?
If one does not possess a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm, this one mind will certainly not be possessed; as for the others, they may or may not be possessed.
If one does not possess an unwholesome mind, two minds will certainly not be possessed; as for the others, they may or may not be possessed.
If one does not possess the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the desire realm, this one mind is definitely not possessed; as for the others, they may or may not be possessed.

If one does not possess a mind that is unobscured-neutral and bound to the desire realm, seven minds are certainly not possessed, one mind is certainly possessed, and the remainder may or may not be possessed.
If one does not possess a wholesome mind associated with the form realm (*rūpāvacara-kuśala-citta*), two minds will certainly not be possessed, while the remaining ones may or may not be possessed.

If one does not possess a mind that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) associated with the form realm, three minds will certainly not be possessed, one mind will certainly be possessed, and the remaining ones may or may not be possessed.
If one does not possess the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the form realm, this one mind is definitely not possessed; as for the others, they may or may not be possessed.

If one does not achieve a wholesome mind associated with the formless realm, three minds are definitely not achieved, and three minds are definitely achieved; as for the remaining [minds], they may or may not be achieved.

If one does not possess the obscured-unspecified mind associated with the formless realm, five minds are definitely not possessed, two minds are definitely possessed, and as for the remaining ones, they may or may not be possessed.
If one does not possess the unobscured-neutral mind associated with the formless realm, this one mind is certainly not possessed; as for the others, they may or may not be possessed.
If the mind of one in training (śaikṣa-citta) is not accomplished, this one mind is certainly not accomplished; as for the others, they may be accomplished or not accomplished.

If the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-citta) is not accomplished, this one mind is certainly not accomplished; one mind is certainly accomplished, and as for the others, they may be accomplished or not accomplished.

There are twelve types of mind: namely, the wholesome mind, the unwholesome mind, the obscured-neutral mind, and the unobscured-neutral mind bound to the desire realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-neutral mind, and the unobscured-neutral mind bound to the form realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-neutral mind, and the unobscured-neutral mind bound to the formless realm; as well as the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, there are three types of persons (pudgala):
first, the person who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm; second, the person who has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm;
[and third, the person who has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm].

3. Regarding the person who has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm and the person who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm: among these twelve types of mind, how many are possessed and how many are not possessed?
Regarding a person who has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), how many of these twelve minds do they possess and how many do they not possess?
Regarding a person who has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), how many of these twelve minds do they possess and how many do they not possess?

A person who has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm definitely accomplishes four minds and definitely does not accomplish four minds; as for the remaining ones, they may or may not be accomplished.

For a person who has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), three minds are necessarily accomplished, two minds are necessarily not accomplished, and the remaining ones may or may not be accomplished.

For a person who has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, they necessarily possess one-pointed concentration, while they do not necessarily possess it; as for the remaining [faculties], they may or may not be possessed.

The twelve types of mind are: the wholesome mind, unwholesome mind, obscured-unspecified mind, and unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the desire realm; the wholesome mind, obscured-unspecified mind, and unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm; the wholesome mind, obscured-unspecified mind, and unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the formless realm; as well as the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, there are three types of persons (pudgala):
first, persons who have already abandoned craving for the desire realm;
second, persons who have already abandoned craving for the form realm.

3. Regarding the person (*pudgala*) who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and the person who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): among these twelve minds, how many are not possessed (*asamanvāgata*) and how many are possessed (*samanvāgata*)?
For a person who has already abandoned craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), how many of these twelve minds are not possessed and how many are possessed?
For a person who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), how many of these twelve minds are not possessed and how many are possessed?
A person who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm definitely does not possess two minds; as for the others, they may or may not possess them.
A person who has already abandoned craving for the form realm definitely does not possess three minds, definitely possesses one mind, and as for the others, they may or may not possess them.

For a person (pudgala) who has already abandoned craving for the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), five minds are definitely not attained, two minds are definitely attained, and the remainder are either attained or not attained.
If, at the very beginning, a wholesome mind bound to the Brahma-world manifests, is it immediately preceded by all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm?
If, at the very beginning of the preparatory practice, a wholesome mind bound to the Brahma-world manifests, it is immediately preceded by all wholesome minds bound to the desire realm.

Alternatively, at the very beginning, a wholesome mind bound to the Brahma-world manifests, but it is not preceded immediately by a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm; that is to say, when one passes away from a higher Brahma-world and is reborn within the Brahma-world, that initial wholesome mind bound to the Brahma-world manifests.

Furthermore, when a wholesome mind bound to the first sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) manifests, is it preceded immediately by all wholesome minds bound to the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*)?

If, at the very beginning of the preparatory practice, a wholesome mind associated with the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) manifests, it is immediately preceded by all wholesome minds associated with the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Or, there is a case where a wholesome mind bound to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) manifests initially, but it is not immediately preceded by a wholesome mind bound to the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). This refers to one who passes away from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and is reborn in the sphere of nothingness; at that moment, a wholesome mind bound to the sphere of nothingness manifests for the first time.

There are twelve types of mind: the wholesome mind, the unwholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the desire realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the form realm; the wholesome mind, the obscured-unspecified mind, and the unobscured-unspecified mind bound to the formless realm; as well as the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

If, in the case of the mind of training (*śaikṣa-citta*), one achieves its relinquishment and does not achieve its acquisition, then among these twelve minds, how many achieve relinquishment and do not achieve acquisition, and how many do not achieve relinquishment and achieve acquisition?

If the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is relinquished as accomplished and attained as unaccomplished, then among these twelve minds, how many are relinquished as accomplished and attained as unaccomplished, and how many are relinquished as unaccomplished and attained as accomplished?

If the mind of training (śaikṣa-citta) abandons its possession and does not attain it, two minds certainly abandon their possession and do not attain them, and one mind certainly abandons its non-possession and attains it; for the remainder, there is neither the case of abandoning possession and not attaining it, nor the case of abandoning non-possession and attaining it.

If there is the abandonment of the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), its possession (*prāpti*) is lost and its non-possession (*aprāpti*) is attained; for one mind, its abandonment is certainly lost and its non-possession is certainly attained; for two minds, their non-abandonment is certainly lost and their possession is certainly attained; for two minds, either their abandonment is lost and their non-possession is attained, or their non-abandonment is lost and their possession is attained; for five minds, neither is there the case where abandonment is lost and non-possession is attained, nor is there the case where non-abandonment is lost and possession is attained.

There are twelve types of mind: namely, the wholesome mind, unwholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and unobscured-neutral mind bound to the desire realm; the wholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and unobscured-neutral mind bound to the form realm; the wholesome mind, obscured-neutral mind, and unobscured-neutral mind bound to the formless realm; as well as the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

If, regarding the mind of training (*śaikṣa-citta*), there is the non-attainment of abandonment and the attainment [of it], how many among these twelve minds involve the non-attainment of abandonment and the attainment [of it], and how many involve the attainment of abandonment and the non-attainment [of it]?

If, regarding the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-citta*), there is the relinquishing of non-acquisition and the attainment of acquisition, then among these twelve minds, how many involve the relinquishing of non-acquisition and the attainment of acquisition, and how many involve the relinquishing of acquisition and the attainment of non-acquisition?

If, in the case of the mind of training (*śaikṣa-citta*), there is non-attainment of relinquishment and attainment [of it], or if there are two minds where there is necessarily non-attainment of relinquishment and attainment [of it], one mind where there is necessarily attainment of relinquishment and non-attainment [of it], two minds where there is either non-attainment of relinquishment and attainment [of it] or attainment of relinquishment and non-attainment [of it], or if there is attainment [of something] with no relinquishing at all—then in these five cases, there is neither non-attainment of relinquishment and attainment [of it], nor attainment of relinquishment and non-attainment [of it].

If the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) abandons non-possession and achieves possession, then for one mind it is certain that non-possession is abandoned and possession is achieved; for two minds it is certain that possession is abandoned and non-possession is achieved.
The *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume Sixteen.
